items.title: Physical quantity
items.content: A physical quantity is a quantity that can be measured and expressed by a numerical value and a unit.

items.title: Unit
items.content: A unit is a fixed standard quantity used for measuring a physical quantity.

items.title: SI base quantities
items.content: Length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), thermodynamic temperature (K), amount of substance (mol), luminous intensity (cd).

items.title: SI base units
items.content: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

items.title: Derived quantity
items.content: A physical quantity obtained from base quantities through mathematical relations is called a derived quantity.

items.title: SI prefixes
items.content: Common prefixes: kilo = 10^3, mega = 10^6, giga = 10^9, milli = 10^-3, micro = 10^-6, nano = 10^-9, pico = 10^-12.

items.title: Dimension
items.content: Dimensions of a physical quantity indicate how it depends on the fundamental quantities.

items.title: Dimensional formula
items.content: A dimensional formula represents a physical quantity in terms of powers of fundamental quantities such as mass, length and time.

items.title: General dimensional formula
items.content: [Q] = M^a L^b T^c ... where a, b, c are powers of the corresponding fundamental quantities.

items.title: Dimension of displacement
items.content: [x] = L

items.title: Dimension of force
items.content: [F] = MLT^-2

items.title: Dimension of momentum
items.content: [p] = MLT^-1

items.title: Dimension of density
items.content: [rho] = ML^-3

items.title: Dimension of angular velocity
items.content: [omega] = T^-1

items.title: Dimension of impulse
items.content: [J] = MLT^-1

items.title: Dimension of torque
items.content: [tau] = ML^2T^-2

items.title: Dimension of coefficient of viscosity
items.content: [eta] = ML^-1T^-1

items.title: Accuracy
items.content: Accuracy indicates how close a measured value is to the true value.

items.title: Precision
items.content: Precision indicates how closely repeated measurements agree with one another.

items.title: Systematic error
items.content: An error that occurs in a consistent manner due to an identifiable cause is called systematic error.

items.title: Random error
items.content: An error that varies unpredictably from one measurement to another is called random error.

items.title: Mean value
items.content: For measurements x1, x2, ..., xn: x_mean = (x1 + x2 + ... + xn) / n

items.title: Absolute error
items.content: Absolute error in a measurement xi: Delta xi = |xi - x_mean|

items.title: Mean absolute error
items.content: Mean absolute error = (Delta x1 + Delta x2 + ... + Delta xn) / n

items.title: Relative error
items.content: Relative error = mean absolute error / mean measured value

items.title: Percentage error
items.content: Percentage error = relative error x 100

items.title: Addition and subtraction of errors
items.content: For addition or subtraction, the maximum absolute error in the result is the sum of the absolute errors of the measured quantities.

items.title: Multiplication and division of errors
items.content: For multiplication or division, the maximum fractional error is the sum of the fractional errors of the measured quantities.

items.title: Power of a measured quantity
items.content: If Q = A^n, the maximum fractional error in Q is n times the fractional error in A.

items.title: Significant figures
items.content: Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a measured quantity, including all certain digits and the first uncertain digit.

items.title: Non-zero digits
items.content: All non-zero digits in a measured quantity are significant.

items.title: Zeros between non-zero digits
items.content: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant.

items.title: Leading zeros
items.content: Zeros to the left of the first non-zero digit are not significant.

items.title: Trailing zeros in decimal numbers
items.content: Trailing zeros to the right of a decimal point are significant when they indicate measured precision.

items.title: Multiplication and division significant figures
items.content: The result should have the same number of significant figures as the quantity having the fewest significant figures.

items.title: Addition and subtraction decimal places
items.content: The result should be retained to the same number of decimal places as the quantity having the fewest decimal places.

items.title: Rounding off
items.content: If the digit to be removed is greater than 5, increase the preceding digit by 1. If it is less than 5, leave it unchanged. For exactly 5, follow the prescribed rounding convention.

items.title: Least count
items.content: Least count is the smallest measurement that can be measured reliably by a measuring instrument.

items.title: Vernier calipers
items.content: Vernier calipers are used for measuring small lengths and dimensions such as internal and external diameters and depth.

items.title: Vernier calipers least count
items.content: Least count = 1 main scale division - 1 vernier scale division.

items.title: Screw gauge
items.content: A screw gauge is used for measuring very small lengths such as the diameter of a thin wire or thickness of a sheet.

items.title: Pitch of screw gauge
items.content: Pitch = distance moved by the screw / number of complete rotations.

items.title: Screw gauge least count
items.content: Least count = pitch / number of divisions on the circular scale.

items.title: Dimensional consistency
items.content: Every term added or subtracted in a physically meaningful equation must have the same dimensions.

items.title: Uses of dimensional analysis
items.content: Dimensional analysis can check dimensional consistency, derive relations between physical quantities, and convert units from one system to another.

items.title: Limitation of dimensional analysis
items.content: Dimensional analysis cannot determine dimensionless numerical constants, distinguish quantities with the same dimensions, or establish relations involving addition of different functions such as trigonometric or exponential terms.

items.title: Motion
items.content: An object is in motion if its position changes with time relative to a chosen reference frame.

items.title: Rest
items.content: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to a chosen reference frame.

items.title: Position
items.content: Position specifies the location of an object relative to a chosen reference point or origin.

items.title: Distance
items.content: Distance is the total length of the actual path travelled by an object. It is a scalar quantity.

items.title: Displacement
items.content: Displacement is the change in position of an object. It is a vector quantity directed from initial position to final position.

items.title: Distance-displacement relation
items.content: Distance travelled is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement.

items.title: Zero displacement
items.content: If an object returns to its initial position, its displacement is zero even though the distance travelled may be non-zero.

items.title: Displacement in one dimension
items.content: Delta x = x2 - x1

items.title: Speed
items.content: Speed is the rate of change of distance with time. It is a scalar quantity.

items.title: Average speed
items.content: Average speed = total distance travelled / total time taken

items.title: Velocity
items.content: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with time. It is a vector quantity.

items.title: Average velocity
items.content: Average velocity = total displacement / total time taken

items.title: Instantaneous velocity
items.content: v = dx/dt

items.title: Instantaneous speed
items.content: Instantaneous speed = |v| = |dx/dt|

items.title: Acceleration
items.content: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time.

items.title: Average acceleration
items.content: a_avg = (v2 - v1) / (t2 - t1) = Delta v / Delta t

items.title: Instantaneous acceleration
items.content: a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2

items.title: Uniform motion
items.content: Motion is uniform when an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.

items.title: Uniformly accelerated motion
items.content: Motion is uniformly accelerated when the velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time.

items.title: First equation of motion
items.content: v = u + at

items.title: Average velocity for uniform acceleration
items.content: v_avg = (u + v) / 2

items.title: Distance travelled in nth second
items.content: For uniformly accelerated motion, distance travelled during the nth second: s_n = u + (a/2)(2n - 1).

items.title: Position-time relation
items.content: For constant acceleration: x = x0 + ut + (1/2)at^2

items.title: Free fall as one-dimensional motion
items.content: For vertical motion near Earth, acceleration due to gravity is approximately constant and directed downward.

items.title: Free-fall equations
items.content: For downward-positive motion under gravity: v = u + gt, s = ut + (1/2)gt^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2gs.

items.title: Upward motion under gravity
items.content: Taking upward as positive: v = u - gt, y = ut - (1/2)gt^2, v^2 = u^2 - 2gy.

items.title: Maximum height in vertical upward motion
items.content: At maximum height, final velocity is zero. Therefore H = u^2/(2g), when air resistance is neglected.

items.title: Time to reach maximum height
items.content: t_up = u/g

items.title: Total time of flight for vertical projection
items.content: For an object projected vertically upward and returning to the same level: T = 2u/g.

items.title: Sign convention
items.content: Choose a positive direction and assign signs consistently to position, velocity, acceleration and displacement.

items.title: Position-time graph
items.content: The slope of a position-time graph gives velocity.

items.title: Velocity from position-time graph
items.content: v = slope of x-t graph = dx/dt

items.title: Velocity-time graph
items.content: The slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, while the area under the graph gives displacement.

items.title: Acceleration from velocity-time graph
items.content: a = slope of v-t graph = dv/dt

items.title: Displacement from velocity-time graph
items.content: Displacement = signed area under the velocity-time graph.

items.title: Acceleration-time graph
items.content: The area under an acceleration-time graph gives the change in velocity.

items.title: Change in velocity from acceleration-time graph
items.content: Delta v = signed area under the a-t graph.

items.title: Horizontal x-t graph
items.content: A horizontal position-time graph represents zero velocity, so the object is at rest in the chosen frame.

items.title: Straight-line x-t graph
items.content: A straight position-time graph with constant slope represents uniform velocity.

items.title: Horizontal v-t graph
items.content: A horizontal velocity-time graph represents constant velocity and therefore zero acceleration.

items.title: Straight-line v-t graph
items.content: A straight velocity-time graph with constant slope represents uniform acceleration.

items.title: Relative position in one dimension
items.content: The position of A relative to B is x_AB = x_A - x_B.

items.title: Relative velocity
items.content: Velocity of A relative to B: v_AB = v_A - v_B.

items.title: Relative speed in same direction
items.content: For two objects moving in the same direction, relative speed is the magnitude of the difference of their speeds.

items.title: Relative speed in opposite directions
items.content: For two objects moving in opposite directions, relative speed is the sum of their speeds.

items.title: SI unit of speed
items.content: metre per second (m s^-1)

items.title: SI unit of acceleration
items.content: metre per second squared (m s^-2)

items.title: Speed and velocity
items.content: Speed is scalar and cannot be negative. Velocity is vector and may be positive, negative or zero depending on the chosen direction.

items.title: Negative acceleration
items.content: Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down. Whether speed increases or decreases depends on the relative signs of velocity and acceleration.

items.title: Retardation
items.content: Retardation refers to acceleration opposite to the instantaneous velocity, causing the speed to decrease.

items.title: Uniform velocity condition
items.content: If acceleration is zero, velocity remains constant.

items.title: Instantaneous rest
items.content: An object is instantaneously at rest when its instantaneous velocity is zero, although its acceleration may be non-zero.

items.title: Scalar quantity
items.content: A scalar quantity has magnitude only and is completely specified by its magnitude.

items.title: Vector quantity
items.content: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction and follows the rules of vector addition.

items.title: Vector notation
items.content: A vector can be represented by an arrow. Its length represents magnitude and its arrowhead represents direction.

items.title: Magnitude of a vector
items.content: For vector A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k: |A| = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2).

items.title: Unit vector
items.content: Unit vector along A: A_hat = A / |A|.

items.title: Standard unit vectors
items.content: i, j and k are unit vectors along the positive x, y and z axes respectively.

items.title: Vector components in two dimensions
items.content: If A makes angle theta with the positive x-axis: A_x = A cos(theta), A_y = A sin(theta).

items.title: Direction angle from components
items.content: tan(theta) = A_y / A_x, with the quadrant determined from the signs of A_x and A_y.

items.title: Vector addition
items.content: For A = A_x i + A_y j and B = B_x i + B_y j: A + B = (A_x + B_x)i + (A_y + B_y)j.

items.title: Resultant of two vectors
items.content: If vectors A and B make angle theta: R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos(theta)).

items.title: Resultant direction
items.content: If resultant R makes angle alpha with A: tan(alpha) = B sin(theta) / (A + B cos(theta)).

items.title: Parallel vectors
items.content: For two vectors in the same direction, resultant magnitude is A + B.

items.title: Opposite vectors
items.content: For two vectors in opposite directions, resultant magnitude is |A - B|.

items.title: Perpendicular vectors
items.content: For perpendicular vectors, resultant magnitude is R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2).

items.title: Triangle law of vector addition
items.content: If two vectors are represented by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their resultant is represented by the third side taken from the tail of the first to the head of the second.

items.title: Parallelogram law of vector addition
items.content: If two vectors acting from the same point are represented by adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is represented by the diagonal from the common origin.

items.title: Vector subtraction
items.content: A - B = A + (-B), where -B has the same magnitude as B but opposite direction.

items.title: Vector multiplication by scalar
items.content: Multiplying a vector by a positive scalar changes its magnitude without changing direction. A negative scalar reverses its direction.

items.title: Position vector
items.content: Position vector of a point P(x,y,z): r = x i + y j + z k.

items.title: Displacement vector
items.content: Displacement from r1 to r2: Delta r = r2 - r1.

items.title: Velocity vector
items.content: Instantaneous velocity vector: v = dr/dt.

items.title: Acceleration vector
items.content: Instantaneous acceleration vector: a = dv/dt = d^2r/dt^2.

items.title: Projectile
items.content: A projectile is an object projected into air that subsequently moves under the influence of gravity, neglecting air resistance.

items.title: Projectile horizontal velocity
items.content: For projection speed u at angle theta: u_x = u cos(theta).

items.title: Projectile vertical velocity
items.content: For projection speed u at angle theta: u_y = u sin(theta).

items.title: Horizontal displacement of projectile
items.content: x = u cos(theta) t.

items.title: Vertical displacement of projectile
items.content: y = u sin(theta)t - (1/2)gt^2.

items.title: Trajectory equation
items.content: y = x tan(theta) - [g x^2 / (2u^2 cos^2(theta))].

items.title: Time of flight
items.content: For a projectile returning to its original level: T = 2u sin(theta) / g.

items.title: Maximum height of projectile
items.content: H = u^2 sin^2(theta) / (2g).

items.title: Horizontal range of projectile
items.content: R = u^2 sin(2theta) / g.

items.title: Maximum range condition
items.content: For a given projection speed and level ground, horizontal range is maximum when theta = 45 degrees.

items.title: Maximum range
items.content: For a projectile on level ground, maximum range is R_max = u^2/g.

items.title: Complementary angles
items.content: Two projection angles theta and (90 degrees - theta) give the same horizontal range for the same initial speed on level ground.

items.title: Velocity at highest point of projectile
items.content: At the highest point, the vertical component of velocity is zero and the horizontal component remains u cos(theta).

items.title: Projectile speed at any point
items.content: v = sqrt[(u cos(theta))^2 + (u sin(theta) - gt)^2].

items.title: Independence of horizontal and vertical motion
items.content: In ideal projectile motion, horizontal motion has constant velocity while vertical motion has constant acceleration g downward.

items.title: Uniform circular motion
items.content: Motion of an object along a circular path with constant speed is called uniform circular motion.

items.title: Angular displacement
items.content: Angular displacement: theta = s/r, where s is arc length and r is radius.

items.title: Angular velocity
items.content: omega = dtheta/dt.

items.title: Relation between linear and angular velocity
items.content: v = r omega.

items.title: Angular speed and frequency
items.content: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi/T.

items.title: Linear speed in circular motion
items.content: v = 2 pi r/T = 2 pi r f.

items.title: Centripetal acceleration
items.content: a_c = v^2/r = r omega^2.

items.title: Centripetal acceleration
items.content: The acceleration directed towards the centre of a circular path is called centripetal acceleration.

items.title: Direction of velocity in circular motion
items.content: The instantaneous velocity of an object in circular motion is tangential to the circular path.

items.title: Direction of centripetal acceleration
items.content: Centripetal acceleration always points radially inward towards the centre of the circular path.

items.title: Speed versus velocity in uniform circular motion
items.content: In uniform circular motion, speed remains constant but velocity continuously changes direction, so acceleration is non-zero.

items.title: Centripetal force
items.content: F_c = mv^2/r = mr omega^2.

items.title: Angular displacement unit
items.content: The SI unit of angular displacement is radian (rad).

items.title: One complete revolution
items.content: One complete revolution corresponds to 2 pi radians or 360 degrees.

items.title: Arc length
items.content: s = r theta, when theta is measured in radians.

items.title: Relative velocity in vector form
items.content: v_AB = v_A - v_B.

items.title: Vector equality
items.content: Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and the same direction, irrespective of their positions.

items.title: Null vector
items.content: A null vector has zero magnitude and no definite direction.

items.title: Negative of a vector
items.content: The negative of a vector has the same magnitude but opposite direction.

items.title: Vector addition is commutative
items.content: A + B = B + A.

items.title: Condition for zero resultant of two vectors
items.content: Two vectors have zero resultant only when they have equal magnitudes and opposite directions.

items.title: Force
items.content: Force is an interaction that can change the state of motion of an object or produce deformation.

items.title: Inertia
items.content: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of rest or uniform motion.

items.title: Inertia of rest
items.content: The tendency of an object at rest to remain at rest is called inertia of rest.

items.title: Inertia of motion
items.content: The tendency of a moving object to continue moving with uniform velocity is called inertia of motion.

items.title: Inertia of direction
items.content: The tendency of an object to resist a change in its direction of motion is called inertia of direction.

items.title: Newton first law
items.content: An object remains at rest or continues in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force.

items.title: Newton second law
items.content: F_net = dp/dt, where p is linear momentum.

items.title: Newton second law for constant mass
items.content: F_net = ma.

items.title: Newton third law
items.content: When one object exerts a force on another object, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal-magnitude force in the opposite direction on the first.

items.title: Action and reaction forces
items.content: Action and reaction forces act on two different interacting bodies, so they do not cancel each other on a single free-body diagram.

items.title: Linear momentum
items.content: p = mv.

items.title: Momentum
items.content: Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity. It is a vector quantity.

items.title: SI unit of momentum
items.content: kg m s^-1, equivalently N s.

items.title: Impulse
items.content: J = Delta p = p2 - p1.

items.title: Impulse for constant force
items.content: J = F Delta t.

items.title: Impulse-momentum theorem
items.content: The impulse delivered to an object equals its change in linear momentum.

items.title: Conservation of linear momentum
items.content: If the net external force on an isolated system is zero, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant.

items.title: Two-body momentum conservation
items.content: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2, when external impulse is negligible.

items.title: System of particles
items.content: A system of particles is a collection of particles considered together for analysing their motion and interactions.

items.title: Free-body diagram
items.content: A free-body diagram represents all external forces acting on a selected body.

items.title: Net force
items.content: The net force on a body is the vector sum of all external forces acting on it.

items.title: Net force in components
items.content: F_net = (sum Fx)i + (sum Fy)j + (sum Fz)k.

items.title: Equilibrium
items.content: A body is in translational equilibrium when the vector sum of all external forces acting on it is zero.

items.title: Condition for translational equilibrium
items.content: sum F = 0.

items.title: Equilibrium and acceleration
items.content: If the net external force is zero, the acceleration of the centre of mass is zero.

items.title: Friction
items.content: Friction is a contact force that opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion between surfaces in contact.

items.title: Static friction
items.content: Static friction acts between surfaces when there is no relative motion between them and adjusts up to a maximum value.

items.title: Static friction range
items.content: 0 <= f_s <= f_s,max.

items.title: Limiting friction
items.content: f_s,max = mu_s N.

items.title: Limiting friction
items.content: The maximum value of static friction just before relative motion begins is called limiting friction.

items.title: Coefficient of static friction
items.content: The coefficient of static friction is the ratio of limiting friction to normal reaction.

items.title: Kinetic friction
items.content: Kinetic friction acts when two surfaces are sliding relative to each other.

items.title: Kinetic friction
items.content: f_k = mu_k N.

items.title: Static versus kinetic friction
items.content: For typical dry surfaces, the coefficient of static friction is greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction: mu_s > mu_k.

items.title: Normal reaction
items.content: Normal reaction is the contact force exerted by a surface perpendicular to the contact surface.

items.title: Normal reaction on horizontal surface
items.content: For a body at rest on a horizontal surface with no other vertical force, N = mg.

items.title: Friction on an inclined plane
items.content: For a body on an incline, the normal reaction is N = mg cos(theta), when no other force has a perpendicular component.

items.title: Component of weight along incline
items.content: Component of weight parallel to an inclined plane = mg sin(theta).

items.title: Component of weight perpendicular to incline
items.content: Component of weight perpendicular to an inclined plane = mg cos(theta).

items.title: Acceleration down a smooth incline
items.content: For a frictionless incline of angle theta, acceleration down the plane is a = g sin(theta).

items.title: Acceleration down a rough incline
items.content: For sliding down an incline with kinetic friction: a = g(sin(theta) - mu_k cos(theta)).

items.title: Coefficient of friction and angle of repose
items.content: At limiting equilibrium on an inclined plane, the coefficient of static friction is related to the angle of repose by mu_s = tan(theta_r).

items.title: Angle of repose
items.content: The angle of inclination of a plane at which a body just begins to slide down is called the angle of repose.

items.title: Centripetal force requirement
items.content: For circular motion of radius r at speed v, the required inward net force is F_c = mv^2/r.

items.title: Centripetal force using angular speed
items.content: F_c = mr omega^2.

items.title: Centripetal force is not a new force
items.content: Centripetal force is the name given to the net inward radial force required for circular motion; it may be provided by tension, friction, gravity, normal force, or their combination.

items.title: Vehicle on level circular road
items.content: For ideal circular motion on a level road, maximum speed without skidding is v_max = sqrt(mu_s r g).

items.title: Banking of roads without friction
items.content: For a frictionless banked road: tan(theta) = v^2/(rg).

items.title: Banking angle relation
items.content: For a given speed v and radius r, a suitable banking angle satisfies tan(theta) = v^2/(rg) when friction is neglected.

items.title: Tension in an ideal string
items.content: For an ideal massless and inextensible string passing over an ideal pulley, the tension is the same throughout the string.

items.title: Atwood machine
items.content: For two masses m1 and m2 connected by a light inextensible string over an ideal pulley, the heavier mass accelerates downward and the lighter mass upward.

items.title: Atwood machine acceleration
items.content: For m2 > m1: a = (m2 - m1)g/(m1 + m2), assuming an ideal setup.

items.title: Atwood machine tension
items.content: For an ideal Atwood machine, T = 2m1m2g/(m1 + m2).

items.title: Pseudo force
items.content: A pseudo force is introduced when applying Newtonian mechanics from a non-inertial reference frame. It acts opposite to the acceleration of the frame.

items.title: Pseudo force
items.content: F_pseudo = -m a_frame.

items.title: Inertial frame
items.content: An inertial frame is a reference frame in which Newton first law holds and no pseudo force is required for Newtonian analysis.

items.title: Non-inertial frame
items.content: A non-inertial frame is an accelerating reference frame in which pseudo forces may be introduced to apply Newton second law.

items.title: Force and acceleration direction
items.content: For a single body of constant mass, acceleration is in the direction of the net force.

items.title: Mass and inertia
items.content: Mass is a measure of the inertia of a body. Greater mass means greater resistance to a given change in velocity.

items.title: SI unit of force
items.content: The SI unit of force is newton (N), where 1 N = 1 kg m s^-2.

items.title: SI unit of impulse
items.content: The SI unit of impulse is N s, equivalent to kg m s^-1.

items.title: Work
items.content: Work is done by a force when its point of application undergoes displacement and the force has a component along the displacement.

items.title: Work by constant force
items.content: W = F s cos(theta), where theta is the angle between force and displacement.

items.title: Positive work
items.content: Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement.

items.title: Negative work
items.content: Work is negative when the force has a component opposite to the displacement.

items.title: Zero work
items.content: Work is zero when the force is perpendicular to displacement or when there is no displacement.

items.title: Work by variable force
items.content: W = integral(F . dr), evaluated along the path of motion.

items.title: Work from force-displacement graph
items.content: The work done by a variable force is the signed area under the force-displacement graph.

items.title: SI unit of work
items.content: The SI unit of work is joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.

items.title: Energy
items.content: Energy is the capacity of a system to do work.

items.title: Kinetic energy
items.content: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion.

items.title: Kinetic energy in terms of momentum
Work-energy theorem
items.content: The net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy.

items.title: Work-energy theorem formula
items.content: W_net = Delta K = K_f - K_i.

items.title: Potential energy
items.content: Potential energy is energy associated with the configuration or position of a system.

items.title: Gravitational potential energy near Earth
items.content: U = mgh, taking the chosen zero level as reference.

items.title: Change in gravitational potential energy
items.content: Delta U = mg(h2 - h1), near Earth where g is approximately constant.

items.title: Conservative force
items.content: A force is conservative if the work done by it between two points is independent of the path taken.

items.title: Work by conservative force
items.content: The work done by a conservative force around a closed path is zero.

items.title: Work and potential energy
items.content: For a conservative force: W_conservative = -Delta U.

items.title: Non-conservative force
items.content: A force is non-conservative when the work it does depends on the path followed between two points.

items.title: Examples of conservative forces
items.content: Gravitational force and ideal spring force are conservative forces.

items.title: Example of non-conservative force
items.content: Kinetic friction is a common non-conservative force because its work depends on the path length.

items.title: Spring force
items.content: For an ideal spring: F = -kx.

items.title: Spring constant
items.content: The spring constant k measures the stiffness of an ideal spring and appears in Hooke law F = -kx.

items.title: Work done in stretching a spring
items.content: Work required to stretch an ideal spring from 0 to x: W = (1/2)kx^2.

items.title: Work done by spring
items.content: When a spring changes extension from x1 to x2, work done by the spring is W_spring = (1/2)k(x1^2 - x2^2).

items.title: Mechanical energy
items.content: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies.

items.title: Mechanical energy
items.content: E_mechanical = K + U.

items.title: Conservation of mechanical energy
items.content: If only conservative forces do work, the total mechanical energy remains constant.

items.title: Conservation of mechanical energy
items.content: K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f.

items.title: Mechanical energy with non-conservative work
items.content: K_i + U_i + W_nc = K_f + U_f, where W_nc is work done by non-conservative forces.

items.title: Power
items.content: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.

items.title: Average power
items.content: P_avg = W/Delta t.

items.title: Instantaneous power
items.content: P = dW/dt.

items.title: Power by a force
items.content: P = F . v = Fv cos(theta).

items.title: SI unit of power
items.content: The SI unit of power is watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s^-1.

items.title: Efficiency
items.content: Efficiency is the ratio of useful output energy or power to the input energy or power, usually expressed as a percentage.

items.title: Efficiency formula
items.content: Efficiency = (useful output / input) x 100%.

items.title: Potential energy from force
items.content: For a one-dimensional conservative force, F(x) = -dU/dx.

items.title: Zero of potential energy
items.content: The zero level of potential energy can be chosen arbitrarily; only differences in potential energy affect physical predictions.

items.title: Work by gravity
items.content: For motion near Earth from height h1 to h2, work done by gravity is W_g = mg(h1 - h2).

items.title: Work done in uniform circular motion
items.content: The centripetal force does zero work because it is perpendicular to instantaneous displacement.

items.title: Kinetic energy and speed
items.content: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed: K is proportional to v^2.

items.title: Effect of doubling speed
items.content: If mass remains constant and speed doubles, kinetic energy becomes four times its original value.

items.title: Effect of doubling mass
items.content: If speed remains constant and mass doubles, kinetic energy becomes twice its original value.

items.title: Work-energy theorem and net force
items.content: The work-energy theorem applies to the net work done by all forces acting on the object.

items.title: Zero net work
items.content: If net work on an object is zero, its kinetic energy remains unchanged.

items.title: Work is scalar
items.content: Work is a scalar quantity even though it is calculated using the scalar product of force and displacement vectors.

items.title: Power is scalar
items.content: Power is a scalar quantity representing the rate of work or energy transfer.

items.title: Power for constant force and constant velocity
items.content: If force and velocity are constant, P = Fv cos(theta).

items.title: Work by normal force
items.content: When a normal force is perpendicular to the displacement, its work is zero.

items.title: Energy conservation
items.content: Energy can change from one form to another, but total energy of an isolated system remains conserved.

chapters.name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

items.title: System of particles
items.content: A system of particles is a collection of particles considered together for analysing its overall motion and interactions.

items.title: Centre of mass
items.content: The centre of mass is the point whose position represents the mass-weighted average position of the particles of a system.

items.title: Centre of mass for two particles
Centre of mass x-coordinate
items.content: x_cm = (sum mi xi)/(sum mi).

items.title: Centre of mass y-coordinate
items.content: y_cm = (sum mi yi)/(sum mi).

items.title: Centre of mass z-coordinate
items.content: z_cm = (sum mi zi)/(sum mi).

items.title: Centre of mass of two equal masses
items.content: For two equal masses, the centre of mass lies at the midpoint of the line joining them.

items.title: Centre of mass of a uniform symmetric body
items.content: For a uniform body having suitable symmetry, the centre of mass lies at its geometrical centre or symmetry point.

items.title: Centre of mass velocity
items.content: V_cm = (sum mi vi)/(sum mi).

items.title: Centre of mass momentum
items.content: P_total = M V_cm, where M is the total mass of the system.

items.title: Centre of mass acceleration
items.content: A_cm = (sum mi ai)/(sum mi).

items.title: Equation of motion of centre of mass
items.content: F_ext = M A_cm.

items.title: Centre of mass with zero external force
items.content: If net external force on a system is zero, its centre of mass moves with constant velocity.

items.title: Rigid body
items.content: A rigid body is an idealised body in which the distance between every pair of particles remains constant.

items.title: Rotational motion
items.content: Motion in which a rigid body rotates about an axis is called rotational motion.

items.title: Angular displacement
items.content: Angular displacement is the change in angular position of a rotating body and is measured in radians in SI.

items.title: Angular velocity
items.content: omega = dtheta/dt.

items.title: Average angular velocity
items.content: omega_avg = Delta theta/Delta t.

items.title: Angular acceleration
items.content: alpha = domega/dt = d^2theta/dt^2.

items.title: Average angular acceleration
items.content: alpha_avg = Delta omega/Delta t.

items.title: Linear-angular velocity relation
items.content: v = r omega.

items.title: Tangential acceleration
items.content: a_t = r alpha.

items.title: Radial acceleration
items.content: a_r = v^2/r = r omega^2.

items.title: Total acceleration in circular motion
items.content: a = sqrt(a_t^2 + a_r^2), since tangential and radial components are perpendicular.

items.title: Rotational kinematic equation 1
items.content: omega = omega_0 + alpha t, for constant angular acceleration.

items.title: Rotational kinematic equation 2
items.content: theta = omega_0 t + (1/2)alpha t^2, for constant angular acceleration.

items.title: Rotational kinematic equation 3
items.content: omega^2 = omega_0^2 + 2 alpha theta, for constant angular acceleration.

items.title: Torque
items.content: Torque is the turning effect of a force about a chosen point or axis.

items.title: Torque vector
items.content: tau = r x F.

items.title: Magnitude of torque
items.content: tau = r F sin(theta), where theta is the angle between r and F.

items.title: Torque is maximum
items.content: Torque magnitude is maximum when the force is perpendicular to the position vector: theta = 90 degrees.

items.title: Torque is zero
items.content: Torque is zero when the line of action of the force passes through the chosen axis or when the force is zero.

items.title: Moment arm
items.content: The perpendicular distance from the axis or pivot to the line of action of a force is called the moment arm.

items.title: Torque using moment arm
items.content: tau = F x perpendicular distance from axis to line of action.

items.title: Rotational Newton second law
items.content: For rotation about a fixed axis: tau_net = I alpha.

items.title: Moment of inertia
items.content: Moment of inertia measures the rotational inertia of a body about a specified axis.

items.title: Moment of inertia for particles
items.content: I = sum mi ri^2.

items.title: Moment of inertia for continuous body
items.content: I = integral r^2 dm.

items.title: Dependence of moment of inertia
items.content: Moment of inertia depends on the mass distribution relative to the chosen axis, not only on total mass.

items.title: Radius of gyration
items.content: I = M k^2, where k is the radius of gyration about the specified axis.

items.title: Radius of gyration
items.content: Radius of gyration is the distance from the axis at which the whole mass could be concentrated to produce the same moment of inertia.

items.title: Parallel axis theorem
items.content: I = I_cm + M d^2, where d is the perpendicular distance between the parallel axes.

items.title: Perpendicular axis theorem
items.content: For a plane lamina: I_z = I_x + I_y, where x and y are mutually perpendicular axes in the plane and z is perpendicular to the plane through their intersection.

items.title: Moment of inertia of a thin ring
items.content: About an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane: I = MR^2.

items.title: Moment of inertia of a disc
items.content: About an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane: I = (1/2)MR^2.

items.title: Moment of inertia of a solid sphere
items.content: About a diameter: I = (2/5)MR^2.

items.title: Moment of inertia of a hollow sphere
items.content: For a thin hollow spherical shell about a diameter: I = (2/3)MR^2.

items.title: Moment of inertia of a rod about centre
items.content: For a uniform thin rod of length L about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to the rod: I = (1/12)ML^2.

items.title: Moment of inertia of a rod about end
items.content: For a uniform thin rod of length L about an axis through one end and perpendicular to the rod: I = (1/3)ML^2.

items.title: Rotational kinetic energy
items.content: K_rot = (1/2)I omega^2.

items.title: Rotational work
items.content: For constant torque: W = tau theta.

items.title: Rotational power
items.content: P = tau omega.

items.title: Angular momentum
items.content: Angular momentum is the rotational analogue of linear momentum.

items.title: Angular momentum of a particle
items.content: L = r x p.

items.title: Magnitude of angular momentum
items.content: L = r p sin(theta).

items.title: Angular momentum of rigid body
items.content: For rotation about a fixed principal axis: L = I omega.

items.title: Torque-angular momentum relation
items.content: tau_ext = dL/dt.

items.title: Conservation of angular momentum
items.content: If the net external torque on a system is zero, its total angular momentum remains constant.

items.title: Angular momentum conservation
items.content: I1 omega1 = I2 omega2, when external torque is zero about the chosen axis.

items.title: Rotational equilibrium
items.content: A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium when the net external torque about the chosen axis is zero.

items.title: Condition for rotational equilibrium
items.content: sum tau = 0.

items.title: Translational and rotational equilibrium
items.content: For complete static equilibrium of a rigid body, both net force and net torque must be zero.

items.title: Conditions for static equilibrium
items.content: sum F = 0 and sum tau = 0.

items.title: Rolling motion
items.content: Rolling motion is a combination of translational motion of the centre of mass and rotational motion about the centre of mass.

items.title: Rolling without slipping
items.content: v_cm = R omega.

items.title: Rolling acceleration relation
items.content: a_cm = R alpha for rolling without slipping.

items.title: Total kinetic energy of rolling body
items.content: K = (1/2)M v_cm^2 + (1/2)I_cm omega^2.

items.title: Instantaneous point of contact in pure rolling
items.content: For ideal rolling without slipping on a stationary surface, the point of contact is instantaneously at rest relative to the surface.

items.title: SI unit of torque
items.content: The SI unit of torque is N m.

items.title: SI unit of angular momentum
items.content: The SI unit of angular momentum is kg m^2 s^-1.

items.title: Dimensions of torque
items.content: [tau] = ML^2T^-2.

items.title: Gravitation
items.content: Gravitation is the universal force of attraction between any two masses.

items.title: Gravitational force
items.content: The gravitational force between two masses is always attractive and acts along the line joining their centres.

items.title: Newton law of gravitation
items.content: F = G m1 m2 / r^2.

items.title: Universal gravitational constant
items.content: G is the universal gravitational constant appearing in Newton law of gravitation.

items.title: SI unit of G
items.content: The SI unit of G is N m^2 kg^-2.

items.title: Inverse square dependence
items.content: For fixed masses, gravitational force varies inversely as the square of the distance between their centres.

items.title: Gravitational field
items.content: g = F/m, where F is the gravitational force on a test mass m.

items.title: Gravitational field due to a point mass
items.content: g = GM/r^2.

items.title: Direction of gravitational field
items.content: The gravitational field due to an isolated mass is directed towards the mass.

items.title: Acceleration due to gravity at Earth surface
items.content: g = GM/R^2, where M is Earth mass and R is Earth radius.

items.title: Weight of a body
items.content: W = mg.

items.title: Mass versus weight
items.content: Mass is an intrinsic property of a body, while weight is the gravitational force acting on the body and depends on the local value of g.

items.title: Potential energy near Earth surface
items.content: U = mgh, when the gravitational field is treated as uniform over the height considered.

items.title: Gravitational potential
items.content: Gravitational potential at a point is the gravitational potential energy per unit mass placed at that point.

items.title: Gravitational potential due to point mass
items.content: V = -GM/r, taking gravitational potential to be zero at infinity.

items.title: Potential energy of two masses
items.content: U = -G m1 m2 / r, taking potential energy to be zero at infinite separation.

items.title: Why gravitational potential energy is negative
items.content: With zero potential energy chosen at infinity, a bound gravitational system has negative potential energy.

items.title: Relation between potential and field
items.content: g = -dV/dr for a radial gravitational field.

items.title: Escape speed
items.content: v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) from the surface of a spherical body of mass M and radius R.

items.title: Escape speed and orbital speed
items.content: For an object close to the surface of the same spherical body, v_e = sqrt(2) v_o.

items.title: Escape speed independence from mass
items.content: For a given spherical body, escape speed does not depend on the mass of the escaping object when air resistance is neglected.

items.title: Escape speed at Earth surface
items.content: v_e = sqrt(2gR).

items.title: Orbital velocity
items.content: Orbital velocity is the speed required for a satellite to maintain a circular orbit around a central body.

items.title: Orbital velocity
items.content: v_o = sqrt(GM/r) for a circular orbit of radius r.

items.title: Orbital velocity near Earth surface
items.content: v_o = sqrt(gR).

items.title: Satellite orbital period
items.content: T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/GM) for a circular orbit.

items.title: Kepler third law
items.content: T^2 proportional to r^3 for bodies orbiting the same central mass in circular or elliptical orbits.

items.title: Centripetal force for satellite
items.content: GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r for a circular orbit.

items.title: Satellite orbital speed independence from satellite mass
items.content: For a given orbit around a central mass, orbital speed does not depend on the mass of the satellite.

items.title: Geostationary satellite
items.content: A geostationary satellite appears stationary relative to a point on Earth because its orbital motion matches Earth rotation appropriately.

items.title: Conditions for geostationary orbit
items.content: A geostationary satellite must orbit in the equatorial plane, move in the same direction as Earth rotation, and have an orbital period equal to Earth rotational period.

items.title: Gravitational potential energy of a system
items.content: It is the work required to assemble the masses of the system from infinite separation, with zero potential energy at infinity.

items.title: Potential energy of multiple particles
items.content: The total gravitational potential energy is the sum of pairwise potential energies: U = -G sum(mi mj / rij), over each distinct pair.

items.title: Gravitational force vector
items.content: For two point masses, the force magnitude is Gm1m2/r^2 and its direction is along the line joining the masses.

items.title: Superposition of gravitational fields
items.content: The net gravitational field at a point is the vector sum of the gravitational fields produced by all masses.

items.title: Superposition of gravitational forces
items.content: The net gravitational force on a mass is the vector sum of the individual gravitational forces due to all other masses.

items.title: g at height h above Earth
g at small height
items.content: For h much smaller than R: g_h approximately equals g(1 - 2h/R).

items.title: g at depth d
items.content: For an ideal uniform Earth model: g_d = g(1 - d/R).

items.title: g at Earth centre
items.content: In the ideal uniform spherical Earth model, g becomes zero at the centre.

items.title: Variation of g with altitude
items.content: The value of g decreases as altitude above Earth surface increases.

items.title: Variation of g with depth
items.content: For the ideal uniform Earth model, g decreases approximately linearly with depth and becomes zero at the centre.

items.title: Gravitational potential at infinity
items.content: The conventional reference for gravitational potential in this chapter is V = 0 at infinity.

items.title: Work done by gravity
items.content: Work done by gravity equals the negative change in gravitational potential energy: W_gravity = -Delta U.

items.title: Change in gravitational potential energy
items.content: Delta U = U_final - U_initial.

items.title: Conservative nature of gravitational force
items.content: Gravitational force is conservative, so work done by gravity between two points is independent of the path taken.

items.title: Closed path work by gravity
items.content: The net work done by gravity over a closed path is zero.

items.title: Total mechanical energy of satellite
items.content: E = K + U.

items.title: Kinetic energy of circular-orbit satellite
items.content: K = GMm/(2r).

items.title: Potential energy of circular-orbit satellite
items.content: U = -GMm/r.

items.title: Total energy of circular-orbit satellite
items.content: E = -GMm/(2r).

items.title: Energy relation for circular satellite orbit
items.content: For a circular orbit, U = -2K and E = -K = U/2.

items.title: Bound gravitational orbit
items.content: A negative total mechanical energy corresponds to a bound gravitational state when zero energy is chosen at infinity.

items.title: Weightlessness
items.content: Apparent weightlessness occurs when a body has no normal reaction force supporting it, such as during free fall.

items.title: Weightlessness in an orbiting satellite
items.content: Astronauts in an orbiting satellite experience apparent weightlessness because the satellite and its contents are continuously in free fall under gravity.

items.title: Kepler first law
items.content: Planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.

items.title: Kepler second law
items.content: The line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.

items.title: Kepler third law
items.content: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis for bodies orbiting the same central mass.

items.title: Areal velocity
items.content: Kepler second law implies that the areal velocity of a planet is constant.

items.title: Areal velocity
items.content: Areal velocity = dA/dt = constant for a planet under a central gravitational force.

items.title: Relation between G and g
items.content: g = GM/R^2.

items.title: Approximate value of g
items.content: Near Earth surface, g is approximately 9.8 m s^-2.

items.title: Approximate value of G
items.content: G is approximately 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2.

items.title: Gravity inside a spherical shell
items.content: Inside an ideal uniform spherical shell, the net gravitational field is zero.

items.title: Gravitational potential inside a spherical shell
items.content: Inside an ideal spherical shell, gravitational potential is constant throughout the interior and equals the potential at the surface.

items.title: Gravitational potential of a spherical shell outside
items.content: Outside a spherically symmetric body, its gravitational field and potential are the same as those of a point mass concentrated at its centre.

items.title: Shell theorem
items.content: For a spherically symmetric mass distribution, the gravitational effect outside is equivalent to that of the total mass concentrated at the centre.

items.title: Orbital energy change with radius
items.content: For a circular orbit, E = -GMm/(2r), so increasing orbital radius makes the total energy less negative.

items.title: Escape and bound orbit
items.content: An object escapes the gravitational field when its total mechanical energy reaches zero or greater, under the usual reference of zero energy at infinity.

items.title: Minimum escape energy from surface
items.content: For a body of mass m at the surface of a spherical body: K_escape = GMm/R = (1/2)m v_e^2.

items.title: Orbital period in terms of radius
items.content: T^2 = (4 pi^2/GM) r^3 for a circular orbit.

items.title: Gravitational force versus electrostatic force
items.content: Both gravitational and electrostatic point-force laws have inverse-square dependence on separation, but gravitational interaction between ordinary masses is always attractive.

items.title: Gravitational field lines
items.content: Gravitational field lines point towards masses and, for a spherically symmetric isolated mass, are radial.

items.title: SI unit of gravitational potential
items.content: The SI unit of gravitational potential is J kg^-1, equivalent to m^2 s^-2.

items.title: SI unit of gravitational potential energy
items.content: The SI unit of gravitational potential energy is joule (J).

items.title: Gravity inside a spherical shell
items.content: Inside an ideal uniform spherical shell, the net gravitational field is zero.

items.title: Gravitational potential inside a spherical shell
items.content: Inside an ideal spherical shell, gravitational potential is constant throughout the interior and equals the potential at the surface.

items.title: Gravitational potential of a spherical shell outside
items.content: Outside a spherically symmetric body, its gravitational field and potential are the same as those of a point mass concentrated at its centre.

items.title: Shell theorem
items.content: For a spherically symmetric mass distribution, the gravitational effect outside is equivalent to that of the total mass concentrated at the centre.

items.title: Orbital energy change with radius
items.content: For a circular orbit, E = -GMm/(2r), so increasing orbital radius makes the total energy less negative.

items.title: Escape and bound orbit
items.content: An object escapes the gravitational field when its total mechanical energy reaches zero or greater, under the usual reference of zero energy at infinity.

items.title: Minimum escape energy from surface
items.content: For a body of mass m at the surface of a spherical body: K_escape = GMm/R = (1/2)m v_e^2.

items.title: Orbital period in terms of radius
items.content: T^2 = (4 pi^2/GM) r^3 for a circular orbit.

items.title: Gravitational force versus electrostatic force
items.content: Both gravitational and electrostatic point-force laws have inverse-square dependence on separation, but gravitational interaction between ordinary masses is always attractive.

items.title: Gravitational field lines
items.content: Gravitational field lines point towards masses and, for a spherically symmetric isolated mass, are radial.

items.title: SI unit of gravitational potential
items.content: The SI unit of gravitational potential is J kg^-1, equivalent to m^2 s^-2.

items.title: SI unit of gravitational potential energy
items.content: The SI unit of gravitational potential energy is joule (J).

items.title: Fluid
items.content: A fluid is a substance that can flow and cannot sustain a tangential shear stress at rest.

items.title: Density
items.content: ρ = m/V, where ρ is density, m is mass and V is volume.

items.title: Relative Density
items.content: Relative density = density of substance / density of water.

items.title: Pressure
items.content: P = F/A, where F is normal force and A is area over which it acts.

items.title: SI Unit of Pressure
items.content: The SI unit of pressure is pascal (Pa). 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².

items.title: Pressure as a Scalar
items.content: Pressure at a point in a fluid at rest acts normally to every surface and has no preferred tangential direction.

items.title: Pascal's Law
items.content: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the walls of its container.

items.title: Hydraulic Lift
items.content: For an ideal hydraulic lift, F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

items.title: Hydraulic Mechanical Advantage
items.content: F₂/F₁ = A₂/A₁ for an ideal hydraulic lift.

items.title: Hydrostatic Pressure
items.content: Pressure at depth h in a liquid of density ρ is P = P₀ + ρgh, where P₀ is pressure at the surface.

items.title: Gauge Pressure
items.content: Gauge pressure = P − P₀ = ρgh for a liquid at depth h.

items.title: Atmospheric Pressure
items.content: Atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the Earth's atmosphere on surfaces.

items.title: Barometer
items.content: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. For a mercury barometer, P_atm = ρgh.

items.title: Manometer
items.content: A manometer measures pressure difference using the height difference of a liquid column.

items.title: Pressure Variation with Depth
items.content: For a liquid of constant density at rest, pressure increases linearly with depth: ΔP = ρgΔh.

items.title: Buoyant Force
items.content: The buoyant force on an immersed body is the upward force exerted by the surrounding fluid.

items.title: Archimedes' Principle
items.content: A body immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.

items.title: Buoyant Force Formula
items.content: F_B = ρ_fluid V_displaced g.

items.title: Apparent Weight in a Fluid
items.content: Apparent weight = actual weight − buoyant force.

items.title: Condition for Floating
items.content: A body floats when the buoyant force balances its weight: F_B = mg.

items.title: Floating Equilibrium
items.content: For a freely floating body, the weight of the body equals the buoyant force.

items.title: Fraction of Volume Submerged
items.content: For a floating body, V_submerged/V_body = ρ_body/ρ_fluid.

items.title: Streamline Flow
items.content: In streamline flow, the velocity of a fluid particle at a point remains steady with time and the flow follows smooth paths.

items.title: Turbulent Flow
items.content: Turbulent flow is irregular fluid motion in which velocity and pressure can fluctuate significantly with time.

items.title: Ideal Fluid
items.content: An ideal fluid is treated as incompressible and non-viscous for simplified fluid-flow analysis.

items.title: Viscosity
items.content: Viscosity is the property of a fluid that opposes relative motion between adjacent layers.

items.title: Newton's Law of Viscosity
items.content: F/A = η(dv/dx), where η is the coefficient of viscosity and dv/dx is the velocity gradient.

items.title: Coefficient of Viscosity
items.content: The SI unit of coefficient of viscosity is Pa·s or N s m⁻².

items.title: Dimensions of Viscosity
items.content: Dimensional formula of coefficient of viscosity: [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹].

items.title: Stokes' Law
items.content: For a small spherical body moving slowly through a viscous fluid, viscous force F = 6πηrv.

items.title: Terminal Velocity
items.content: Terminal velocity is the constant speed reached when the net force on a falling body in a viscous fluid becomes zero.

items.title: Terminal Velocity of a Small Sphere
items.content: v_t = 2r²(ρ_s − ρ_f)g/(9η), for a small sphere under Stokes' law conditions.

items.title: Reynolds Number
items.content: Re = ρvd/η, where ρ is fluid density, v is speed, d is characteristic length and η is viscosity.

items.title: Reynolds Number Meaning
items.content: Reynolds number compares inertial effects with viscous effects in fluid flow.

items.title: Continuity Equation
items.content: For steady incompressible flow, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

items.title: Mass Conservation in Fluid Flow
items.content: In steady flow, the mass crossing each cross-section per unit time remains constant.

items.title: Volume Flow Rate
items.content: Q = Av, where A is cross-sectional area and v is average fluid speed.

items.title: Bernoulli's Principle
items.content: For steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow along a streamline, the total mechanical energy per unit volume remains constant.

items.title: Bernoulli Equation
items.content: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant.

items.title: Bernoulli Energy Terms
items.content: P is pressure energy per unit volume, ½ρv² is kinetic energy per unit volume, and ρgh is gravitational potential energy per unit volume.

items.title: Torricelli's Law
items.content: The speed of efflux of a liquid through a small orifice at depth h below the free surface is v = √(2gh), under ideal-flow conditions.

items.title: Efflux
items.content: Efflux is the outflow of a liquid through a small opening in a container.

items.title: Dynamic Pressure
items.content: Dynamic pressure associated with fluid speed v is ½ρv².

items.title: Surface Tension
items.content: Surface tension is the tangential force per unit length acting at a liquid surface.

items.title: Surface Tension Formula
items.content: T = F/l, where F is the tangential force acting normally to a line of length l on the liquid surface.

items.title: SI Unit of Surface Tension
items.content: The SI unit of surface tension is N m⁻¹.

items.title: Dimensions of Surface Tension
items.content: Dimensional formula of surface tension: [M T⁻²].

items.title: Cohesive Force
items.content: Cohesive force is the intermolecular attraction between molecules of the same substance.

items.title: Adhesive Force
items.content: Adhesive force is the intermolecular attraction between molecules of different substances.

items.title: Angle of Contact
items.content: The angle of contact is the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid.

items.title: Concave Meniscus
items.content: A liquid forms a concave meniscus when adhesive attraction between the liquid and container is stronger than cohesive attraction within the liquid.

items.title: Convex Meniscus
items.content: A liquid forms a convex meniscus when cohesive attraction is stronger than adhesive attraction.

items.title: Capillarity
items.content: Capillarity is the rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube due to surface tension and interaction between the liquid and tube.

items.title: Capillary Rise
items.content: h = 2T cosθ/(ρgr), where T is surface tension, θ is angle of contact, ρ is liquid density and r is capillary radius.

items.title: Capillary Rise Result
items.content: Capillary rise increases when surface tension increases and decreases when liquid density or capillary radius increases.

items.title: Excess Pressure in a Liquid Drop
items.content: For a liquid drop of radius R, excess pressure ΔP = 2T/R.

items.title: Excess Pressure in a Soap Bubble
items.content: For a soap bubble of radius R, excess pressure ΔP = 4T/R because the bubble has two liquid surfaces.

items.title: Pressure Difference Across Curved Surface
items.content: Surface tension produces a pressure difference across a curved liquid surface.

items.title: Effect of Temperature on Surface Tension
items.content: Surface tension generally decreases as temperature increases.

items.title: Effect of Impurities on Surface Tension
items.content: Impurities can change the surface tension of a liquid; the effect depends on the nature of the impurity.

items.title: Pressure Force on a Surface
items.content: For uniform pressure P acting normally over area A, force F = PA.

items.title: Hydrostatic Equilibrium
items.content: In a fluid at rest, pressure varies with depth so that the pressure force balances the weight of the fluid.

items.title: Pressure at Same Depth
items.content: For a connected liquid at rest with the same density, pressure is the same at points at the same horizontal depth.

items.title: Pascal Unit Conversion
items.content: 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Also, 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.

items.title: Density of Water
items.content: For standard school-level calculations, density of water is commonly taken as 1000 kg/m³.

items.title: Specific Gravity
items.content: Specific gravity is another name commonly used for relative density: density of substance divided by density of water.

items.title: Buoyancy and Displaced Volume
items.content: For a completely immersed body, V_displaced equals the volume of the body.

items.title: Floating Body Displacement
items.content: For a floating body, only the submerged portion displaces liquid, so the displaced volume is the submerged volume.

items.title: Continuity for Constant Area
items.content: If the cross-sectional area of a fluid pipe is constant, the speed remains constant for steady incompressible flow.

items.title: Continuity Speed-Area Relation
items.content: For steady incompressible flow, v₂/v₁ = A₁/A₂. Fluid speed increases when the cross-sectional area decreases.

items.title: Bernoulli Pressure-Speed Relation
items.content: At the same height in ideal steady flow, P + ½ρv² is constant, so higher fluid speed corresponds to lower pressure.

items.title: Bernoulli Height Effect
items.content: At the same fluid speed, pressure decreases as height increases because the gravitational term ρgh increases.

items.title: Venturi Effect
items.content: In a narrowed region of a flowing fluid, speed increases and static pressure decreases under ideal-flow conditions.

items.title: Viscosity and Fluid Layers
items.content: Viscosity produces internal friction between neighbouring layers moving with different velocities.

items.title: Viscous Force Dependence
items.content: For laminar flow between nearby layers, viscous force increases with the area of contact and velocity gradient.

items.title: Stokes' Law Dependence
items.content: For a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid, viscous force is proportional to radius, viscosity and speed.

items.title: Terminal Velocity Dependence
items.content: Under Stokes' law conditions, terminal velocity of a small sphere is proportional to r² and the density difference, and inversely proportional to viscosity.

items.title: Surface Energy
items.content: Surface energy is the work required to increase the surface area of a liquid by overcoming surface tension.

items.title: Surface Energy of a Liquid Surface
items.content: For a single liquid surface, work done to increase area by ΔA is W = TΔA.

items.title: Fluid Mechanics Quick Relation
items.content: Key Class 11 fluid relations: P = F/A, P = P₀ + ρgh, F_B = ρVg, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant.

items.title: Temperature
items.content: Temperature indicates the degree of hotness or coldness of a body and determines the direction of heat flow.

items.title: Heat
items.content: Heat is energy transferred between bodies because of a temperature difference.

items.title: Thermal Equilibrium
items.content: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when there is no net heat transfer between them.

items.title: Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
items.content: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

items.title: Absolute Zero
items.content: Absolute zero is 0 K, corresponding to −273.15 °C.

items.title: Heat Capacity
items.content: Heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of a body by one degree.

items.title: Heat Capacity Formula
items.content: C = Q/ΔT.

items.title: Specific Heat Capacity
items.content: Specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise unit mass of a substance by one degree.

items.title: Specific Heat Formula
items.content: c = Q/(mΔT).

items.title: Heat Transfer by Temperature Change
items.content: Q = mcΔT.

items.title: SI Unit of Specific Heat
items.content: The SI unit of specific heat capacity is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

items.title: Molar Heat Capacity
items.content: Molar heat capacity is the heat required to raise one mole of a substance by one kelvin.

items.title: Molar Heat Capacity Formula
items.content: Cₘ = Q/(nΔT).

items.title: Latent Heat
items.content: Latent heat is heat absorbed or released during a change of state without a temperature change.

items.title: Latent Heat Formula
items.content: Q = mL.

items.title: Specific Latent Heat
items.content: Specific latent heat is the heat required to change the state of unit mass at constant temperature.

items.title: Thermal Expansion
items.content: Thermal expansion is the increase in dimensions of a substance when its temperature increases.

items.title: Linear Expansion
items.content: ΔL = αL₀ΔT.

items.title: Coefficient of Linear Expansion
items.content: α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT).

items.title: Area Expansion
items.content: ΔA = βA₀ΔT.

items.title: Coefficient of Area Expansion
items.content: β = ΔA/(A₀ΔT).

items.title: Volume Expansion
items.content: ΔV = γV₀ΔT.

items.title: Coefficient of Volume Expansion
items.content: γ = ΔV/(V₀ΔT).

items.title: Expansion Coefficient Relation
items.content: For an isotropic solid, β ≈ 2α and γ ≈ 3α.

items.title: SI Unit of Expansion Coefficients
items.content: The SI unit of α, β and γ is K⁻¹.

items.title: Dimensions of Expansion Coefficient
items.content: Thermal expansion coefficients have dimensions [Θ⁻¹].

items.title: Area Expansion Relation
items.content: For small temperature changes, ΔA/A₀ ≈ 2αΔT.

items.title: Volume Expansion Relation
items.content: For small temperature changes, ΔV/V₀ ≈ 3αΔT.

items.title: Apparent Expansion of Liquid
items.content: Observed liquid expansion depends on both the liquid's expansion and the expansion of its container.

items.title: Real and Apparent Expansion
items.content: Real expansion = apparent expansion + expansion of container.

items.title: Anomalous Expansion of Water
items.content: Water contracts when heated from 0 °C to 4 °C and expands when heated above 4 °C.

items.title: Maximum Density of Water
items.content: Water has maximum density at approximately 4 °C.

items.title: Thermal Stress
items.content: If thermal expansion or contraction is prevented, internal stress can develop.

items.title: Thermal Expansion in Solids
items.content: For a freely expanding solid, thermal strain is approximately proportional to temperature change.

items.title: Bimetallic Strip
items.content: A bimetallic strip bends on heating because its two metals have different expansion coefficients.

items.title: Thermal Expansion of a Hole
items.content: A hole in a uniformly heated solid expands as though the material occupying the hole also expanded.

items.title: Heat Transfer
items.content: Heat can be transferred by conduction, convection or radiation.

items.title: Conduction
items.content: Conduction is heat transfer through a material without bulk motion of the material.

items.title: Thermal Conductivity
items.content: Thermal conductivity measures a material's ability to conduct heat.

items.title: Fourier's Law
items.content: H = kAΔT/L for steady conduction through a uniform slab.

items.title: Heat Current
items.content: H = Q/t.

items.title: Thermal Conductivity Formula
items.content: k = HL/(AΔT).

items.title: SI Unit of Thermal Conductivity
items.content: The SI unit of thermal conductivity is W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

items.title: Dimensions of Thermal Conductivity
items.content: Dimensional formula of thermal conductivity: [M L T⁻³ Θ⁻¹].

items.title: Thermal Resistance
items.content: Rth = L/(kA).

items.title: Heat Current and Thermal Resistance
items.content: H = ΔT/Rth.

items.title: Conductors and Insulators
items.content: Good thermal conductors transfer heat readily, while insulators resist heat flow.

items.title: Convection
items.content: Convection is heat transfer through bulk motion of a fluid.

items.title: Natural Convection
items.content: Natural convection results from density differences produced by temperature differences.

items.title: Forced Convection
items.content: Forced convection occurs when fluid motion is produced or enhanced externally.

items.title: Radiation
items.content: Thermal radiation is energy transfer by electromagnetic waves and does not require a material medium.

items.title: Thermal Radiation
items.content: All bodies above absolute zero emit thermal radiation.

items.title: Black Body
items.content: A black body is an ideal body that absorbs all incident radiation and is an ideal emitter.

items.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Law
items.content: For a black body, emitted power per unit area E = σT⁴.

items.title: Total Black Body Radiation
items.content: P = σAT⁴ for a black body of area A.

items.title: Net Radiation Exchange
items.content: Pnet = σA(T⁴ − T₀⁴) for an ideal radiator exchanging radiation with surroundings.

items.title: Newton's Law of Cooling
items.content: For small temperature differences, rate of cooling is approximately proportional to the temperature difference from surroundings.

items.title: Newton's Cooling Relation
items.content: dT/dt ∝ −(T − Ts).

items.title: Cooling Curve
items.content: A body generally cools faster when its temperature is much higher than its surroundings.

items.title: Wien's Displacement Law
items.content: λmT = b.

items.title: Radiation Power and Temperature
items.content: Black-body radiation power per unit area is proportional to T⁴.

items.title: Radiation and Surface Nature
items.content: Thermal radiation depends on the nature and temperature of the surface.

items.title: Absorptivity
items.content: Absorptivity is the fraction of incident radiation absorbed by a surface.

items.title: Emissivity
items.content: Emissivity measures how effectively a real surface emits radiation compared with a black body at the same temperature.

items.title: Good Absorber and Good Emitter
items.content: A good absorber of thermal radiation is generally also a good emitter.

items.title: Kirchhoff's Law of Thermal Radiation
items.content: At thermal equilibrium, the ratio of emissive power to absorptive power is the same for bodies at a given temperature.

items.title: Thermal Equilibrium and Radiation
items.content: At thermal equilibrium, absorption and emission of radiation balance on average.

items.title: Heat Capacity and Specific Heat Relation
items.content: C = mc.

items.title: Calorimetry Principle
items.content: In an isolated calorimetry system, heat lost by hotter bodies equals heat gained by colder bodies.

items.title: Calorimetry Equation
items.content: Heat lost = heat gained, for an ideal isolated calorimetry system.

items.title: Phase Change Temperature
items.content: During a phase change of a pure substance at constant pressure, temperature remains constant.

items.title: Specific Heat During Heating
items.content: Without a phase change, heat required depends on mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change.

items.title: Heat and Work as Energy Transfer
items.content: Heat and work are two modes of transferring energy between a system and its surroundings.

items.title: Thermal Properties Quick Reference
items.content: Key relations: Q = mcΔT, Q = mL, ΔL = αL₀ΔT, ΔA = βA₀ΔT, ΔV = γV₀ΔT, H = kAΔT/L, P = σAT⁴, λmT = b.

items.title: Thermodynamic System
items.content: A thermodynamic system is a specified part of the universe chosen for study, separated from its surroundings by a boundary.

items.title: Surroundings
items.content: Everything outside the thermodynamic system that can interact with it is called its surroundings.

items.title: Boundary of a System
items.content: The boundary separates a thermodynamic system from its surroundings and may allow transfer of energy or matter.

items.title: Open System
items.content: An open system can exchange both energy and matter with its surroundings.

items.title: Closed System
items.content: A closed system can exchange energy but not matter with its surroundings.

items.title: Isolated System
items.content: An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.

items.title: Thermodynamic State
items.content: The state of a thermodynamic system is specified by macroscopic variables such as pressure, volume and temperature.

items.title: State Variables
items.content: State variables are physical quantities whose values depend only on the state of a system, not on the path taken.

items.title: Path Function
items.content: A path function depends on the process or path followed between two states.

items.title: Thermodynamic Equilibrium
items.content: A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when its macroscopic properties do not change with time and thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium conditions are satisfied.

items.title: Thermal Equilibrium
items.content: Thermal equilibrium means there is no net heat transfer within the system or between systems in contact.

items.title: Mechanical Equilibrium
items.content: Mechanical equilibrium exists when there is no unbalanced pressure force or mechanical tendency to change the state.

items.title: Thermodynamic Process
items.content: A thermodynamic process is a change of a system from one equilibrium state to another.

items.title: Quasi-Static Process
items.content: A quasi-static process proceeds through a continuous sequence of states very close to equilibrium.

items.title: Isothermal Process
items.content: An isothermal process occurs at constant temperature.

items.title: Isobaric Process
items.content: An isobaric process occurs at constant pressure.

items.title: Isochoric Process
items.content: An isochoric process occurs at constant volume.

items.title: Adiabatic Process
items.content: An adiabatic process occurs without heat exchange between the system and surroundings.

items.title: Cyclic Process
items.content: A cyclic process returns the system to its initial thermodynamic state.

items.title: Equation of State of an Ideal Gas
items.content: PV = nRT.

items.title: Universal Gas Constant
items.content: R ≈ 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

items.title: Ideal Gas Equation in Terms of Number of Molecules
items.content: PV = NkBT.

items.title: Boltzmann Constant
items.content: kB = R/NA.

items.title: Work Done by a Gas
items.content: For a quasistatic process, W = ∫P dV.

items.title: Work Done at Constant Pressure
items.content: W = P(V₂ − V₁).

items.title: Work Sign Convention
items.content: In the convention commonly used in NCERT thermodynamics, work done by the system is taken as positive and work done on the system as negative.

items.title: Expansion Work
items.content: During expansion, ΔV > 0 and the work done by the gas is positive under the NCERT sign convention.

items.title: Compression Work
items.content: During compression, ΔV < 0 and the work done by the gas is negative under the NCERT sign convention.

items.title: Work from a P-V Diagram
items.content: The work done by a gas in a quasistatic process equals the area under the process curve on a pressure-volume diagram.

items.title: Work in a Cyclic Process
items.content: For a cyclic process, net work is represented by the area enclosed by the cycle on a P-V diagram.

items.title: Heat
items.content: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.

items.title: Internal Energy
items.content: Internal energy is the total microscopic energy associated with the random molecular motion and interactions within a system.

items.title: Internal Energy of an Ideal Gas
items.content: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature.

items.title: Change in Internal Energy
items.content: ΔU = U₂ − U₁.

items.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
items.content: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW, where ΔW is work done by the system.

items.title: First Law Energy Interpretation
