items.content: The first law expresses conservation of energy for thermodynamic processes.

items.title: Heat Supplied to a System
items.content: Energy supplied as heat may increase internal energy and/or be used for work done by the system.

items.title: Heat Capacity at Constant Volume
items.content: CV = (ΔQ/ΔT)V.

items.title: Heat Capacity at Constant Pressure
items.content: CP = (ΔQ/ΔT)P.

items.title: Relation Between CP and CV
items.content: For one mole of an ideal gas, CP − CV = R.

items.title: Ratio of Heat Capacities
items.content: γ = CP/CV.

items.title: Molar Heat Capacity at Constant Volume for a Monatomic Ideal Gas
Molar Heat Capacity at Constant Pressure for a Monatomic Ideal Gas
γ for a Monatomic Ideal Gas
items.content: For a monatomic ideal gas, γ = 5/3.

items.title: Molar Heat Capacity at Constant Volume for a Diatomic Ideal Gas
items.content: In the classical room-temperature model, CV = 5R/2.

items.title: Molar Heat Capacity at Constant Pressure for a Diatomic Ideal Gas
items.content: In the classical room-temperature model, CP = 7R/2.

items.title: γ for a Diatomic Ideal Gas
items.content: In the classical room-temperature model, γ = 7/5.

items.title: Isothermal Ideal Gas Relation
items.content: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, PV = constant.

items.title: Isothermal Work
items.content: For reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).

items.title: Isothermal Internal Energy Change
items.content: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, ΔU = 0.

items.title: Isothermal Heat Transfer
items.content: For an ideal gas in a reversible isothermal process, Q = W.

items.title: Adiabatic Condition
items.content: For an adiabatic process, Q = 0.

items.title: Adiabatic Ideal Gas Relation
items.content: For a reversible adiabatic process, PV^γ = constant.

items.title: Adiabatic Temperature-Volume Relation
items.content: For a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process, TV^(γ−1) = constant.

items.title: Adiabatic Pressure-Temperature Relation
items.content: For a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process, T^γ/P^(γ−1) = constant.

items.title: Adiabatic Work
items.content: For an ideal gas undergoing a reversible adiabatic process, W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1).

items.title: Adiabatic Expansion
items.content: In an adiabatic expansion, the gas does work without receiving heat, so its internal energy and temperature decrease.

items.title: Adiabatic Compression
items.content: In an adiabatic compression, work is done on the gas and its internal energy and temperature increase.

items.title: Isochoric Process Heat
items.content: For a constant-volume process, W = 0, so Q = ΔU.

items.title: Isobaric Process Work
items.content: For a constant-pressure process, W = PΔV.

items.title: Isobaric Process Heat
items.content: At constant pressure, QP = ΔU + PΔV.

items.title: Cyclic Process Internal Energy
items.content: For a complete cycle, the system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0.

items.title: Cyclic Process Heat and Work
items.content: For a complete cycle, net heat supplied equals net work done by the system.

items.title: Reversible Process
items.content: A reversible process is an ideal process that can be reversed by an infinitesimal change, restoring both system and surroundings to their original states.

items.title: Irreversible Process
items.content: An irreversible process cannot be exactly reversed so that both system and surroundings return to their original states.

items.title: Thermal Reservoir
items.content: A thermal reservoir is an ideal body that can exchange heat while maintaining essentially constant temperature.

items.title: Heat Engine
items.content: A heat engine is a device that converts part of the heat absorbed from a high-temperature reservoir into work while rejecting some heat to a low-temperature reservoir.

items.title: Heat Engine Efficiency
items.content: η = W/QH = 1 − QC/QH.

items.title: Efficiency Limitation
items.content: The efficiency of a heat engine is always less than 100% for a cyclic engine operating between finite temperature reservoirs.

items.title: Refrigerator
items.content: A refrigerator is a device that transfers heat from a low-temperature region to a high-temperature region using external work.

items.title: Coefficient of Performance of Refrigerator
items.content: COPR = QC/W.

items.title: Heat Pump
items.content: A heat pump transfers heat from a low-temperature reservoir to a high-temperature reservoir using external work.

items.title: Coefficient of Performance of Heat Pump
items.content: COPHP = QH/W.

items.title: COP Relation
items.content: For an ideal refrigerator and heat pump operating between the same reservoirs, COPHP = COPR + 1.

items.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics
items.content: The second law determines the direction of spontaneous thermodynamic processes and places limits on the conversion of heat into work.

items.title: Kelvin-Planck Statement
items.content: No cyclic heat engine can convert all the heat absorbed from a single reservoir completely into work.

items.title: Clausius Statement
items.content: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter body without external work.

items.title: Carnot Engine
items.content: A Carnot engine is an ideal reversible heat engine operating between two temperatures through two isothermal and two adiabatic processes.

items.title: Carnot Efficiency
items.content: For a Carnot engine, η = 1 − TC/TH, with temperatures measured in kelvin.

items.title: Carnot Efficiency Limitation
items.content: For fixed source and sink temperatures, no heat engine operating between them can have efficiency greater than that of a reversible Carnot engine.

items.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases
items.content: Kinetic theory explains the macroscopic properties of gases in terms of the motion and interactions of their microscopic particles.

items.title: Ideal Gas
items.content: An ideal gas is a model gas whose molecules are treated as point particles with negligible volume and negligible intermolecular forces except during collisions.

items.title: Kinetic Theory Assumption: Molecular Motion
items.content: Gas molecules are in continuous random motion.

items.title: Kinetic Theory Assumption: Molecular Size
items.content: The individual volume of gas molecules is assumed negligible compared with the volume occupied by the gas.

items.title: Kinetic Theory Assumption: Intermolecular Force
items.content: In an ideal gas, intermolecular forces are neglected except during collisions.

items.title: Kinetic Theory Assumption: Collisions
items.content: Molecular collisions with one another and with container walls are treated as elastic.

items.title: Elastic Collision
items.content: An elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy and momentum.

items.title: Random Motion
items.content: Random molecular motion means the molecules move in different directions with no preferred direction in equilibrium.

items.title: Molecular Number Density
items.content: Number density is the number of molecules per unit volume.

items.title: Number Density Formula
items.content: Number density = N/V.

items.title: Pressure of an Ideal Gas
items.content: Gas pressure arises from the impacts of molecules on the walls of the container.

items.title: Pressure-Molecular Motion Relation
items.content: P = (1/3)ρc_rms².

items.title: Mass Density of Gas
items.content: ρ = Nm/V, where N is the number of molecules, m is molecular mass and V is volume.

items.title: Pressure in Terms of Molecular Mass
items.content: P = Nm c_rms²/(3V).

items.title: Mean Square Speed
items.content: Mean square speed is the average of the squares of the molecular speeds.

items.title: RMS Speed
items.content: Root mean square speed is the square root of the mean of the squares of molecular speeds.

items.title: RMS Speed Formula
items.content: c_rms = √⟨c²⟩.

items.title: RMS Speed from Pressure
items.content: c_rms = √(3P/ρ).

items.title: RMS Speed of Ideal Gas
items.content: c_rms = √(3RT/M).

items.title: Molar Mass
items.content: Molar mass M is the mass of one mole of a substance.

items.title: Avogadro Constant
items.content: NA ≈ 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

items.title: Number of Molecules
items.content: N = nNA.

items.title: Molecular Mass and Molar Mass
items.content: M = mNA, where m is the mass of one molecule.

items.title: Ideal Gas Equation
items.content: PV = nRT.

items.title: Ideal Gas Equation in Molecular Form
items.content: PV = NkBT.

items.title: Boltzmann Constant
items.content: kB = R/NA.

items.title: Gas Constant and Boltzmann Constant
items.content: R = NAkB.

items.title: Temperature in Kinetic Theory
items.content: Absolute temperature is directly related to the average translational kinetic energy of gas molecules.

items.title: Average Translational Kinetic Energy
items.content: Average translational kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2)kBT.

items.title: Total Translational Kinetic Energy
items.content: Total translational kinetic energy of N molecules = (3/2)NkBT.

items.title: Total Translational Kinetic Energy in Moles
items.content: Total translational kinetic energy = (3/2)nRT.

items.title: Temperature-Kinetic Energy Relation
items.content: At a given temperature, the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is the same for all ideal gases.

items.title: Average Kinetic Energy and Temperature
items.content: kBT = (2/3) × average translational kinetic energy per molecule.

items.title: Pressure in Terms of Temperature
items.content: PV = (2/3) × total translational kinetic energy.

items.title: RMS Speed and Temperature
items.content: For a fixed gas, c_rms ∝ √T.

items.title: RMS Speed and Molar Mass
items.content: At fixed temperature, c_rms ∝ 1/√M.

items.title: RMS Speed Comparison
items.content: For two gases at the same temperature, c_rms,1/c_rms,2 = √(M₂/M₁).

items.title: Degrees of Freedom
items.content: The degrees of freedom of a molecule are the independent ways in which it can possess energy.

items.title: Translational Degrees of Freedom
items.content: A molecule moving freely in three-dimensional space has three translational degrees of freedom.

items.title: Monatomic Gas Degrees of Freedom
items.content: A monatomic ideal gas has three translational degrees of freedom in the basic model.

items.title: Diatomic Gas Degrees of Freedom
items.content: At ordinary temperatures, a diatomic molecule is commonly treated as having translational and rotational degrees of freedom; vibrational modes may become active at higher temperatures.

items.title: Law of Equipartition of Energy
items.content: For each quadratic degree of freedom, the average energy contribution per molecule is (1/2)kBT.

items.title: Energy Per Degree of Freedom
items.content: Average energy per quadratic degree of freedom = (1/2)kBT.

items.title: Monatomic Gas Internal Energy
items.content: For n moles of a monatomic ideal gas, U = (3/2)nRT.

items.title: Diatomic Gas Internal Energy
items.content: In the ordinary-temperature classical model with five active degrees of freedom, U = (5/2)nRT.

items.title: Internal Energy and Degrees of Freedom
items.content: For f active quadratic degrees of freedom, U = (f/2)nRT.

items.title: Molar Internal Energy
items.content: For f active quadratic degrees of freedom, U/n = (f/2)RT.

items.title: Specific Heat and Degrees of Freedom
items.content: For an ideal gas with f active degrees of freedom, CV = (f/2)R.

items.title: Constant Pressure Molar Heat Capacity
items.content: For an ideal gas, CP = CV + R.

items.title: Heat Capacity Difference
items.content: CP − CV = R for one mole of an ideal gas.

items.title: Heat Capacity Ratio
items.content: γ = CP/CV.

items.title: Monatomic Gas CV
items.content: For a monatomic ideal gas, CV = (3/2)R.

items.title: Monatomic Gas CP
items.content: For a monatomic ideal gas, CP = (5/2)R.

items.title: Monatomic Gas Gamma
items.content: For a monatomic ideal gas, γ = 5/3.

items.title: Diatomic Gas CV
items.content: In the classical ordinary-temperature model, CV = (5/2)R.

items.title: Diatomic Gas CP
items.content: In the classical ordinary-temperature model, CP = (7/2)R.

items.title: Diatomic Gas Gamma
items.content: In the classical ordinary-temperature model, γ = 7/5.

items.title: Equipartition and Heat Capacity
items.content: Increasing the number of active energy degrees of freedom increases the heat capacity of a gas.

items.title: Vibrational Degrees of Freedom
items.content: Vibrational modes can become active at sufficiently high temperatures and contribute additional energy degrees of freedom.

items.title: Mean Free Path
items.content: Mean free path is the average distance travelled by a gas molecule between successive collisions.

items.title: Mean Free Path Symbol
items.content: Mean free path is commonly represented by λ.

items.title: Collision Frequency
items.content: Collision frequency is the average number of molecular collisions experienced by a molecule per unit time.

items.title: Mean Free Path Dependence
items.content: For a dilute gas, mean free path decreases as molecular number density increases.

items.title: Mean Free Path and Pressure
items.content: At fixed temperature, increasing pressure generally decreases the mean free path of gas molecules.

items.title: Mean Free Path and Temperature
items.content: For a gas at fixed pressure, increasing temperature tends to increase the mean free path in the simple kinetic-theory model.

items.title: Gas Molecule Speed Distribution
items.content: Gas molecules in thermal equilibrium have a distribution of speeds rather than one common speed.

items.title: Most Probable Speed
items.content: The most probable speed is the speed corresponding to the maximum of the molecular speed distribution.

items.title: Average Speed
items.content: Average speed is the arithmetic mean of the speeds of the gas molecules.

items.title: RMS Speed vs Average Speed
items.content: For a gas in thermal equilibrium, the RMS speed is greater than the average speed, which is greater than the most probable speed.

items.title: Speed Ordering
items.content: c_rms > c_avg > c_mp for a gas in thermal equilibrium.

items.title: Temperature Effect on Speed Distribution
items.content: Increasing temperature shifts the molecular speed distribution toward higher speeds and broadens it.

items.title: Gas Pressure and Temperature
items.content: For a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature.

items.title: Gas Volume and Temperature
items.content: For a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature.

items.title: Boyle's Law
items.content: For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, PV = constant.

items.title: Charles' Law
items.content: For a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, V/T = constant.

items.title: Pressure Law
items.content: For a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, P/T = constant.

items.title: Absolute Zero
items.content: Absolute zero is the theoretical lower limit of temperature, corresponding to 0 K.

items.title: Periodic Motion
items.content: A motion that repeats itself at regular intervals of time is called periodic motion.

items.title: Time Period
items.content: Time period T is the time taken by a periodically moving particle to complete one cycle.

items.title: Frequency
items.content: Frequency f is the number of complete oscillations made per unit time.

items.title: Angular Frequency
items.content: ω = 2πf = 2π/T.

items.title: Oscillation
items.content: An oscillation is a to-and-fro periodic motion about a mean or equilibrium position.

items.title: Mean Position
items.content: The mean position is the equilibrium position about which an oscillator moves.

items.title: Amplitude
items.content: Amplitude A is the maximum displacement of an oscillating particle from its mean position.

items.title: Displacement in SHM
items.content: x = A cos(ωt + φ), for a suitable choice of phase.

items.title: Phase
items.content: The phase specifies the state of oscillation of a particle at a given instant.

items.title: Initial Phase
items.content: The constant φ in a harmonic displacement equation represents the initial phase.

items.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
items.content: A particle executes SHM when its acceleration is directly proportional to its displacement from the mean position and directed towards the mean position.

items.title: SHM Acceleration Condition
items.content: a = −ω²x.

items.title: Restoring Acceleration
items.content: The negative sign in a = −ω²x indicates that acceleration is directed opposite to displacement.

items.title: Restoring Force in SHM
items.content: F = −kx.

items.title: Force-Acceleration Relation
items.content: F = ma.

items.title: SHM Force and Angular Frequency
items.content: k = mω².

items.title: Velocity in SHM
items.content: v = −Aω sin(ωt + φ) for x = A cos(ωt + φ).

items.title: Acceleration in SHM
items.content: a = −Aω² cos(ωt + φ) = −ω²x.

items.title: Maximum Displacement
items.content: Maximum displacement in SHM is A.

items.title: Maximum Velocity
items.content: v_max = Aω.

items.title: Maximum Acceleration
items.content: a_max = Aω².

items.title: Velocity-Displacement Relation in SHM
items.content: v² = ω²(A² − x²).

items.title: Acceleration-Displacement Relation
items.content: a = −ω²x.

items.title: Velocity at Mean Position
items.content: At the mean position x = 0, the speed in SHM is maximum: v = Aω.

items.title: Acceleration at Mean Position
items.content: At the mean position x = 0, acceleration in SHM is zero.

items.title: Velocity at Extreme Position
items.content: At x = ±A, velocity is zero.

items.title: Acceleration at Extreme Position
items.content: At x = ±A, acceleration has maximum magnitude Aω².

items.title: Phase Difference of Displacement and Velocity
items.content: In SHM, velocity differs in phase from displacement by π/2.

items.title: Phase Difference of Displacement and Acceleration
items.content: In SHM, acceleration differs in phase from displacement by π.

items.title: Phase Difference of Velocity and Acceleration
items.content: In SHM, velocity and acceleration differ in phase by π/2.

items.title: SHM Equation from Differential Form
items.content: d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0.

items.title: General SHM Solution
items.content: x = A cos(ωt + φ) or equivalently x = A sin(ωt + φ).

items.title: Period from Angular Frequency
items.content: T = 2π/ω.

items.title: Energy in SHM
items.content: The total mechanical energy of an ideal SHM oscillator remains constant when no dissipative force acts.

items.title: Total Energy in SHM
items.content: E = (1/2)kA² = (1/2)mω²A².

items.title: Energy at Mean Position
items.content: At x = 0, kinetic energy is maximum and potential energy is minimum.

items.title: Energy at Extreme Position
items.content: At x = ±A, potential energy is maximum and kinetic energy is zero.

items.title: Maximum Kinetic Energy
items.content: K_max = (1/2)kA² = (1/2)mω²A².

items.title: Maximum Potential Energy
items.content: U_max = (1/2)kA².

items.title: Energy Distribution in SHM
items.content: K/E = 1 − x²/A² and U/E = x²/A².

items.title: Equal Kinetic and Potential Energy
items.content: K = U when |x| = A/√2.

items.title: Energy Dependence on Amplitude
items.content: For fixed angular frequency and mass, total energy is proportional to A².

items.title: Spring-Mass Oscillator
items.content: A mass attached to an ideal spring can execute SHM when the restoring force obeys Hooke's law.

items.title: Spring Stiffness Effect
items.content: For a given mass, increasing spring constant k decreases the time period.

items.title: Mass Effect on Spring Period
items.content: For a given spring, increasing mass m increases the time period.

items.title: Amplitude Effect on Ideal Spring Period
items.content: For ideal SHM of a spring-mass system, the time period is independent of amplitude.

items.title: Simple Pendulum
items.content: A simple pendulum consists of a small bob suspended by a light inextensible string from a fixed support.

items.title: Small-Angle Approximation
items.content: For small angular displacement measured in radians, sin θ ≈ θ.

items.title: Simple Pendulum SHM Condition
items.content: For small angular displacements, the motion of a simple pendulum approximates SHM.

items.title: Simple Pendulum Angular Frequency
items.content: ω = √(g/l) for small oscillations.

items.title: Simple Pendulum Time Period
items.content: T = 2π√(l/g) for small oscillations.

items.title: Simple Pendulum Frequency
items.content: f = (1/2π)√(g/l) for small oscillations.

items.title: Pendulum Length Effect
items.content: The time period of a simple pendulum is proportional to √l.

items.title: Gravity Effect on Pendulum Period
items.content: The time period of a simple pendulum is proportional to 1/√g.

items.title: Pendulum Mass Effect
items.content: For small oscillations, the time period of an ideal simple pendulum is independent of bob mass.

items.title: Pendulum Amplitude Effect
items.content: For sufficiently small oscillations, the time period is approximately independent of amplitude.

items.title: SHM and Circular Motion
items.content: Uniform circular motion projected on any diameter produces simple harmonic motion.

items.title: Reference Circle Radius
items.content: For the circular-motion representation of SHM, the radius of the reference circle equals the SHM amplitude.

items.title: Angular Speed in Reference Circle
items.content: The angular speed of the reference circular motion equals the angular frequency ω of SHM.

items.title: SHM at t = 0
items.content: If x = A cos(ωt), then at t = 0 the particle starts at x = A with zero velocity.

items.title: SHM Starting at Mean Position
items.content: If x = A sin(ωt), then at t = 0 the particle starts at the mean position with maximum positive velocity.

items.title: One Complete Oscillation
items.content: One complete SHM cycle corresponds to a phase change of 2π radians.

items.title: Half Oscillation
items.content: A half cycle corresponds to a phase change of π radians.

items.title: Quarter Oscillation
items.content: A quarter cycle corresponds to a phase change of π/2 radians.

items.title: Time from Mean to Extreme
items.content: For SHM, the time taken to move from the mean position to an extreme position is T/4.

items.title: Time Between Extreme Positions
items.content: The time taken to move from one extreme position to the opposite extreme is T/2.

items.title: Time from Extreme to Mean
items.content: The time taken to move from an extreme position to the mean position is T/4.

items.title: Oscillation Graphs
items.content: Displacement, velocity and acceleration in SHM vary sinusoidally with time.

items.title: Displacement-Amplitude Limit
items.content: The displacement of an SHM particle always satisfies |x| ≤ A.

items.title: Speed in SHM
items.content: Speed = ω√(A² − x²).

items.title: Restoring Force and Displacement Graph
items.content: For SHM, the restoring force-displacement graph is a straight line through the origin with negative slope −k.

items.title: SHM Differential Equation
items.content: The equation d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0 is the standard differential equation of SHM.

items.title: Oscillations Quick Reference
items.content: Core SHM relations: x=A cos(ωt+φ), a=−ω²x, v²=ω²(A²−x²), E=(1/2)mω²A², T_spring=2π√(m/k), T_pendulum=2π√(l/g).

items.title: Wave
items.content: A wave is a disturbance that propagates through space and time, transferring energy without net transport of matter.

items.title: Mechanical Wave
items.content: A mechanical wave requires a material medium for propagation.

items.title: Transverse Wave
items.content: In a transverse wave, particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

items.title: Longitudinal Wave
items.content: In a longitudinal wave, particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.

items.title: Pulse
items.content: A pulse is a single non-repetitive disturbance travelling through a medium.

items.title: Periodic Wave
items.content: A periodic wave is a wave produced by a disturbance that repeats regularly with time.

items.title: Amplitude of Wave
items.content: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its mean position.

items.title: Wavelength
items.content: Wavelength λ is the distance between two nearest particles that are in the same phase.

items.title: Frequency of Wave
items.content: Frequency f is the number of complete wave cycles passing a fixed point per unit time.

items.title: Time Period of Wave
items.content: Time period T is the time taken for one complete cycle of oscillation.

items.title: Wave Speed
items.content: v = λf = λ/T.

items.title: Angular Frequency of Wave
items.content: ω = 2πf = 2π/T.

items.title: Wave Number
items.content: k = 2π/λ.

items.title: Angular Frequency-Wave Number Relation
items.content: v = ω/k.

items.title: Phase
items.content: The phase of a particle describes the state of its oscillation at a given instant.

items.title: Phase Difference
items.content: For separation Δx along a progressive wave, phase difference Δφ = 2πΔx/λ.

items.title: Phase Difference by Time
items.content: For time difference Δt at a fixed position, Δφ = 2πΔt/T.

items.title: In-Phase Points
items.content: Two points are in phase when they have the same displacement and velocity state at the same instant.

items.title: Phase Difference for Same Phase
items.content: Points separated by nλ have phase difference 2nπ and are in phase.

items.title: Phase Difference for Opposite Phase
items.content: Points separated by an odd multiple of λ/2 have phase difference π modulo 2π.

items.title: Wave Equation
items.content: A sinusoidal progressive wave can be written as y(x,t) = A sin(kx − ωt + φ).

items.title: Wave Travelling in Positive x Direction
items.content: A wave travelling in the +x direction can be represented by y = A sin(kx − ωt + φ).

items.title: Wave Travelling in Negative x Direction
items.content: A wave travelling in the −x direction can be represented by y = A sin(kx + ωt + φ).

items.title: Progressive Wave
items.content: A progressive wave travels through the medium and carries energy from one region to another.

items.title: Stationary Wave
items.content: A stationary wave is formed by the superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions.

items.title: Superposition Principle
items.content: When waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.

items.title: Interference
items.content: Interference is the redistribution of intensity produced by superposition of waves.

items.title: Constructive Interference
items.content: Constructive interference occurs when waves combine to produce maximum resultant amplitude.

items.title: Destructive Interference
items.content: Destructive interference occurs when waves combine to reduce the resultant amplitude.

items.title: Reflection of Waves
items.content: Reflection is the change in direction of a wave when it encounters a boundary and returns into the original medium.

items.title: Refraction of Waves
items.content: Refraction is the change in wave propagation direction caused by a change in wave speed on entering another medium.

items.title: Diffraction
items.content: Diffraction is the spreading or bending of waves around obstacles or through openings.

items.title: Particle Velocity in Wave
items.content: The velocity of a medium particle oscillating in a wave is generally different from the propagation speed of the wave.

items.title: Wave Velocity vs Particle Velocity
items.content: Wave velocity describes propagation of the disturbance, whereas particle velocity describes motion of an individual medium particle.

items.title: Transverse Wave Example
items.content: Waves on a stretched string are a common example of transverse mechanical waves.

items.title: Longitudinal Wave Example
items.content: Sound waves in air are longitudinal mechanical waves.

items.title: Compression
items.content: A compression in a longitudinal wave is a region where particles are closer together and pressure or density is relatively high.

items.title: Rarefaction
items.content: A rarefaction is a region in a longitudinal wave where particles are farther apart and pressure or density is relatively low.

items.title: Longitudinal Wavelength
items.content: The distance between two successive compressions or two successive rarefactions equals one wavelength λ.

items.title: Transverse Wavelength
items.content: The distance between two successive crests or two successive troughs equals one wavelength λ.

items.title: Crest
items.content: A crest is the point of maximum positive displacement in a transverse wave.

items.title: Trough
items.content: A trough is the point of maximum negative displacement in a transverse wave.

items.title: Sound Wave
items.content: Sound is a mechanical wave that requires a material medium for propagation.

items.title: Sound in Vacuum
items.content: Sound cannot propagate through vacuum because it requires a material medium.

items.title: Speed of Sound in Medium
items.content: The speed of sound depends on the elastic and inertial properties of the medium.

items.title: Speed of Sound in Fluid
items.content: For an ideal fluid, v = √(B/ρ), where B is bulk modulus and ρ is density.

items.title: Speed of Sound in Gas
items.content: For an ideal gas, v = √(γP/ρ).

items.title: Gas Sound Speed Using Temperature
items.content: For an ideal gas, v = √(γRT/M).

items.title: Newton's Formula for Sound Speed
items.content: Newton's early expression used v = √(P/ρ) for gases but did not account for adiabatic changes.

items.title: Laplace Correction
items.content: Laplace corrected Newton's result by using the adiabatic relation, giving v = √(γP/ρ).

items.title: Speed of Sound Temperature Trend
items.content: For a given gas under suitable conditions, the speed of sound increases as temperature increases.

items.title: Speed of Sound in Solids
items.content: Sound generally travels faster in solids because of their high elastic stiffness.

items.title: Sound Speed and Frequency
items.content: For a fixed medium, wave speed is determined by medium properties and is not changed simply by changing frequency.

items.title: Wavelength-Frequency Relation for Sound
items.content: For sound in a fixed medium, λ = v/f.

items.title: Audible Frequency Range
items.content: For humans, the commonly quoted audible frequency range is approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

items.title: Infrasonic Sound
items.content: Sound with frequency below about 20 Hz is called infrasonic.

items.title: Ultrasonic Sound
items.content: Sound with frequency above about 20 kHz is called ultrasonic.

items.title: Organ Pipe
items.content: An organ pipe is an air column that can support standing longitudinal waves and resonant modes.

items.title: Open Pipe
items.content: An ideal open pipe has displacement antinodes at both open ends.

items.title: Closed Pipe
items.content: An ideal pipe closed at one end has a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.

items.title: Open Pipe Fundamental
items.content: For an ideal open pipe of length L, the fundamental wavelength is λ₁ = 2L.

items.title: Open Pipe Fundamental Frequency
items.content: For an ideal open pipe, f₁ = v/(2L).

items.title: Open Pipe Harmonics
items.content: For an ideal open pipe, f_n = nv/(2L), where n = 1, 2, 3, ...

items.title: Closed Pipe Fundamental
items.content: For an ideal pipe closed at one end, the fundamental wavelength is λ₁ = 4L.

items.title: Closed Pipe Fundamental Frequency
items.content: For an ideal closed pipe, f₁ = v/(4L).

items.title: Closed Pipe Harmonics
items.content: For an ideal closed pipe, f_n = (2n−1)v/(4L), where n = 1, 2, 3, ...

items.title: Closed Pipe Harmonic Pattern
items.content: An ideal closed pipe supports only odd harmonics: 1st, 3rd, 5th, and so on.

items.title: Beats
items.content: Beats are periodic variations in sound intensity produced by superposition of waves having slightly different frequencies.

items.title: Beat Frequency
items.content: f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|.

items.title: Beat Period
items.content: T_beat = 1/f_beat.

items.title: Resonance
items.content: Resonance occurs when a system is driven at or near its natural frequency, producing a large amplitude response.

items.title: Natural Frequency
items.content: Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system oscillates freely after being disturbed.

items.title: Stationary Wave Nodes
items.content: A node is a point in a stationary wave where the displacement amplitude is always zero.

items.title: Stationary Wave Antinodes
items.content: An antinode is a point in a stationary wave where the displacement amplitude is maximum.

items.title: Node-Antinode Separation
items.content: The distance between a node and its nearest antinode is λ/4.

items.title: Adjacent Node Separation
items.content: The distance between two successive nodes is λ/2.

items.title: Adjacent Antinode Separation
items.content: The distance between two successive antinodes is λ/2.

items.title: Stationary Wave Energy
items.content: An ideal stationary wave does not transport net energy along the medium, although particles oscillate.

items.title: Wave Quick Reference
items.content: Core wave relations: v=λf, ω=2πf, k=2π/λ, v=ω/k, Δφ=2πΔx/λ, f_beat=|f₁−f₂|.

items.title: Matter
items.content: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.

items.title: Law of Conservation of Mass
items.content: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; total mass remains conserved.

items.title: Law of Definite Proportions
items.content: A pure chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass.

items.title: Law of Multiple Proportions
items.content: When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratios.

items.title: Dalton's Atomic Theory
items.content: Matter is composed of atoms, atoms of an element have characteristic properties, and chemical reactions involve rearrangement of atoms.

items.title: Atomic Mass
items.content: Atomic mass is the relative mass of an atom compared with 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

items.title: Atomic Mass Unit
items.content: One atomic mass unit, u, is defined as 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

items.title: Molecular Mass
items.content: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms present in one molecule.

items.title: Formula Mass
items.content: Formula mass is the sum of atomic masses represented by a chemical formula, especially for ionic compounds.

items.title: Molar Mass
items.content: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, expressed commonly in g mol⁻¹.

items.title: Mole
items.content: One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities.

items.title: Number of Moles from Number of Particles
items.content: n = N/N_A.

items.title: Number of Particles from Moles
items.content: N = nN_A.

items.title: Moles from Given Mass
items.content: n = m/M, where m is given mass and M is molar mass.

items.title: Mass from Moles
items.content: m = nM.

items.title: Molar Mass from Mass and Moles
items.content: M = m/n.

items.title: Moles of Gas from Volume
items.content: At a specified temperature and pressure, n = V/V_m when V_m is the molar volume under those conditions.

items.title: Molar Volume at STP
items.content: For the commonly used NCERT STP convention, one mole of an ideal gas occupies approximately 22.4 L at 273.15 K and 1 atm.

items.title: Percentage Composition
items.content: Mass percentage of an element = (mass of the element in one mole of compound / molar mass of compound) × 100.

items.title: Mass Percentage
items.content: Mass percentage = (mass of component / total mass of sample) × 100.

items.title: Mole Fraction
items.content: Mole fraction of component i, x_i = n_i / Σn.

items.title: Sum of Mole Fractions
items.content: For a mixture, Σx_i = 1.

items.title: Molarity
items.content: Molarity is the number of moles of solute present per litre of solution.

items.title: Molarity Formula
items.content: M = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres.

items.title: Molarity from Mass
items.content: M = m/(M_molar × V), when V is in litres.

items.title: Molality
items.content: Molality is the number of moles of solute present per kilogram of solvent.

items.title: Molality Formula
items.content: m = moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg.

items.title: Mass Percentage of Solution
items.content: Mass percentage = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100.

items.title: Parts Per Million
items.content: ppm = (number of parts of component / total number of parts) × 10⁶.

items.title: Parts Per Billion
items.content: ppb = (number of parts of component / total number of parts) × 10⁹.

items.title: Dilution Relation
items.content: For dilution of the same solute, M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

items.title: Empirical Formula
items.content: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of different elements in a compound.

items.title: Molecular Formula
items.content: The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.

items.title: Molecular Formula from Empirical Formula
items.content: Molecular formula = (Empirical formula) × n, where n = molar mass / empirical formula mass.

items.title: Empirical Formula Mass
items.content: Empirical formula mass is the sum of atomic masses represented by the empirical formula.

items.title: Molecular Formula Factor
items.content: n = Molecular molar mass / Empirical formula mass.

items.title: Stoichiometry
items.content: Stoichiometry deals with quantitative relationships between reactants and products in chemical reactions.

items.title: Balanced Chemical Equation
items.content: A chemical equation must have equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides.

items.title: Stoichiometric Coefficients
items.content: The coefficients in a balanced equation represent the relative numbers of molecules or moles participating in the reaction.

items.title: Limiting Reagent
items.content: The limiting reagent is the reactant that is completely consumed first and limits the amount of product formed.

items.title: Excess Reagent
items.content: An excess reagent is present in an amount greater than required by the stoichiometric ratio.

items.title: Theoretical Yield
items.content: Theoretical yield is the maximum amount of product predicted from stoichiometric calculations.

items.title: Actual Yield
items.content: Actual yield is the amount of product obtained experimentally.

items.title: Percentage Yield
items.content: Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100.

items.title: Reaction Quotient in Stoichiometric Context
items.content: For stoichiometric calculations, mole ratios are obtained directly from coefficients of the balanced chemical equation.

items.title: Mass-Mass Stoichiometry
items.content: Convert the given mass to moles, use the balanced-equation mole ratio, then convert product moles to the required quantity.

items.title: Mass-Mole Stoichiometry
items.content: Convert the given mass to moles, apply the balanced-equation mole ratio, and report the required moles.

items.title: Mole-Mass Stoichiometry
items.content: Use the balanced-equation mole ratio to obtain product moles, then convert them to mass using molar mass.

items.title: Mole-Mole Stoichiometry
items.content: Use the coefficients of the balanced chemical equation to establish the mole ratio between substances.

items.title: Volume-Volume Gas Stoichiometry
items.content: At the same temperature and pressure, reacting gas volumes are proportional to their stoichiometric coefficients.

items.title: Avogadro's Law
items.content: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

items.title: Significant Figures
items.content: Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a measured quantity, including all certain digits and the first uncertain digit.

items.title: Non-Zero Significant Digits
items.content: All non-zero digits are significant.

items.title: Interior Zeros
items.content: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant.

items.title: Leading Zeros
items.content: Zeros to the left of the first non-zero digit are not significant.

items.title: Trailing Zeros with Decimal
items.content: Trailing zeros in a number containing a decimal point are significant.

items.title: Trailing Zeros without Decimal
items.content: Trailing zeros in a whole number without an indicated decimal point may be ambiguous and should be expressed in scientific notation when precision matters.

items.title: Addition and Subtraction Rule
items.content: The result is rounded to the least number of decimal places among the quantities being added or subtracted.

items.title: Multiplication and Division Rule
items.content: The result contains the same number of significant figures as the quantity with the fewest significant figures.

items.title: Rounding Off
items.content: If the digit immediately after the retained digit is 5 or greater, the retained digit is increased by one; otherwise it remains unchanged.

items.title: Scientific Notation
items.content: A number in scientific notation is written as a coefficient between 1 and 10 multiplied by an integral power of 10.

items.title: Dimensional Analysis
items.content: Dimensional analysis uses dimensions of physical quantities to check equations and convert units.

items.title: Density
items.content: Density ρ = mass/volume.

items.title: Relative Density
items.content: Relative density = density of substance / density of reference substance.

items.title: Atomicity
items.content: Atomicity is the number of atoms present in one molecule of an element.

items.title: Average Atomic Mass
items.content: Average atomic mass = Σ(isotopic abundance × isotopic mass), with abundances expressed as fractions.

items.title: Percentage Isotopic Abundance
items.content: Percentage abundance = (number or fraction of atoms of an isotope / total atoms) × 100.

items.title: Mass Fraction
items.content: Mass fraction of a component = mass of component / total mass of mixture.

items.title: Mole Fraction from Moles
items.content: x_i = n_i/(n₁ + n₂ + ...).

items.title: Molarity and Temperature
items.content: Molarity depends on solution volume and therefore can change with temperature.

items.title: Molality and Temperature
items.content: Molality is based on mass of solvent and is independent of temperature under ordinary conditions.

items.title: Concentration Conversion
items.content: For a solution, amount of solute = concentration × appropriate quantity of solution or solvent, according to the concentration definition.

items.title: Mole Concept Particle Conversion
items.content: Mass ↔ moles ↔ number of particles can be converted using n = m/M and N = nN_A.

items.title: Stoichiometric Ratio
items.content: For a balanced equation aA + bB → cC + dD, n_A/a = n_B/b = n_C/c = n_D/d for stoichiometric quantities.

items.title: Limiting Reagent Test
items.content: Compare available moles divided by their stoichiometric coefficients; the smallest value identifies the limiting reagent.

items.title: Excess Reactant Remaining
items.content: Excess reactant remaining = initial amount − amount consumed according to the limiting reagent.

items.title: Purity Percentage
items.content: Percentage purity = (mass of pure substance / mass of impure sample) × 100.

items.title: Elemental Analysis
items.content: Determine the mass or percentage of each element present and use atomic masses to obtain the simplest mole ratio.

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core relations: n=m/M, N=nN_A, Molarity=n/V, Molality=n/mass of solvent, x_i=n_i/Σn, % yield=(actual/theoretical)×100, and % composition=(mass of element/molar mass of compound)×100.

items.title: Electron
items.content: An electron is a negatively charged subatomic particle present in atoms.

items.title: Proton
items.content: A proton is a positively charged subatomic particle present in the nucleus.

items.title: Neutron
items.content: A neutron is a neutral subatomic particle present in the nucleus.

items.title: Electron Charge
items.content: The magnitude of electronic charge is approximately 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

items.title: Atomic Number
items.content: Atomic number Z is the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom.

items.title: Mass Number
items.content: Mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

items.title: Mass Number Relation
items.content: A = Z + N, where N is the number of neutrons.

items.title: Number of Neutrons
items.content: N = A − Z.

items.title: Neutral Atom
items.content: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

items.title: Isotopes
items.content: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

items.title: Isobars
items.content: Isobars are atoms of different elements having the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

items.title: Thomson Atomic Model
items.content: Thomson proposed that positive charge was distributed throughout the atom with electrons embedded in it.

items.title: Rutherford Nuclear Model
items.content: Rutherford's scattering experiment led to the conclusion that an atom has a tiny dense positively charged nucleus and is mostly empty space.

items.title: Rutherford Scattering
items.content: Most alpha particles passed through the foil undeflected, while a small fraction were strongly deflected.

items.title: Electromagnetic Radiation
items.content: Electromagnetic radiation consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that propagate through space.

items.title: Wavelength
items.content: Wavelength λ is the distance between two successive points in the same phase of a wave.

items.title: Frequency
items.content: Frequency ν is the number of wave cycles passing a point per unit time.

items.title: Wave Velocity
items.content: c = λν for electromagnetic radiation in vacuum.

items.title: Speed of Light
items.content: The speed of electromagnetic radiation in vacuum is approximately 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

items.title: Wave Number
items.content: Wavenumber ṽ = 1/λ, when wavelength is expressed in the corresponding reciprocal unit.

items.title: Frequency-Wavelength Relation
items.content: ν = c/λ for electromagnetic radiation in vacuum.

items.title: Planck Quantum
items.content: Planck proposed that electromagnetic energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets called quanta.

items.title: Photon Energy
items.content: E = hν.

items.title: Photon Energy Using Wavelength
items.content: E = hc/λ.

items.title: Photon Momentum
items.content: p = h/λ for a photon.

items.title: Photoelectric Effect
items.content: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when suitable electromagnetic radiation falls on it.

items.title: Threshold Frequency
items.content: Threshold frequency is the minimum frequency of incident radiation required to eject electrons from a particular metal.

items.title: Work Function
items.content: Work function is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a metal.

items.title: Einstein Photoelectric Equation
items.content: hν = hν₀ + K_max.

items.title: Maximum Kinetic Energy
items.content: K_max = h(ν − ν₀).

items.title: Stopping Potential
items.content: K_max = eV₀.

items.title: Hydrogen Spectrum
items.content: The hydrogen emission spectrum consists of discrete lines corresponding to transitions between quantized energy levels.

items.title: Bohr Model
items.content: Bohr proposed that electrons move in certain permitted stationary orbits having definite energies.

items.title: Bohr Quantization Condition
items.content: mvr = nh/(2π), where n = 1, 2, 3, ...

items.title: Bohr Angular Momentum
items.content: L = nħ, where ħ = h/(2π).

items.title: Bohr Radius
items.content: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is approximately 0.529 Å.

items.title: Bohr Radius Relation
items.content: For a hydrogen-like species, r_n = a₀ n²/Z.

items.title: Hydrogen-Like Species
items.content: A hydrogen-like species has only one electron, such as H, He⁺, Li²⁺, etc.

items.title: Energy of Hydrogen-Like Atom
items.content: E_n = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ Z²/n² J per atom.

items.title: Energy in Electron Volt
items.content: E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV for a hydrogen-like species.

items.title: Ground State
items.content: The ground state is the lowest-energy state of an atom.

items.title: Excited State
items.content: An excited state is a state in which an electron has higher energy than the ground state.

items.title: Energy Transition
items.content: For a transition between levels, ΔE = E_final − E_initial.

items.title: Photon Emission
items.content: When an electron moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level, energy is emitted as a photon.

items.title: Photon Absorption
items.content: When an electron absorbs energy equal to the difference between two permitted levels, it can move to a higher level.

items.title: Rydberg Equation
items.content: 1/λ = RZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), for n₂ > n₁ in hydrogen-like species.

items.title: Rydberg Constant
items.content: R is approximately 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.

items.title: Lyman Series
items.content: The Lyman series corresponds to electronic transitions ending at n = 1 and lies in the ultraviolet region.

items.title: Balmer Series
items.content: The Balmer series corresponds to transitions ending at n = 2 and lies mainly in the visible region.

items.title: Paschen Series
items.content: The Paschen series corresponds to transitions ending at n = 3 and lies in the infrared region.

items.title: Brackett Series
items.content: The Brackett series corresponds to transitions ending at n = 4 and lies in the infrared region.

items.title: Pfund Series
items.content: The Pfund series corresponds to transitions ending at n = 5 and lies in the infrared region.

items.title: Energy-Frequency Trend
items.content: Photon energy increases with frequency because E = hν.

items.title: Energy-Wavelength Trend
items.content: Photon energy decreases as wavelength increases because E = hc/λ.

items.title: de Broglie Hypothesis
items.content: de Broglie proposed that moving particles have wave-like properties.

items.title: de Broglie Wavelength
items.content: λ = h/p.

items.title: de Broglie Wavelength Using Momentum
items.content: λ = h/(mv) for a non-relativistic particle.

items.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
items.content: It is impossible to simultaneously determine the exact position and exact momentum of a microscopic particle.

items.title: Uncertainty Relation
items.content: Δx Δp ≥ h/(4π).

items.title: Quantum Mechanical Model
items.content: The quantum mechanical model describes electrons using wave functions and probability distributions rather than fixed classical orbits.

items.title: Orbital
items.content: An orbital is a region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is high.

items.title: Principal Quantum Number
items.content: The principal quantum number n specifies the main energy level or shell and has values 1, 2, 3, ...

items.title: Azimuthal Quantum Number
items.content: The azimuthal quantum number l specifies the subshell and has values from 0 to n−1.

items.title: Magnetic Quantum Number
items.content: The magnetic quantum number m_l specifies the orientation of an orbital and has values from −l to +l.

items.title: Spin Quantum Number
items.content: The spin quantum number m_s specifies electron spin and has values +1/2 or −1/2.

items.title: Subshell Labels
items.content: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 correspond to s, p, d, f subshells respectively.

items.title: Number of Orbitals in Subshell
items.content: Number of orbitals in a subshell = 2l + 1.

items.title: Maximum Electrons in Subshell
items.content: Maximum number of electrons in a subshell = 2(2l + 1).

items.title: Number of Orbitals in Shell
items.content: The nth shell contains n² orbitals.

items.title: Maximum Electrons in Shell
items.content: The nth shell can contain a maximum of 2n² electrons.

items.title: s Subshell
items.content: An s subshell has l = 0, one orbital, and a maximum capacity of 2 electrons.

items.title: p Subshell
items.content: A p subshell has l = 1, three orbitals, and a maximum capacity of 6 electrons.

items.title: d Subshell
items.content: A d subshell has l = 2, five orbitals, and a maximum capacity of 10 electrons.

items.title: f Subshell
items.content: An f subshell has l = 3, seven orbitals, and a maximum capacity of 14 electrons.

items.title: Aufbau Principle
items.content: Electrons occupy available orbitals in order of increasing energy.

items.title: Pauli Exclusion Principle
items.content: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers.

items.title: Hund's Rule
items.content: Degenerate orbitals are singly occupied with parallel spins before pairing occurs.

items.title: Electronic Configuration
items.content: Electronic configuration describes the distribution of electrons among shells, subshells, and orbitals.

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core relations: c=λν, E=hν=hc/λ, p=h/λ, λ=h/(mv), ΔxΔp≥h/(4π), 2n² electrons per shell, and 2(2l+1) electrons per subshell.

chapters.name: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

items.title: Modern Periodic Law
items.content: The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

items.title: Periodic Table
items.content: The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number so that recurring properties can be studied.

items.title: Period
items.content: A period is a horizontal row in the modern periodic table.

items.title: Group
items.content: A group is a vertical column in the modern periodic table.

items.title: Block
items.content: A block is a region of the periodic table containing elements in which the last electron enters a particular type of subshell.

items.title: s-Block
items.content: The s-block contains elements in which the differentiating electron enters an s subshell.

items.title: p-Block
items.content: The p-block contains elements in which the differentiating electron enters a p subshell.

items.title: d-Block
items.content: The d-block contains elements in which the differentiating electron enters a d subshell.

items.title: f-Block
items.content: The f-block contains elements in which the differentiating electron enters an f subshell.

items.title: Period Number and Shell
items.content: The period number generally corresponds to the highest principal quantum number n in the ground-state electronic configuration.

items.title: Group 1
items.content: Group 1 elements are called alkali metals, except hydrogen which has distinct properties.

items.title: Group 2
items.content: Group 2 elements are called alkaline earth metals.

items.title: Group 17
items.content: Group 17 elements are called halogens.

items.title: Group 18
items.content: Group 18 elements are called noble gases.

items.title: Metals
items.content: Metals generally show lustre, malleability, ductility and good electrical and thermal conductivity.

items.title: Non-Metals
items.content: Non-metals generally lack metallic properties and often have relatively high ionisation energies and electron-gain tendencies.

items.title: Metalloids
items.content: Metalloids show properties intermediate between metals and non-metals.

items.title: Valence Electrons
items.content: Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell that participate most directly in chemical bonding.

items.title: Atomic Radius
items.content: Atomic radius is a measure of the size of an atom, commonly estimated from internuclear distances in bonded or neighbouring atoms.

items.title: Covalent Radius
items.content: Covalent radius is half the internuclear distance between two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond.

items.title: Van der Waals Radius
items.content: Van der Waals radius is associated with the non-bonded contact distance between atoms in neighbouring molecules.

items.title: Atomic Radius Across Period
items.content: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period.

items.title: Atomic Radius Down Group
items.content: Atomic radius generally increases down a group because additional electron shells are occupied.

items.title: Effective Nuclear Charge
items.content: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive attraction experienced by an electron after accounting for shielding by other electrons.

items.title: Effective Nuclear Charge Across Period
items.content: Effective nuclear charge generally increases across a period because nuclear charge increases while shielding does not increase proportionally.

items.title: Shielding Effect
items.content: Shielding effect is the reduction in attraction between the nucleus and an electron caused by intervening electrons.

items.title: Shielding Down Group
items.content: Shielding generally increases down a group because additional inner shells are present.

items.title: Ionisation Enthalpy
items.content: Ionisation enthalpy is the enthalpy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state.

items.title: First Ionisation Enthalpy
items.content: First ionisation enthalpy is the enthalpy required to remove the first electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

items.title: Second Ionisation Enthalpy
items.content: Second ionisation enthalpy is the enthalpy required to remove the second electron from a gaseous unipositive ion.

items.title: Successive Ionisation Enthalpies
items.content: Successive ionisation enthalpies generally increase because removal of each additional electron occurs from an increasingly positive species.

items.title: Ionisation Enthalpy Across Period
items.content: Ionisation enthalpy generally increases from left to right across a period.

items.title: Ionisation Enthalpy Down Group
items.content: Ionisation enthalpy generally decreases down a group.

items.title: Ionisation Enthalpy and Atomic Size
items.content: Smaller atomic size generally corresponds to greater attraction for the valence electron and hence higher ionisation enthalpy.

items.title: Electron Gain Enthalpy
items.content: Electron gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom to form a gaseous anion.

items.title: Electron Gain Enthalpy Across Period
items.content: Electron gain enthalpy generally becomes more negative across a period, with important exceptions.

items.title: Electron Gain Enthalpy Down Group
items.content: Electron gain enthalpy generally becomes less negative down a group, though the trend has exceptions.

items.title: Electron Gain Enthalpy of Noble Gases
items.content: Noble gases generally have positive electron gain enthalpy because adding an electron requires entering a new shell.

items.title: Electronegativity
items.content: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself.

items.title: Electronegativity Across Period
items.content: Electronegativity generally increases from left to right across a period.

items.title: Electronegativity Down Group
items.content: Electronegativity generally decreases down a group.

items.title: Fluorine Electronegativity
items.content: Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the Pauling scale.

items.title: Electropositivity
items.content: Electropositivity is the tendency of an atom to lose electrons and form positive ions.

items.title: Electropositivity Across Period
items.content: Electropositive character generally decreases from left to right across a period.

items.title: Electropositivity Down Group
items.content: Electropositive character generally increases down a group.

items.title: Metallic Character Across Period
items.content: Metallic character generally decreases from left to right across a period.

items.title: Metallic Character Down Group
items.content: Metallic character generally increases down a group.

items.title: Non-Metallic Character Across Period
items.content: Non-metallic character generally increases from left to right across a period.

items.title: Non-Metallic Character Down Group
items.content: Non-metallic character generally decreases down a group.

items.title: Valency Across a Period
items.content: For main-group elements, valency with respect to hydrogen or chlorine generally increases from 1 to 4 and then decreases to 0 across a period.

items.title: Oxidation State
items.content: Oxidation state is the apparent charge assigned to an atom in a compound according to agreed electronegativity conventions.

items.title: Oxidation State of Group 1
items.content: Group 1 elements generally show oxidation state +1 in their compounds.

items.title: Oxidation State of Group 2
items.content: Group 2 elements generally show oxidation state +2 in their compounds.

items.title: Oxidation State of Fluorine
items.content: Fluorine generally shows oxidation state −1 in its compounds.

items.title: Oxidation State of Oxygen
items.content: Oxygen generally shows oxidation state −2, with important exceptions such as peroxides and OF₂.

items.title: Oxidation State of Hydrogen
items.content: Hydrogen generally shows +1 with non-metals and −1 in metal hydrides.

items.title: Diagonal Relationship
items.content: A diagonal relationship refers to similarities between certain elements of the second and third periods placed diagonally in the periodic table.

items.title: Anomalous Behaviour of First Element
items.content: The first element of a group can show distinctive behaviour because of its small size, high ionisation enthalpy and absence of inner shells.

items.title: Periodic Trend
items.content: A periodic trend is a systematic variation in a property of elements with increasing atomic number.

items.title: Periodicity
items.content: Periodicity is the repetition of similar properties at regular intervals when elements are arranged by atomic number.

items.title: Noble Gas Configuration
items.content: A noble gas configuration refers to a completely filled valence shell characteristic of noble gases.

items.title: Octet Rule
items.content: Many main-group atoms tend to attain a stable valence-shell configuration resembling a noble gas, often an octet.

items.title: Stable Duplet
items.content: Hydrogen and helium-related configurations can involve a stable two-electron shell, called a duplet.

items.title: Isoelectronic Species
items.content: Isoelectronic species contain the same number of electrons and therefore often have related electron configurations.

items.title: Isoelectronic Radius Trend
items.content: For isoelectronic species, ionic radius generally decreases as nuclear charge increases.

items.title: Cation Size
items.content: A cation is generally smaller than its parent atom because electron loss reduces electron-electron repulsion and may remove an outer shell.

items.title: Anion Size
items.content: An anion is generally larger than its parent atom because added electrons increase electron-electron repulsion.

items.title: Cationic Radius Across Series
items.content: For comparable cations in a period, ionic size generally decreases with increasing effective nuclear charge.

items.title: Anionic Radius Across Series
items.content: For comparable anions in a period, ionic size generally decreases as effective nuclear charge increases.

items.title: Periodic Table Group Number
items.content: For many main-group elements, group number helps determine the number of valence electrons and common oxidation states.

items.title: Electronic Configuration and Position
items.content: The period, block and group of an element can be inferred from its ground-state electronic configuration.

items.title: Last Electron and Block
items.content: The type of subshell receiving the differentiating electron identifies the block of an element.

items.title: s-Block Valence Configuration
items.content: Typical s-block valence configurations are ns¹ and ns².

items.title: p-Block Valence Configuration
items.content: Typical p-block valence configuration is ns²np¹ to ns²np⁶.

items.title: d-Block Valence Configuration
items.content: Typical d-block valence configuration involves (n−1)d¹–¹⁰ ns⁰–².

items.title: f-Block Valence Configuration
items.content: Typical f-block valence configuration involves filling of a (n−2)f subshell.

items.title: Period Lengths
items.content: The first period contains 2 elements, the second and third contain 8 each, the fourth and fifth contain 18 each, and the sixth and seventh can accommodate 32 each in the long form.

items.title: Lanthanides
items.content: Lanthanides are the fourteen elements associated with progressive filling of the 4f subshell, commonly shown separately below the main table.

items.title: Actinides
items.content: Actinides are the fourteen elements associated with progressive filling of the 5f subshell, commonly shown separately below the main table.

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core trends: atomic radius decreases across and increases down; ionisation enthalpy generally increases across and decreases down; electronegativity generally increases across and decreases down; metallic character generally shows the opposite trend.

items.title: Chemical Bond
items.content: A chemical bond is the attractive force that holds atoms or ions together in a stable chemical species.

items.title: Kossel-Lewis Approach
items.content: Kossel and Lewis related chemical bonding to attainment of stable noble-gas-like electronic configurations.

items.title: Lewis Symbols
items.content: A Lewis symbol represents the valence electrons of an atom as dots around its chemical symbol.

items.title: Octet Rule
items.content: Atoms generally tend to attain eight electrons in their valence shell by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.

items.title: Duplet Rule
items.content: Hydrogen and helium can attain stability with two electrons in the first shell.

items.title: Ionic Bond
items.content: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.

items.title: Electrovalent Bond
items.content: Electrovalent bond is another term for ionic bond, emphasizing electron transfer and resulting ions.

items.title: Formation of NaCl
items.content: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming Na+ and Cl−, which are held together by electrostatic attraction.

items.title: Lattice Enthalpy
items.content: Lattice enthalpy is the enthalpy change associated with the formation or separation of an ionic solid from its gaseous ions, depending on convention.

items.title: Lattice Enthalpy Trend
items.content: Lattice enthalpy generally increases in magnitude when ionic charges increase and ionic sizes decrease.

items.title: Born-Haber Cycle
items.content: A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to ionic compounds to relate lattice enthalpy to other measurable enthalpy changes.

items.title: Fajan's Rule
items.content: Fajan's rules help predict covalent character in ionic compounds from factors such as cation size, cation charge and anion size.

items.title: Polarisation
items.content: Polarisation is distortion of an anion's electron cloud by a nearby cation.

items.title: Polarising Power
items.content: Polarising power is the ability of a cation to distort the electron cloud of an anion.

items.title: Polarizability
items.content: Polarizability is the ease with which an anion's electron cloud can be distorted.

items.title: Covalent Bond
items.content: A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

items.title: Single Covalent Bond
items.content: A single covalent bond involves one shared electron pair.

items.title: Double Covalent Bond
items.content: A double covalent bond involves two shared electron pairs.

items.title: Triple Covalent Bond
items.content: A triple covalent bond involves three shared electron pairs.

items.title: Coordinate Bond
items.content: A coordinate bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom.

items.title: Lewis Structure
items.content: A Lewis structure shows valence electrons, bonding pairs and lone pairs around atoms in a molecule or ion.

items.title: Formal Charge
items.content: Formal charge = valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − 1/2(bonding electrons).

items.title: Formal Charge Sum
items.content: The sum of formal charges in a species equals its overall charge.

items.title: Resonance
items.content: Resonance occurs when a species is represented by two or more valid Lewis structures differing only in electron arrangement.

items.title: Resonance Hybrid
items.content: The actual structure of a resonance-stabilized species is a resonance hybrid rather than any single canonical structure.

items.title: Resonance Energy
items.content: Resonance energy is the stabilization associated with the resonance hybrid relative to the most stable contributing structure.

items.title: Bond Length
items.content: Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms.

items.title: Bond Length and Bond Order
items.content: Bond length generally decreases as bond order increases for comparable bonds.

items.title: Bond Enthalpy
items.content: Bond enthalpy is the enthalpy required to break one mole of a particular type of bond in gaseous molecules.

items.title: Bond Enthalpy and Bond Strength
items.content: Higher bond enthalpy generally indicates a stronger bond.

items.title: Bond Angle
items.content: Bond angle is the angle between two bonds originating from the same central atom.

items.title: Bond Order
items.content: Bond order indicates the number of bonding electron pairs or the effective bond multiplicity between two atoms.

items.title: Bond Order and Stability
items.content: Higher bond order generally corresponds to greater bond strength and shorter bond length.

items.title: Electronegativity Difference
items.content: Difference in electronegativity between bonded atoms helps determine the polarity and character of a bond.

items.title: Polar Covalent Bond
items.content: A polar covalent bond has unequal sharing of the bonding electron pair because the bonded atoms have different electronegativities.

items.title: Nonpolar Covalent Bond
items.content: A nonpolar covalent bond has equal or nearly equal sharing of electrons between bonded atoms.

items.title: Dipole Moment
items.content: Dipole moment measures the separation of positive and negative charge in a bond or molecule.

items.title: Dipole Moment Formula
items.content: For a simple bond, μ = q × r, where q is charge magnitude and r is charge separation.

items.title: Dipole Moment Unit
items.content: The SI unit of dipole moment is C m; Debye is also commonly used.

items.title: Molecular Dipole Moment
items.content: The molecular dipole moment is the vector sum of the individual bond dipole moments and any relevant lone-pair effects.

items.title: VSEPR Theory
items.content: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory predicts molecular shapes by considering repulsions among electron pairs around a central atom.

items.title: Electron Pair Repulsion Order
items.content: The general repulsion order is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

items.title: Lone Pair Effect on Bond Angle
items.content: Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs and generally compress bond angles.

items.title: Electron Domain
items.content: An electron domain is a region around a central atom occupied by a bonding pair, lone pair or multiple bond.

items.title: Steric Number
items.content: Steric number is the total number of electron domains around a central atom.

items.title: Steric Number Formula
items.content: Steric number = number of sigma bonds + number of lone pairs on the central atom.

items.title: Linear Shape
items.content: A species with two electron domains around the central atom generally has a linear electron-domain geometry with bond angle 180°.

items.title: Trigonal Planar Shape
items.content: A species with three electron domains and no lone pair on the central atom has trigonal planar geometry with bond angles near 120°.

items.title: Tetrahedral Shape
items.content: A species with four electron domains and no lone pair on the central atom has tetrahedral geometry with bond angles near 109.5°.

items.title: Trigonal Bipyramidal Shape
items.content: Five electron domains around a central atom give trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry.

items.title: Octahedral Shape
items.content: Six electron domains around a central atom give octahedral electron-domain geometry.

items.title: VSEPR Multiple Bonds
items.content: A multiple bond is treated as one electron domain in VSEPR geometry, although it can exert greater repulsion than a single bond.

items.title: Hybridisation
items.content: Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals of comparable energy on the same atom to form equivalent hybrid orbitals.

items.title: sp Hybridisation
items.content: sp hybridisation gives two hybrid orbitals and is associated with linear electron-domain geometry.

items.title: sp2 Hybridisation
items.content: sp2 hybridisation gives three hybrid orbitals and is associated with trigonal planar electron-domain geometry.

items.title: sp3 Hybridisation
items.content: sp3 hybridisation gives four hybrid orbitals and is associated with tetrahedral electron-domain geometry.

items.title: sp3d Hybridisation
items.content: sp3d hybridisation gives five hybrid orbitals and is associated with trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry.

items.title: sp3d2 Hybridisation
items.content: sp3d2 hybridisation gives six hybrid orbitals and is associated with octahedral electron-domain geometry.

items.title: Sigma Bond
items.content: A sigma bond is formed by head-on overlap along the internuclear axis.

items.title: Pi Bond
items.content: A pi bond is formed by lateral overlap of parallel orbitals above and below the internuclear axis.

items.title: Sigma and Pi in Single Bond
items.content: A single covalent bond consists of one sigma bond.

items.title: Sigma and Pi in Double Bond
items.content: A double covalent bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond.

items.title: Sigma and Pi in Triple Bond
items.content: A triple covalent bond consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

items.title: Valence Bond Theory
items.content: Valence bond theory describes covalent bonding in terms of overlap of atomic orbitals containing electrons of suitable spin.

items.title: Orbital Overlap
items.content: Orbital overlap is the interpenetration of atomic orbitals involved in bond formation.

items.title: Hydrogen Molecule Bonding
items.content: In H2, the two hydrogen 1s orbitals overlap head-on to form a sigma bond.

items.title: Molecular Orbital Theory
items.content: Molecular orbital theory describes electrons as occupying molecular orbitals extending over the entire molecule.

items.title: Bonding Molecular Orbital
items.content: A bonding molecular orbital has lower energy than the combining atomic orbitals and increases electron density between nuclei.

items.title: Antibonding Molecular Orbital
items.content: An antibonding molecular orbital has higher energy and a node between nuclei relative to the corresponding bonding orbital.

items.title: Molecular Orbital Formation
items.content: The number of molecular orbitals formed equals the number of atomic orbitals combined.

items.title: Bond Order MOT
items.content: Bond order = 1/2(Nb − Na), where Nb and Na are electrons in bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals.

items.title: Bond Order and Stability MOT
items.content: A positive bond order generally indicates a stable bonded species, and larger bond order generally means greater stability.

items.title: Magnetic Behaviour
items.content: A species is paramagnetic if it has one or more unpaired electrons and diamagnetic if all electrons are paired.

items.title: Hydrogen Bond
items.content: A hydrogen bond is an attractive interaction involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom and another electronegative atom with a lone pair.

items.title: Intermolecular Hydrogen Bond
items.content: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding occurs between separate molecules.

items.title: Intramolecular Hydrogen Bond
items.content: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding occurs between suitable donor and acceptor groups within the same molecule.

items.title: Hydrogen Bond Strength
items.content: Hydrogen bonding is generally stronger when hydrogen is bonded to highly electronegative, small atoms such as F, O or N.

items.title: Dipole Moment and Symmetry
items.content: A highly symmetrical molecule can have zero net dipole moment even when individual bonds are polar because bond dipoles may cancel.

items.title: Limitations of Octet Rule
items.content: The octet rule does not adequately explain electron-deficient, odd-electron and expanded-valence species and is therefore not universally applicable.

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core ideas: octet rule, ionic/covalent bonding, Lewis structures, formal charge, resonance, VSEPR shapes, hybridisation, sigma/pi bonds, molecular orbital theory, bond order, polarity and hydrogen bonding.

items.title: Thermodynamic System
items.content: A thermodynamic system is the part of the universe selected for study.

items.title: Surroundings
items.content: The surroundings are everything outside the thermodynamic system that can interact with it.

items.title: Universe
items.content: The universe in thermodynamics consists of the system and its surroundings.

items.title: Open System
items.content: An open system can exchange both matter and energy with its surroundings.

items.title: Closed System
items.content: A closed system can exchange energy but not matter with its surroundings.

items.title: Isolated System
items.content: An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.

items.title: State of a System
items.content: The state of a thermodynamic system is specified by measurable macroscopic properties such as pressure, volume and temperature.

items.title: State Variables
items.content: State variables are properties whose values depend only on the state of the system and not on the path used to reach it.

items.title: State Function
items.content: A state function depends only on the initial and final states and not on the path between them.

items.title: Path Function
items.content: A path function depends on the process or path followed between two states.

items.title: Examples of State Functions
items.content: Internal energy, enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy are state functions.

items.title: Examples of Path Functions
items.content: Heat and work are path functions.

items.title: Intensive Property
items.content: An intensive property does not depend on the amount of substance present.

items.title: Extensive Property
items.content: An extensive property depends on the amount of substance present.

items.title: Examples Intensive
