items.content: Temperature, pressure, density and concentration are intensive properties.

items.title: Examples Extensive
items.content: Mass, volume, internal energy and enthalpy are extensive properties.

items.title: Thermodynamic Process
items.content: A thermodynamic process is a change of a system from one state to another.

items.title: Isothermal Process
items.content: An isothermal process occurs at constant temperature.

items.title: Isobaric Process
items.content: An isobaric process occurs at constant pressure.

items.title: Isochoric Process
items.content: An isochoric process occurs at constant volume.

items.title: Adiabatic Process
items.content: An adiabatic process occurs without transfer of heat between system and surroundings.

items.title: Cyclic Process
items.content: A cyclic process returns the system to its initial state after a sequence of changes.

items.title: Reversible Process
items.content: A reversible process is an ideal process that can be reversed by an infinitesimal change so that both system and surroundings return to their original states.

items.title: Irreversible Process
items.content: An irreversible process cannot be exactly reversed to restore both system and surroundings to their initial states.

items.title: Zeroth Law
items.content: If system A is in thermal equilibrium with B and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A is in thermal equilibrium with C.

items.title: Heat
items.content: Heat is energy transferred between a system and surroundings because of a temperature difference.

items.title: Work
items.content: Work is energy transferred when a force or generalized force causes a displacement or change in a system.

items.title: Sign Convention Chemistry
items.content: In the chemistry convention, heat absorbed by the system is positive and work done on the system is positive.

items.title: Heat Symbol
items.content: Heat is commonly represented by q.

items.title: Work Symbol
items.content: Work is commonly represented by w.

items.title: Expansion Work
items.content: For pressure-volume work, w = −P_ext ΔV.

items.title: Constant External Pressure Work
items.content: At constant external pressure, w = −P_ext(V2 − V1).

items.title: Expansion Work Sign
items.content: For expansion, ΔV > 0 and pressure-volume work is negative in the chemistry sign convention.

items.title: Compression Work Sign
items.content: For compression, ΔV < 0 and pressure-volume work is positive in the chemistry sign convention.

items.title: Free Expansion
items.content: In free expansion against negligible external pressure, pressure-volume work is zero.

items.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
items.content: The first law states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.

items.title: First Law Equation
items.content: ΔU = q + w.

items.title: Internal Energy
items.content: Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy contained within a thermodynamic system.

items.title: Internal Energy Change
items.content: ΔU = U_final − U_initial.

items.title: Cyclic Internal Energy
items.content: For a complete cycle, ΔU = 0 because internal energy is a state function.

items.title: Constant Volume Heat
items.content: At constant volume, when only pressure-volume work is involved, q_v = ΔU.

items.title: Enthalpy
items.content: Enthalpy is defined as H = U + PV.

items.title: Enthalpy Change
items.content: ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV).

items.title: Constant Pressure Heat
items.content: At constant pressure, when only pressure-volume work is involved, q_p = ΔH.

items.title: Ideal Gas Enthalpy Relation
items.content: For an ideal gas, ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT for a reaction involving gaseous species.

items.title: Molar Enthalpy
items.content: Molar enthalpy change is the enthalpy change per mole of the relevant substance or reaction as specified.

items.title: Thermochemical Equation
items.content: A thermochemical equation is a balanced chemical equation accompanied by the enthalpy change for the reaction as written.

items.title: Standard State
items.content: The standard state is the reference state of a substance at a specified standard pressure, commonly 1 bar.

items.title: Standard Enthalpy Change
items.content: Standard enthalpy change is the enthalpy change for a process when reactants and products are in their standard states.

items.title: Standard Enthalpy of Formation
items.content: Standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its constituent elements in their standard states.

items.title: Formation Enthalpy of Element
items.content: The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its most stable standard state is zero.

items.title: Standard Enthalpy of Combustion
items.content: Standard enthalpy of combustion is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions.

items.title: Standard Enthalpy of Atomisation
items.content: Standard enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change required to form one mole of gaseous atoms from an element in its standard state.

items.title: Bond Dissociation Enthalpy
items.content: Bond dissociation enthalpy is the enthalpy required to break one mole of a specified bond in gaseous molecules.

items.title: Mean Bond Enthalpy
items.content: Mean bond enthalpy is the average bond dissociation enthalpy for a particular type of bond across different molecules.

items.title: Enthalpy of Sublimation
items.content: Enthalpy of sublimation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solid changes directly into gaseous atoms or molecules, depending on the specified process.

items.title: Enthalpy of Fusion
items.content: Enthalpy of fusion is the enthalpy required to convert one mole of a solid into liquid at its melting point.

items.title: Enthalpy of Vaporisation
items.content: Enthalpy of vaporisation is the enthalpy required to convert one mole of liquid into gas at its boiling point.

items.title: Enthalpy of Solution
items.content: Enthalpy of solution is the enthalpy change when a specified amount of solute dissolves in a solvent under stated conditions.

items.title: Enthalpy of Hydration
items.content: Enthalpy of hydration is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions becomes hydrated by water.

items.title: Enthalpy of Neutralisation
items.content: Enthalpy of neutralisation is the enthalpy change when an acid and base react to form one mole of water under specified conditions.

items.title: Hess's Law
items.content: The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the pathway and depends only on the initial and final states.

items.title: Hess Law Calculation
items.content: ΔH_reaction = sum of enthalpy changes of the individual steps used to construct the reaction.

items.title: Formation Enthalpy Calculation
items.content: ΔH°_reaction = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants).

items.title: Combustion Enthalpy Calculation
items.content: Reaction enthalpy can be obtained from standard enthalpies of combustion by applying Hess's law to the appropriate thermochemical equations.

items.title: Bond Enthalpy Estimation
items.content: ΔH_reaction ≈ Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed).

items.title: Calorimetry
items.content: Calorimetry is the measurement of heat changes associated with physical or chemical processes.

items.title: Heat Capacity
items.content: Heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of a system by one degree Celsius or one kelvin.

items.title: Heat Capacity Formula
items.content: C = q/ΔT.

items.title: Specific Heat Capacity
items.content: Specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of one unit mass of a substance by one degree.

items.title: Specific Heat Formula
items.content: q = m c ΔT.

items.title: Molar Heat Capacity
items.content: Molar heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by one kelvin.

items.title: Gibbs Energy
items.content: Gibbs energy is defined as G = H − TS and is useful for assessing spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure.

items.title: Gibbs Energy Change
items.content: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS at constant temperature.

items.title: Spontaneous Process Criterion
items.content: At constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous when ΔG < 0.

items.title: Equilibrium Gibbs Criterion
items.content: At equilibrium under constant temperature and pressure, ΔG = 0.

items.title: Nonspontaneous Criterion
items.content: At constant temperature and pressure, a process with ΔG > 0 is nonspontaneous in the forward direction.

items.title: Entropy
items.content: Entropy is a thermodynamic state function associated with energy dispersal and the number of accessible microscopic arrangements.

items.title: Second Law Thermodynamics
items.content: The second law states that the entropy of the universe increases for a spontaneous irreversible process and remains constant for an ideal reversible process.

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core relations: ΔU=q+w; w=−P_extΔV; H=U+PV; ΔH=ΔU+Δn_gRT; ΔH°rxn=ΣΔH°f(products)−ΣΔH°f(reactants); q=mcΔT; ΔG=ΔH−TΔS; spontaneous at constant T,P when ΔG<0.

items.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
items.content: Dynamic equilibrium is a state in a reversible process where the forward and reverse processes occur at equal rates.

items.title: Reversible Reaction
items.content: A reversible reaction can proceed in both forward and backward directions under suitable conditions.

items.title: Irreversible Reaction
items.content: An irreversible reaction proceeds predominantly in one direction under the given conditions.

items.title: Chemical Equilibrium
items.content: Chemical equilibrium is the dynamic state in which the rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal and macroscopic concentrations remain constant.

items.title: Characteristics of Equilibrium
items.content: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic, requires a reversible process, occurs in a closed system for ordinary treatment, and has constant macroscopic properties at equilibrium.

items.title: Law of Mass Action
items.content: At a fixed temperature, the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses or concentrations of reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.

items.title: Equilibrium Constant
items.content: The equilibrium constant expresses the ratio of equilibrium activities or concentrations of products to reactants according to the balanced equation.

items.title: Kc Definition
items.content: For a reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c[D]^d/[A]^a[B]^b at equilibrium.

items.title: Kp Definition
items.content: For gaseous reactions, Kp is expressed using the equilibrium partial pressures of gaseous species.

items.title: Homogeneous Equilibrium
items.content: A homogeneous equilibrium contains all reacting species in the same phase.

items.title: Heterogeneous Equilibrium
items.content: A heterogeneous equilibrium contains reacting species in more than one phase.

items.title: Equilibrium Expression
items.content: Only species whose activities change are included in the equilibrium expression; pure solids and pure liquids are omitted.

items.title: Reaction Quotient
items.content: The reaction quotient Q has the same mathematical form as the equilibrium constant but uses concentrations or partial pressures at any instant.

items.title: Q vs K Criterion
items.content: If Q < K the forward reaction is favoured; if Q > K the reverse reaction is favoured; if Q = K the system is at equilibrium.

items.title: Kc and Stoichiometry
items.content: Changing stoichiometric coefficients changes the numerical value of the equilibrium constant according to the transformed equation.

items.title: Kp and Kc Relation
items.content: For gaseous equilibria, Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn_g.

items.title: Gas Constant in Kp Relation
items.content: R is the gas constant and T is the absolute temperature in the relation Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn_g.

items.title: Effect of Equation Reversal
items.content: When a reaction equation is reversed, the new equilibrium constant is the reciprocal of the original: K_new = 1/K.

items.title: Effect of Multiplying Equation
items.content: If all stoichiometric coefficients are multiplied by n, the new equilibrium constant is K_new = K^n.

items.title: Effect of Adding Equations
items.content: When reactions are added, the overall equilibrium constant is the product of the individual equilibrium constants.

items.title: Magnitude of K
items.content: The magnitude of K indicates the relative extent to which reactants are converted into products at equilibrium.

items.title: Large K
items.content: A large equilibrium constant indicates that products are favoured at equilibrium.

items.title: Small K
items.content: A small equilibrium constant indicates that reactants are favoured at equilibrium.

items.title: Pure Solids in K
items.content: Pure solids are omitted from equilibrium constant expressions because their activities are treated as constant.

items.title: Pure Liquids in K
items.content: Pure liquids are omitted from equilibrium constant expressions because their activities are treated as constant.

items.title: Units of Equilibrium Constant
items.content: Depending on the form used and the convention adopted, equilibrium constants may carry units; thermodynamic equilibrium constants based on activities are dimensionless.

items.title: Le Chatelier Principle
items.content: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that tends to oppose the imposed change.

items.title: Effect of Concentration
items.content: Adding a reactant generally shifts equilibrium toward products, while adding a product generally shifts it toward reactants.

items.title: Effect of Pressure
items.content: For gaseous equilibria, increasing pressure generally favours the side with fewer moles of gas.

items.title: Effect of Volume
items.content: For gaseous equilibria, decreasing volume generally favours the side with fewer moles of gas.

items.title: Effect of Inert Gas Constant Volume
items.content: Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change the partial pressures of reacting gases and therefore does not shift the equilibrium.

items.title: Effect of Inert Gas Constant Pressure
items.content: Adding an inert gas at constant pressure can change the volume and may shift a gaseous equilibrium toward the side with more gaseous moles.

items.title: Effect of Temperature
items.content: Changing temperature changes the equilibrium constant and shifts equilibrium in the direction that absorbs the imposed heat change.

items.title: Catalyst and Equilibrium
items.content: A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions and does not change the equilibrium constant or equilibrium composition.

items.title: Equilibrium Constant and Temperature
items.content: The value of an equilibrium constant depends on temperature and is independent of the initial concentrations for a specified reaction.

items.title: Exothermic Equilibrium
items.content: For an exothermic forward reaction, increasing temperature generally shifts equilibrium toward reactants.

items.title: Endothermic Equilibrium
items.content: For an endothermic forward reaction, increasing temperature generally shifts equilibrium toward products.

items.title: Acid Base Equilibrium
items.content: Acid-base equilibrium involves reversible proton-transfer processes between acids, bases and their conjugate species.

items.title: Arrhenius Acid
items.content: An Arrhenius acid produces H+ or H3O+ in aqueous solution.

items.title: Arrhenius Base
items.content: An Arrhenius base produces OH− in aqueous solution.

items.title: Bronsted Lowry Acid
items.content: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor.

items.title: Bronsted Lowry Base
items.content: A Brønsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor.

items.title: Conjugate Acid
items.content: A conjugate acid is formed when a Brønsted-Lowry base accepts a proton.

items.title: Conjugate Base
items.content: A conjugate base is formed when a Brønsted-Lowry acid donates a proton.

items.title: Conjugate Acid-Base Pair
items.content: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by one proton.

items.title: Amphiprotic Species
items.content: An amphiprotic species can both donate and accept a proton, depending on the reaction.

items.title: Lewis Acid
items.content: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor.

items.title: Lewis Base
items.content: A Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.

items.title: Strength of Acid
items.content: Acid strength refers to the extent to which an acid ionises or donates protons in a given solvent.

items.title: Strength of Base
items.content: Base strength refers to the tendency of a base to accept protons or generate hydroxide ions in a given solvent.

items.title: Strong Electrolyte
items.content: A strong electrolyte ionises or dissociates almost completely in aqueous solution.

items.title: Weak Electrolyte
items.content: A weak electrolyte ionises or dissociates only partially in aqueous solution.

items.title: Degree of Ionisation
items.content: Degree of ionisation is the fraction of the initial amount of an electrolyte that ionises.

items.title: Ostwald Dilution Law
items.content: For a weak electrolyte AB ⇌ A+ + B− with concentration C and degree of dissociation α, K = Cα²/(1−α).

items.title: Ionisation Constant
items.content: An ionisation constant measures the equilibrium extent of ionisation of a weak acid or weak base.

items.title: Ka Definition
items.content: For HA ⇌ H+ + A−, Ka = [H+][A−]/[HA].

items.title: Kb Definition
items.content: For B + H2O ⇌ BH+ + OH−, Kb = [BH+][OH−]/[B].

items.title: pKa Definition
items.content: pKa = −log Ka.

items.title: pKb Definition
items.content: pKb = −log Kb.

items.title: Ka and Kb Relation
items.content: For a conjugate acid-base pair at a given temperature, Ka × Kb = Kw.

items.title: Ionic Product of Water
items.content: The ionic product of water is the product of hydrogen-ion and hydroxide-ion concentrations in aqueous solution.

items.title: Kw at 25 C
items.content: At 25 °C, Kw is approximately 1.0 × 10^−14 for dilute aqueous solutions.

items.title: pH Definition
items.content: pH = −log[H+] for hydrogen-ion concentration expressed in mol L^−1.

items.title: pOH Definition
items.content: pOH = −log[OH−] for hydroxide-ion concentration expressed in mol L^−1.

items.title: pH and pOH Relation
items.content: At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.

items.title: pH Strong Acid
items.content: For a strong monoprotic acid in dilute solution, [H+] is approximately equal to its analytical concentration, so pH = −log C.

items.title: pH Strong Base
items.content: For a strong monobasic base in dilute solution, [OH−] is approximately equal to its analytical concentration, so pOH = −log C and pH = 14 − pOH at 25 °C.

items.title: Common Ion Effect
items.content: The common ion effect is the suppression of ionisation of a weak electrolyte when a strong electrolyte provides an ion common to the equilibrium.

items.title: Buffer Solution
items.content: A buffer solution resists significant change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

items.title: Acidic Buffer
items.content: An acidic buffer generally consists of a weak acid and its salt with a strong base.

items.title: Basic Buffer
items.content: A basic buffer generally consists of a weak base and its salt with a strong acid.

items.title: Henderson Hasselbalch Acidic
items.content: For an acidic buffer, pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).

items.title: Henderson Hasselbalch Basic
items.content: For a basic buffer, pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base]).

items.title: Solubility Equilibrium
items.content: Solubility equilibrium is the dynamic equilibrium established between an undissolved sparingly soluble solid and its dissolved ions.

items.title: Solubility Product
items.content: The solubility product Ksp is the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of a sparingly soluble ionic solid, with pure solid omitted.

items.title: Ksp Definition
items.content: For MX(s) ⇌ M+ + X−, Ksp = [M+][X−].

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core relations: Kp=Kc(RT)^Δn_g; Q<K forward, Q>K reverse; Ka=[H+][A−]/[HA]; Kb=[BH+][OH−]/[B]; KaKb=Kw; pH=−log[H+]; pOH=−log[OH−]; at 25 °C pH+pOH=14; buffer pH=pKa+log(salt/acid).

items.title: Redox Reaction
items.content: A redox reaction is a reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.

items.title: Oxidation
items.content: Oxidation is loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number, addition of oxygen, or removal of hydrogen, depending on the context.

items.title: Reduction
items.content: Reduction is gain of electrons, decrease in oxidation number, removal of oxygen, or addition of hydrogen, depending on the context.

items.title: Oxidising Agent
items.content: An oxidising agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced during a redox reaction.

items.title: Reducing Agent
items.content: A reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidised during a redox reaction.

items.title: Oxidation Number
items.content: Oxidation number is the apparent charge assigned to an atom using prescribed rules for electron assignment.

items.title: Oxidation State
items.content: Oxidation state is another term commonly used for the oxidation number of an element in a species.

items.title: Rules Oxidation Number
items.content: Oxidation number is assigned using rules involving free elements, ions, oxygen, hydrogen, halogens and the algebraic sum of oxidation numbers.

items.title: Free Element Oxidation Number
items.content: The oxidation number of an element in its free elemental form is zero.

items.title: Monatomic Ion Oxidation Number
items.content: The oxidation number of a monatomic ion equals its ionic charge.

items.title: Hydrogen Oxidation Number
items.content: Hydrogen is generally +1 in compounds with non-metals and −1 in metal hydrides.

items.title: Oxygen Oxidation Number
items.content: Oxygen is generally −2, but shows −1 in peroxides and positive values in compounds with fluorine.

items.title: Fluorine Oxidation Number
items.content: Fluorine has oxidation number −1 in its compounds.

items.title: Alkali Metal Oxidation Number
items.content: Group 1 metals generally have oxidation number +1 in their compounds.

items.title: Alkaline Earth Oxidation Number
items.content: Group 2 metals generally have oxidation number +2 in their compounds.

items.title: Sum Oxidation Numbers Neutral
items.content: The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral compound is zero.

items.title: Sum Oxidation Numbers Ion
items.content: The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion equals the charge on that ion.

items.title: Oxidation Number Fraction
items.content: An average oxidation number may be fractional when equivalent atoms of an element have different actual oxidation states.

items.title: Oxidation Number Increase
items.content: An increase in oxidation number indicates oxidation.

items.title: Oxidation Number Decrease
items.content: A decrease in oxidation number indicates reduction.

items.title: Oxidation Process
items.content: Oxidation involves electron loss and is represented by an increase in oxidation number.

items.title: Reduction Process
items.content: Reduction involves electron gain and is represented by a decrease in oxidation number.

items.title: Electron Loss
items.content: Loss of electrons corresponds to oxidation.

items.title: Electron Gain
items.content: Gain of electrons corresponds to reduction.

items.title: Classical Oxidation
items.content: In the classical sense, oxidation may involve addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen.

items.title: Classical Reduction
items.content: In the classical sense, reduction may involve removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen.

items.title: Electronic Concept Redox
items.content: The electronic concept defines oxidation as electron loss and reduction as electron gain.

items.title: Oxidation and Reduction Together
items.content: Oxidation and reduction must occur together because electrons lost by one species are accepted by another.

items.title: Redox Pair
items.content: A redox pair consists of an oxidised and reduced form of a species that differ by electron transfer.

items.title: Conjugate Redox Pair
items.content: A conjugate redox pair represents the oxidised and reduced forms involved in a redox process.

items.title: Disproportionation
items.content: Disproportionation is a redox process in which the same element in one oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

items.title: Comproportionation
items.content: Comproportionation is a redox process in which two oxidation states of the same element form an intermediate oxidation state.

items.title: Redox in Ionic Reactions
items.content: In ionic redox reactions, oxidation and reduction can be identified by changes in oxidation numbers of the participating ions.

items.title: Redox in Molecular Reactions
items.content: In molecular redox reactions, oxidation states help identify the species undergoing oxidation and reduction.

items.title: Redox Indicator
items.content: A redox indicator changes colour over a characteristic range of electrode potential during a redox titration.

items.title: Balancing Redox Equations
items.content: Redox equations are balanced by conserving atoms and charge while accounting for electron transfer.

items.title: Oxidation Number Method
items.content: The oxidation number method balances redox equations by equalising the total increase and decrease in oxidation numbers.

items.title: Step Oxidation Number Method
items.content: The oxidation number method involves assigning oxidation states, identifying changes, equalising electron changes, and then balancing remaining atoms and charge.

items.title: Charge Balance
items.content: A correctly balanced ionic redox equation must have the same total charge on both sides.

items.title: Atom Balance
items.content: A correctly balanced chemical equation must contain equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides.

items.title: Electron Balance
items.content: In a balanced redox equation, total electrons lost during oxidation equal total electrons gained during reduction.

items.title: Acidic Medium Balance
items.content: In acidic medium, H2O balances oxygen, H+ balances hydrogen, and electrons balance charge.

items.title: Basic Medium Balance
items.content: In basic medium, H2O and OH− are used to balance oxygen and hydrogen, followed by electron balancing.

items.title: Half Reaction Method
items.content: The half-reaction method separates oxidation and reduction into two half-reactions and then combines them after balancing electrons.

items.title: Oxidation Half Reaction
items.content: An oxidation half-reaction represents the species losing electrons.

items.title: Reduction Half Reaction
items.content: A reduction half-reaction represents the species gaining electrons.

items.title: Adding Half Reactions
items.content: After balancing both half-reactions, they are added so that electrons cancel and the overall equation is obtained.

items.title: Electron Cancellation
items.content: The number of electrons in the oxidation and reduction half-reactions must be made equal before addition.

items.title: Acidic Medium H2O
items.content: In acidic-medium balancing, water is added to balance oxygen atoms.

items.title: Acidic Medium H+
items.content: In acidic-medium balancing, H+ ions are added to balance hydrogen atoms.

items.title: Acidic Medium Charge
items.content: Electrons are added to acidic-medium half-reactions to equalise total charge.

items.title: Basic Medium OH−
items.content: In basic-medium balancing, OH− ions are used to balance hydrogen after oxygen has been balanced with water.

items.title: Basic Medium H2O
items.content: Water is used in basic-medium balancing to balance oxygen and hydrogen as required.

items.title: Basic Medium Charge
items.content: Electrons are added in the appropriate half-reaction to balance charge in basic medium.

items.title: Disproportionation Identification
items.content: A disproportionation reaction is identified when the same element undergoes both oxidation and reduction.

items.title: Redox Reaction Identification
items.content: A reaction is redox when at least one element increases and another decreases in oxidation number.

items.title: Oxidising Strength
items.content: Oxidising strength is the tendency of a species to accept electrons and undergo reduction.

items.title: Reducing Strength
items.content: Reducing strength is the tendency of a species to donate electrons and undergo oxidation.

items.title: Electrochemical Series
items.content: The electrochemical series arranges redox couples according to their standard reduction potentials.

items.title: Standard Reduction Potential
items.content: Standard reduction potential E° is the electrode potential for a reduction half-reaction measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions.

items.title: Standard Oxidation Potential
items.content: Standard oxidation potential corresponds to the potential for the reverse oxidation process under standard conditions.

items.title: E°cell Relation
items.content: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, using standard reduction potentials.

items.title: Cell Potential Sign
items.content: For a spontaneous galvanic redox reaction under standard conditions, E°cell is positive.

items.title: Spontaneous Redox Criterion
items.content: Under standard conditions, a redox reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous in the written direction when E°cell > 0.

items.title: Oxidation at Anode
items.content: Oxidation always occurs at the anode.

items.title: Reduction at Cathode
items.content: Reduction always occurs at the cathode.

items.title: Anode Sign Galvanic
items.content: In a galvanic cell, the anode is negative relative to the cathode.

items.title: Cathode Sign Galvanic
items.content: In a galvanic cell, the cathode is positive relative to the anode.

items.title: Electron Flow Galvanic
items.content: Electrons flow through the external circuit from the anode toward the cathode in a galvanic cell.

items.title: Salt Bridge Role
items.content: A salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality and completes the internal ionic circuit of a galvanic cell.

items.title: Redox Titration
items.content: A redox titration determines the amount or concentration of a substance through a reaction involving electron transfer.

items.title: Permanganate Redox
items.content: Permanganate ion is a strong oxidising agent and is commonly used in acidic-medium redox titrations.

items.title: Dichromate Redox
items.content: Dichromate ion is a strong oxidising agent and is commonly used in acidic-medium redox titrations.

items.title: Equivalent Concept Redox
items.content: In redox reactions, one equivalent corresponds to the amount of substance that transfers one mole of electrons under the specified reaction.

items.title: n-Factor Redox
items.content: For a redox substance, the n-factor is the number of electrons lost or gained per formula unit in the specified reaction.

items.title: Equivalent Mass Redox
items.content: Equivalent mass = molar mass / n-factor for the specified redox reaction.

items.title: Internal Redox Reaction
items.content: An internal redox reaction is a redox process occurring between different parts or oxidation states within the same chemical species or system.

items.title: Auto Redox Reaction
items.content: Auto-redox is another term used for disproportionation, where the same element is both oxidised and reduced.

items.title: Oxidation Number and n-Factor
items.content: For redox reactions, the n-factor is determined from the total change in oxidation number or electrons transferred per formula unit.

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core ideas: oxidation = electron loss/increase in oxidation number; reduction = electron gain/decrease; oxidising agent is reduced; reducing agent is oxidised; balance electrons in redox equations; E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.

chapters.name: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

items.title: Organic Chemistry
items.content: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds, especially their structures, properties, reactions and preparation.

items.title: Tetravalency of Carbon
items.content: Carbon has four valence electrons and commonly forms four covalent bonds to complete its valence shell.

items.title: Catenation
items.content: Catenation is the ability of carbon atoms to form stable covalent bonds with one another, producing chains and rings.

items.title: Hybridisation Carbon
items.content: Carbon commonly exhibits sp3, sp2 and sp hybridisation in organic compounds.

items.title: Sigma Bond Carbon
items.content: A sigma bond is formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis.

items.title: Pi Bond Carbon
items.content: A pi bond is formed by lateral overlap of parallel orbitals and occurs in addition to a sigma bond in multiple bonds.

items.title: Structural Formula
items.content: A structural formula shows how atoms are connected within an organic molecule.

items.title: Condensed Formula
items.content: A condensed formula represents groups of atoms in a shortened structural form.

items.title: Bond Line Formula
items.content: A bond-line formula represents carbon skeletons using lines, with carbon atoms at line ends and vertices and attached hydrogens usually omitted.

items.title: Lewis Structure Organic
items.content: A Lewis structure shows valence electrons, bonds and lone pairs of an organic species.

items.title: Functional Group
items.content: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic chemical properties and reactions of an organic compound.

items.title: Homologous Series
items.content: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds having the same functional group and general formula, with successive members differing by CH2.

items.title: Homologue
items.content: A homologue is an individual member of a homologous series.

items.title: General Formula Alkane
items.content: Acyclic saturated hydrocarbons have the general formula CnH2n+2.

items.title: General Formula Alkene
items.content: Acyclic hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon double bond generally have the formula CnH2n.

items.title: General Formula Alkyne
items.content: Acyclic hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon triple bond generally have the formula CnH2n−2.

items.title: General Formula Monocyclic Hydrocarbon
items.content: A monocyclic saturated hydrocarbon generally has the formula CnH2n.

items.title: Degree of Unsaturation
items.content: Degree of unsaturation counts rings and pi bonds present in a molecular structure.

items.title: IHD Formula
items.content: For a hydrocarbon CcHh, degree of unsaturation = (2c + 2 − h)/2.

items.title: Saturated Compound
items.content: A saturated organic compound contains only single carbon-carbon bonds in its carbon framework.

items.title: Unsaturated Compound
items.content: An unsaturated organic compound contains at least one carbon-carbon double or triple bond.

items.title: Acyclic Compound
items.content: An acyclic compound has an open-chain carbon framework rather than a ring.

items.title: Cyclic Compound
items.content: A cyclic compound contains one or more rings of atoms.

items.title: Alicyclic Compound
items.content: An alicyclic compound is cyclic but behaves broadly like an aliphatic compound rather than an aromatic compound.

items.title: Aromatic Compound
items.content: An aromatic compound contains a cyclic conjugated system with aromatic stabilization.

items.title: Heterocyclic Compound
items.content: A heterocyclic compound contains a ring with at least one atom other than carbon.

items.title: Aliphatic Compound
items.content: Aliphatic compounds are non-aromatic organic compounds that may be open-chain or cyclic.

items.title: Classification by Functional Group
items.content: Organic compounds can be classified according to the characteristic functional group present in their structures.

items.title: IUPAC Nomenclature
items.content: IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic rules for assigning unique names to organic compounds.

items.title: Parent Chain
items.content: The parent chain is the principal carbon chain selected as the basis of an organic compound's systematic name.

items.title: Longest Chain Rule
items.content: The parent structure is selected according to IUPAC rules, generally including the principal functional group and the maximum appropriate number of skeletal atoms.

items.title: Numbering Parent Chain
items.content: The parent chain is numbered to give the principal functional group and other required features the lowest possible locants according to IUPAC priority rules.

items.title: Lowest Locant Rule
items.content: When choosing between equivalent numbering directions, the direction giving the lowest appropriate set of locants is preferred.

items.title: Substituent
items.content: A substituent is an atom or group attached to the selected parent structure in place of a hydrogen atom.

items.title: Alkyl Group
items.content: An alkyl group is a monovalent hydrocarbon group obtained by removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane.

items.title: Methyl Group
items.content: The methyl group is −CH3.

items.title: Ethyl Group
items.content: The ethyl group is −C2H5 or −CH2CH3.

items.title: Propyl Group
items.content: The propyl group is −C3H7 and can occur as n-propyl or propan-2-yl forms.

items.title: Isopropyl Group
items.content: Isopropyl, systematically propan-2-yl, has the structure −CH(CH3)2.

items.title: tert-Butyl Group
items.content: tert-Butyl, systematically 1,1-dimethylethyl, has the structure −C(CH3)3.

items.title: Primary Carbon
items.content: A primary carbon atom is directly bonded to one other carbon atom.

items.title: Secondary Carbon
items.content: A secondary carbon atom is directly bonded to two other carbon atoms.

items.title: Tertiary Carbon
items.content: A tertiary carbon atom is directly bonded to three other carbon atoms.

items.title: Quaternary Carbon
items.content: A quaternary carbon atom is directly bonded to four other carbon atoms.

items.title: Primary Hydrogen
items.content: A primary hydrogen is attached to a primary carbon atom.

items.title: Secondary Hydrogen
items.content: A secondary hydrogen is attached to a secondary carbon atom.

items.title: Tertiary Hydrogen
items.content: A tertiary hydrogen is attached to a tertiary carbon atom.

items.title: Primary Alcohol
items.content: A primary alcohol has the hydroxyl-bearing carbon attached to one other carbon atom, except methanol which is treated separately.

items.title: Secondary Alcohol
items.content: A secondary alcohol has the hydroxyl-bearing carbon attached to two carbon atoms.

items.title: Tertiary Alcohol
items.content: A tertiary alcohol has the hydroxyl-bearing carbon attached to three carbon atoms.

items.title: Primary Amine
items.content: A primary amine has one carbon-containing group attached to nitrogen, along with two hydrogens.

items.title: Secondary Amine
items.content: A secondary amine has two carbon-containing groups attached to nitrogen and one hydrogen.

items.title: Tertiary Amine
items.content: A tertiary amine has three carbon-containing groups attached to nitrogen and no N−H bond.

items.title: Nucleophile
items.content: A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre.

items.title: Electrophile
items.content: An electrophile is an electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair.

items.title: Nucleophilic Reagent
items.content: A nucleophilic reagent provides an electron pair for bond formation with an electrophilic centre.

items.title: Electrophilic Reagent
items.content: An electrophilic reagent accepts an electron pair from an electron-rich site.

items.title: Homolytic Fission
items.content: Homolytic bond fission divides a covalent bond so that each bonded atom takes one electron.

items.title: Heterolytic Fission
items.content: Heterolytic bond fission divides a covalent bond so that both bonding electrons go to one atom.

items.title: Free Radical
items.content: A free radical is a species containing an unpaired electron and is commonly formed by homolytic bond fission.

items.title: Carbocation
items.content: A carbocation is an organic cation in which a carbon atom bears a positive charge.

items.title: Carbanion
items.content: A carbanion is an organic anion in which a carbon atom bears a negative charge.

items.title: Carbocation Stability
items.content: For simple alkyl carbocations, stability generally follows tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl due to electron-releasing effects and hyperconjugation.

items.title: Carbanion Stability
items.content: For simple alkyl carbanions, alkyl substitution generally destabilises the negative charge because alkyl groups are electron-releasing.

items.title: Inductive Effect
items.content: The inductive effect is the permanent polarisation of sigma bonds caused by electronegativity differences and transmitted through a carbon chain.

items.title: Electron Releasing Inductive Effect
items.content: A +I group releases electron density through sigma bonds toward the attached carbon framework.

items.title: Electron Withdrawing Inductive Effect
items.content: A −I group withdraws electron density through sigma bonds from the attached carbon framework.

items.title: Resonance Effect
items.content: The resonance effect involves delocalisation of pi electrons or lone pairs through a conjugated system.

items.title: Mesomeric Effect
items.content: Mesomeric effect is another term for the resonance effect involving electron donation or withdrawal through a conjugated system.

items.title: Hyperconjugation
items.content: Hyperconjugation is delocalisation involving electrons of a sigma bond adjacent to a pi system or electron-deficient centre.

items.title: Electromeric Effect
items.content: The electromeric effect is a temporary complete transfer of a shared pi-electron pair toward one atom of a multiple bond under the influence of an attacking reagent.

items.title: Steric Effect
items.content: Steric effects arise when the spatial arrangement and size of groups hinder interactions or affect the stability and reactivity of molecules.

items.title: Resonance Structures
items.content: Resonance structures are alternative Lewis representations of the same species that differ only in electron distribution, not atom connectivity.

items.title: Resonance Hybrid
items.content: The actual resonance-stabilised molecule is represented by a resonance hybrid rather than any single canonical structure.

items.title: Aromaticity
items.content: Aromaticity is the enhanced stability associated with a cyclic, planar, conjugated pi-electron system satisfying the required electron-count rule.

items.title: Markovnikov Rule
items.content: For addition of an unsymmetrical reagent such as HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen generally adds to the carbon already bearing more hydrogen atoms and the other part adds to the more substituted carbon.

items.title: Peroxide Effect
items.content: In the presence of peroxides, HBr can add to an unsymmetrical alkene predominantly in the anti-Markovnikov orientation through a radical mechanism.

items.title: Functional Group Priority
items.content: For systematic nomenclature, functional groups are assigned priority according to IUPAC rules so that the principal characteristic group determines the suffix.

items.title: Distillation
items.content: Distillation separates liquid components based mainly on differences in boiling points and is used for purification of liquids.

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core ideas: carbon tetravalency and catenation; functional groups; homologous series; IUPAC nomenclature; nucleophiles/electrophiles; homolytic/heterolytic fission; carbocations/carbanions; inductive, resonance, hyperconjugation and electromeric effects; aromaticity; Markovnikov and peroxide effects.

items.title: Hydrocarbon
items.content: A hydrocarbon is an organic compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.

items.title: Classification Hydrocarbons
items.content: Hydrocarbons are broadly classified as aliphatic and aromatic; aliphatic compounds include saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.

items.title: Alkane
items.content: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing only carbon-carbon single bonds.

items.title: Alkene
items.content: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.

items.title: Alkyne
items.content: Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon triple bond.

items.title: Aromatic Hydrocarbon
items.content: Aromatic hydrocarbons contain aromatic ring systems with delocalised pi electrons.

items.title: General Formula Alkane
items.content: Acyclic alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2.

items.title: General Formula Alkene
items.content: Acyclic alkenes containing one double bond have the general formula CnH2n.

items.title: General Formula Alkyne
items.content: Acyclic alkynes containing one triple bond have the general formula CnH2n−2.

items.title: General Formula Cycloalkane
items.content: Monocyclic saturated hydrocarbons generally have the formula CnH2n.

items.title: Alkane C-C Bond
items.content: The carbon-carbon bond in an alkane is a sigma bond formed by overlap of sp3 hybrid orbitals.

items.title: Alkane Hybridisation
items.content: Carbon atoms in alkanes are generally sp3 hybridised.

items.title: Alkane Shape
items.content: Each sp3-hybridised carbon in an alkane has approximately tetrahedral geometry with a bond angle near 109.5°.

items.title: Alkane Nomenclature
items.content: Alkanes are named by selecting the appropriate parent chain, numbering it and identifying substituents according to IUPAC rules.

items.title: Alkane Isomerism
items.content: Alkanes can exhibit structural isomerism, especially chain isomerism, when the carbon skeleton can be arranged differently.

items.title: Chain Isomerism
items.content: Chain isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons.

items.title: Conformational Isomerism
items.content: Conformational isomerism arises from different spatial arrangements produced by rotation about single bonds.

items.title: Ethane Conformations
items.content: Ethane commonly exists in staggered and eclipsed conformations due to rotation about its carbon-carbon single bond.

items.title: Staggered Conformation
items.content: In a staggered conformation, bonds on adjacent carbon atoms are maximally separated around the central carbon-carbon bond.

items.title: Eclipsed Conformation
items.content: In an eclipsed conformation, bonds on adjacent carbon atoms are aligned when viewed along the central carbon-carbon bond.

items.title: Newman Projection
items.content: A Newman projection represents the conformation of a molecule viewed along a selected carbon-carbon bond.

items.title: Sawhorse Projection
items.content: A sawhorse projection represents the three-dimensional arrangement around a carbon-carbon single bond using an oblique view.

items.title: Torsional Strain
items.content: Torsional strain arises from repulsion between bonding electron pairs when bonds on adjacent atoms become eclipsed.

items.title: Angle Strain
items.content: Angle strain occurs when bond angles deviate significantly from their preferred values.

items.title: Alkane Preparation
items.content: Alkanes can be prepared by methods including hydrogenation of unsaturated hydrocarbons, Wurtz reaction and decarboxylation.

items.title: Wurtz Reaction
items.content: Wurtz reaction couples two alkyl halide molecules with sodium in dry ether to form a higher alkane.

items.title: Decarboxylation Alkane
items.content: Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime produces an alkane containing one fewer carbon atom than the original acid.

items.title: Kolbe Electrolysis
items.content: Kolbe electrolysis involves electrolysis of aqueous carboxylate salts to produce hydrocarbons by coupling of alkyl radicals.

items.title: Sodium Propionate Decarboxylation
items.content: Sodium propionate on heating with soda lime gives ethane, with loss of carbon dioxide.

items.title: Combustion Alkane
items.content: Alkanes undergo combustion in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water when combustion is complete.

items.title: Halogenation Alkane
items.content: Alkanes react with halogens under suitable conditions, commonly light or heat, through free-radical substitution.

items.title: Free Radical Substitution
items.content: Free-radical substitution replaces a hydrogen atom of an alkane with a halogen atom through radical intermediates.

items.title: Chlorination Methane
items.content: Methane reacts with chlorine in the presence of light or heat to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.

items.title: Methane Chlorination Mechanism
items.content: Chlorination of methane proceeds by initiation, propagation and termination steps involving chlorine and methyl radicals.

items.title: Initiation Step
items.content: In radical chlorination, light or heat causes homolytic cleavage of Cl2 to generate chlorine radicals.

items.title: Propagation Step
items.content: Propagation consists of radical reactions that consume one radical and generate another, allowing the chain reaction to continue.

items.title: Termination Step
items.content: Termination occurs when radicals combine to form stable molecules and remove radicals from the chain.

items.title: Relative Reactivity Halogens
items.content: Halogenation reactivity and selectivity depend on the halogen; fluorination is extremely vigorous while chlorination is generally more reactive than bromination.

items.title: Alkene Structure
items.content: Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond consisting of one sigma bond and one pi bond.

items.title: Alkene Hybridisation
items.content: The carbon atoms involved in a carbon-carbon double bond are generally sp2 hybridised.

items.title: Alkene Geometry
items.content: The carbon atoms of a double bond are approximately trigonal planar, with bond angles near 120°.

items.title: Geometrical Isomerism
items.content: Geometrical isomerism occurs when restricted rotation around a double bond produces distinct spatial arrangements of substituents.

items.title: Cis Trans Isomerism
items.content: Cis-trans isomerism is a form of geometrical isomerism in which similar or specified groups are arranged on the same or opposite sides of a double bond.

items.title: E Z Isomerism
items.content: E-Z nomenclature distinguishes geometrical isomers using priority rules for substituents attached to the double-bonded atoms.

items.title: Alkene Nomenclature
items.content: Alkenes are named by selecting a parent chain containing the double bond, numbering it to give the double bond the appropriate lowest locant, and identifying substituents.

items.title: Alkene Preparation
items.content: Alkenes can be prepared by elimination reactions such as dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides and dehydration of alcohols.

items.title: Dehydrohalogenation
items.content: Dehydrohalogenation removes hydrogen halide from an alkyl halide to form an alkene, commonly using alcoholic KOH.

items.title: Zaitsev Rule
items.content: In many elimination reactions, the major alkene is the more substituted alkene when structural and reaction conditions permit.

items.title: Dehydration Alcohol
items.content: Alcohols can undergo acid-catalysed dehydration on heating to form alkenes and water.

items.title: Dehalogenation Vicinal Dihalide
items.content: Vicinal dihalides can undergo dehalogenation with suitable metals such as zinc to form alkenes.

items.title: Alkene Addition
items.content: The carbon-carbon double bond of an alkene commonly undergoes addition reactions across the pi bond.

items.title: Electrophilic Addition
items.content: Electrophilic addition involves attack of an electrophile on the electron-rich pi bond followed by formation of new sigma bonds.

items.title: Hydrogenation Alkene
items.content: Hydrogenation adds H2 across a carbon-carbon double bond, generally using a catalyst such as Ni, Pt or Pd, to form an alkane.

items.title: Halogenation Alkene
items.content: Alkenes react with halogens such as Br2 or Cl2 by addition across the carbon-carbon double bond.

items.title: Hydrohalogenation
items.content: Hydrohalogenation adds HX such as HCl or HBr across an alkene double bond.

items.title: Hydration Alkene
items.content: Hydration adds H and OH across an alkene double bond to form an alcohol.

items.title: Markovnikov Addition
items.content: For addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene under ordinary ionic conditions, hydrogen generally attaches to the carbon already bearing more hydrogen atoms.

items.title: Anti Markovnikov Addition
items.content: Anti-Markovnikov addition places the incoming group opposite to the orientation predicted by Markovnikov's rule under appropriate radical conditions.

items.title: Peroxide Effect HBr
items.content: In the presence of peroxides, HBr adds to an unsymmetrical alkene predominantly by a radical pathway giving anti-Markovnikov orientation.

items.title: Ozonolysis
items.content: Ozonolysis cleaves a carbon-carbon double bond and, after appropriate work-up, gives carbonyl compounds that help identify the original alkene structure.

items.title: Oxidation Alkene
items.content: Alkenes can undergo oxidation reactions that convert the double bond into oxygen-containing products depending on the oxidising conditions.

items.title: Baeyer Test
items.content: Dilute alkaline KMnO4 decolourisation is a classical test for unsaturation due to oxidation of the multiple bond.

items.title: Alkyne Structure
items.content: Alkynes contain a carbon-carbon triple bond consisting of one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

items.title: Alkyne Hybridisation
items.content: The carbon atoms involved in a carbon-carbon triple bond are generally sp hybridised.

items.title: Alkyne Nomenclature
items.content: Alkynes are named by selecting a parent chain containing the triple bond and assigning the appropriate locant to the multiple bond.

items.title: Alkyne Preparation
items.content: Alkynes can be prepared by double dehydrohalogenation of suitable vicinal or geminal dihalides.

items.title: Double Dehydrohalogenation
items.content: Two successive elimination reactions can remove two molecules of hydrogen halide from a dihalide to form an alkyne.

items.title: Alkyne Addition
items.content: The carbon-carbon triple bond can undergo addition reactions, often in stages, across its pi bonds.

items.title: Hydrogenation Alkyne
items.content: Complete catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne adds two molecules of H2 to form an alkane.

items.title: Partial Hydrogenation Alkyne
items.content: Controlled hydrogenation of an alkyne can stop at an alkene stage.

items.title: Lindlar Catalyst
items.content: Lindlar catalyst enables partial hydrogenation of an alkyne to a cis-alkene under suitable conditions.

items.title: Alkyne Hydration
items.content: Hydration of an alkyne gives an enol that generally undergoes tautomerisation to a carbonyl compound.

items.title: Terminal Alkyne Acidity
items.content: Terminal alkynes are more acidic than alkenes and alkanes because the conjugate base places negative charge on an sp-hybridised carbon.

items.title: Ammoniacal Silver Nitrate Test
items.content: Terminal alkynes can form precipitates of silver acetylides with ammoniacal silver nitrate.

items.title: Ammoniacal Cuprous Chloride Test
items.content: Terminal alkynes can form coloured copper acetylide precipitates with ammoniacal cuprous chloride.

items.title: Aromaticity Benzene
items.content: Benzene is aromatic because it is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated and contains six delocalised pi electrons.

items.title: Benzene Structure
items.content: Benzene has six carbon atoms arranged in a planar hexagonal ring with equivalent carbon-carbon bonds.

items.title: Benzene Resonance
items.content: Benzene is represented by resonance structures, while its actual structure has delocalised pi electrons and equivalent C-C bonds.

items.title: Benzene Electrophilic Substitution
items.content: Benzene commonly undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions in which a hydrogen atom is replaced while aromaticity is restored.

items.title: Chapter Quick Reference
items.content: Core ideas: alkanes are saturated; alkenes contain C=C; alkynes contain C≡C; alkanes mainly undergo substitution, while alkenes and alkynes commonly undergo addition; benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution; remember Wurtz, decarboxylation, Zaitsev rule, Markovnikov rule, peroxide effect, ozonolysis and key tests.

items.title: Set
items.content: A well-defined collection of distinct objects.

items.title: Subset
items.content: A is a subset of B if every element of A is also an element of B. Notation: A ⊆ B.

items.title: Proper Subset
items.content: A is a proper subset of B if A ⊆ B and A ≠ B. Notation: A ⊂ B.

items.title: Universal Set
items.content: The set containing all objects under consideration in a particular discussion.

items.title: Empty Set
items.content: A set containing no elements. Notation: ∅ or { }.

items.title: Finite Set
items.content: A set containing a finite number of elements.

items.title: Infinite Set
items.content: A set containing infinitely many elements.

items.title: Number of Subsets
items.content: If a finite set has n elements, the total number of subsets is 2^n.

items.title: Number of Proper Subsets
items.content: If a finite set has n elements, the number of proper subsets is 2^n − 1.

items.title: Power Set
items.content: The set of all subsets of a set A is called the power set of A and is denoted by P(A).

items.title: Union
items.content: The union A ∪ B contains elements belonging to A or B or both.

items.title: Intersection
items.content: The intersection A ∩ B contains elements common to both A and B.

items.title: Difference of Sets
items.content: A − B contains elements that belong to A but do not belong to B.

items.title: Complement of a Set
items.content: The complement of A contains elements of the universal set that are not in A. It is denoted by A′ or Aᶜ.

items.title: Intersection with Universal Set
items.content: A ∩ U = A.

items.title: Union with Universal Set
items.content: A ∪ U = U.

items.title: Cardinality of Union
items.content: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

items.title: Cardinality of Difference
items.content: n(A − B) = n(A) − n(A ∩ B).

items.title: Disjoint Sets
items.content: Two sets are disjoint if they have no common element, so A ∩ B = ∅.

items.title: Commutative Union
items.content: A ∪ B = B ∪ A.

items.title: Commutative Intersection
items.content: A ∩ B = B ∩ A.

items.title: Ordered Pair
items.content: An ordered pair is written as (a, b), where a is the first component and b is the second component.

items.title: Cartesian Product
items.content: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a,b) where a ∈ A and b ∈ B.

items.title: Number of Elements in Cartesian Product
items.content: If n(A)=m and n(B)=n, then n(A × B)=mn.

items.title: Relation
items.content: A relation from A to B is a subset of A × B.

items.title: Domain of Relation
items.content: The domain of a relation consists of the first components of its ordered pairs.

items.title: Range of Relation
items.content: The range of a relation consists of the second components that occur in its ordered pairs.

items.title: Function
items.content: A function from A to B assigns exactly one element of B to every element of A.

items.title: Domain of Function
items.content: The set of all input values for which a function is defined.

items.title: Codomain
items.content: The set into which a function maps the elements of its domain.

items.title: Range of Function
items.content: The set of actual output values produced by a function.

items.title: Range and Codomain
items.content: The range of a function is a subset of its codomain.

items.title: One-One Function
items.content: A function is one-one if distinct elements of the domain have distinct images.

items.title: Many-One Function
items.content: A function is many-one if two or more distinct elements of the domain can have the same image.

items.title: Onto Function
items.content: A function is onto if every element of its codomain is the image of at least one element of the domain.

items.title: Into Function
items.content: A function is into if at least one element of the codomain is not an image of any element of the domain.

items.title: Bijective Function
items.content: A function that is both one-one and onto is called bijective.

items.title: Identity Function
items.content: The identity function on A maps every element to itself: f(x)=x.

items.title: Constant Function
items.content: A function whose value is the same for every element of its domain: f(x)=c.

items.title: Linear Function
items.content: A linear function can be written as f(x)=ax+b, where a and b are constants.

items.title: Modulus Function
items.content: f(x)=|x| = x for x≥0 and −x for x<0.

items.title: Signum Function
items.content: sgn(x)=1 for x>0, 0 for x=0, and −1 for x<0.

items.title: Greatest Integer Function
items.content: The greatest integer function [x] gives the greatest integer less than or equal to x.

items.title: Vertical Line Test
items.content: A graph represents a function of x if every vertical line intersects the graph at most once.

items.title: Function Equality
items.content: Two functions are equal when they have the same domain and give the same value for every element of that domain.

items.title: Real-Valued Function
items.content: A function whose domain and codomain are subsets of the real numbers.

items.title: Natural-Valued Function
items.content: A function whose output values belong to the set of natural numbers.

items.title: Integer-Valued Function
items.content: A function whose output values belong to the set of integers.

items.title: Rational-Valued Function
items.content: A function whose output values belong to the set of rational numbers.

items.title: Function as a Mapping
items.content: A function maps every domain element to exactly one codomain element.

items.title: Function Range
items.content: For a function f:A→B, Range(f) ⊆ B.

items.title: One-One and Onto
items.content: A function is bijective exactly when it is both one-one and onto.

items.title: Angle in Radians
items.content: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length equals the radius.

items.title: Degree-Radian Conversion
items.content: 180° = π radians; θ° = θπ/180 radians.

items.title: Radian-Degree Conversion
items.content: 1 radian = 180°/π.

items.title: Sine Function
items.content: sin θ = perpendicular/hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle.

items.title: Cosine Function
items.content: cos θ = base/hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle.

items.title: Tangent Function
items.content: tan θ = perpendicular/base in a right-angled triangle.

items.title: Cosecant Function
items.content: cosec θ = 1/sin θ, wherever sin θ ≠ 0.

items.title: Secant Function
items.content: sec θ = 1/cos θ, wherever cos θ ≠ 0.

items.title: Cotangent Function
items.content: cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ/sin θ, wherever defined.

items.title: Reciprocal Identity 1
items.content: cosec θ = 1/sin θ.

items.title: Reciprocal Identity 2
items.content: sec θ = 1/cos θ.

items.title: Reciprocal Identity 3
items.content: cot θ = 1/tan θ.

items.title: Quotient Identity 1
items.content: tan θ = sin θ/cos θ, wherever cos θ ≠ 0.

items.title: Quotient Identity 2
items.content: cot θ = cos θ/sin θ, wherever sin θ ≠ 0.

items.title: Pythagorean Identity 1
items.content: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

items.title: Pythagorean Identity 2
items.content: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ.

items.title: Pythagorean Identity 3
items.content: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

items.title: Even-Odd Property of Sine
items.content: sin(−θ) = −sin θ.

items.title: Even-Odd Property of Cosine
items.content: cos(−θ) = cos θ.

items.title: Even-Odd Property of Tangent
items.content: tan(−θ) = −tan θ.

items.title: Complementary Angle Sine
items.content: sin(π/2 − θ) = cos θ.

items.title: Complementary Angle Cosine
items.content: cos(π/2 − θ) = sin θ.

items.title: Complementary Angle Tangent
items.content: tan(π/2 − θ) = cot θ.

items.title: Complementary Angle Cotangent
items.content: cot(π/2 − θ) = tan θ.

items.title: Complementary Angle Secant
items.content: sec(π/2 − θ) = cosec θ.

items.title: Complementary Angle Cosecant
items.content: cosec(π/2 − θ) = sec θ.

items.title: Period of Sine
items.content: The period of sin x is 2π.

items.title: Period of Cosine
items.content: The period of cos x is 2π.

items.title: Period of Tangent
items.content: The period of tan x is π.

items.title: Standard Value: 90°
items.content: sin 90° = 1, cos 90° = 0; tan 90° is not defined.

items.title: Signs in Quadrants
items.content: ASTC rule: All are positive in I; sine in II; tangent in III; cosine in IV.

items.title: Sine Addition Formula
items.content: sin(A+B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B.

items.title: Sine Subtraction Formula
items.content: sin(A−B) = sin A cos B − cos A sin B.

items.title: Cosine Addition Formula
items.content: cos(A+B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B.

items.title: Cosine Subtraction Formula
items.content: cos(A−B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B.

items.title: Tangent Addition Formula
items.content: tan(A+B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B), when defined.

items.title: Tangent Subtraction Formula
items.content: tan(A−B) = (tan A − tan B)/(1 + tan A tan B), when defined.

items.title: Double Angle Sine
items.content: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A.

items.title: Double Angle Cosine
items.content: cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A.

items.title: Double Angle Tangent
items.content: tan 2A = 2tan A/(1 − tan²A), when defined.

items.title: Half Angle Sine
items.content: sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2.

items.title: Half Angle Cosine
items.content: cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2.

items.title: Half Angle Tangent
items.content: tan²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/(1 + cos A), where defined.

items.title: Product-to-Sum: 2sinAcosB
items.content: 2sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A−B).

items.title: Product-to-Sum: 2cosAsinB
items.content: 2cos A sin B = sin(A+B) − sin(A−B).

items.title: Product-to-Sum: 2cosAcosB
items.content: 2cos A cos B = cos(A+B) + cos(A−B).

items.title: Product-to-Sum: 2sinAsinB
items.content: 2sin A sin B = cos(A−B) − cos(A+B).

items.title: General Solution of sin x = 0
items.content: x = nπ, where n ∈ Z.

items.title: General Solution of cos x = 0
items.content: x = (2n+1)π/2, where n ∈ Z.

items.title: General Solution of tan x = 0
items.content: x = nπ, where n ∈ Z.

items.title: Powers of i
items.content: i⁰ = 1, i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Powers repeat with period 4.

items.title: Complex Number
items.content: A complex number is of the form z = a + ib, where a,b ∈ R and i² = −1.

items.title: Real Part
items.content: For z = a + ib, Re(z) = a.

items.title: Imaginary Part
items.content: For z = a + ib, Im(z) = b.

items.title: Purely Real Complex Number
items.content: z = a + 0i = a is purely real.

items.title: Purely Imaginary Complex Number
items.content: z = 0 + ib = ib is purely imaginary.

items.title: Equality of Complex Numbers
items.content: a + ib = c + id if and only if a = c and b = d.

items.title: Addition of Complex Numbers
items.content: (a+ib)+(c+id) = (a+c)+i(b+d).

items.title: Subtraction of Complex Numbers
items.content: (a+ib)−(c+id) = (a−c)+i(b−d).

items.title: Multiplication of Complex Numbers
items.content: (a+ib)(c+id) = (ac−bd)+i(ad+bc).

items.title: Division of Complex Numbers
items.content: (a+ib)/(c+id) = [(a+ib)(c−id)]/(c²+d²), provided c+id ≠ 0.

items.title: Conjugate of a Complex Number
items.content: If z = a+ib, then z̄ = a−ib.

items.title: Conjugate of a Conjugate
items.content: Conjugate of z̄ is z.

items.title: Sum with Conjugate
items.content: z + z̄ = 2Re(z).

items.title: Difference with Conjugate
items.content: z − z̄ = 2i Im(z).

items.title: Product with Conjugate
items.content: z z̄ = a²+b² for z=a+ib.

items.title: Modulus of a Complex Number
items.content: For z=a+ib, |z| = √(a²+b²).

items.title: Modulus Squared
items.content: |z|² = z z̄ = a²+b².

items.title: Modulus of a Product
items.content: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|.

items.title: Modulus of a Quotient
items.content: |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|, for z₂ ≠ 0.

items.title: Argand Plane
items.content: A complex number a+ib is represented by the point (a,b) in the Argand plane.

items.title: Complex Number Coordinates
items.content: For z=a+ib, a is the horizontal coordinate and b is the vertical coordinate.

items.title: Argument of a Complex Number
items.content: The argument of z is the angle θ made by OP with the positive real axis, where z = r(cosθ+i sinθ).

items.title: Polar Form of a Complex Number
items.content: z = r(cosθ + i sinθ), where r=|z|.

items.title: Cartesian to Polar Relations
items.content: a = r cosθ, b = r sinθ, r = √(a²+b²).

items.title: Argument and Quadrant
items.content: The value of θ must be chosen according to the quadrant containing the point (a,b).

items.title: Multiplication in Polar Form
items.content: r₁(cosθ₁+i sinθ₁) × r₂(cosθ₂+i sinθ₂) = r₁r₂[cos(θ₁+θ₂)+i sin(θ₁+θ₂)].

items.title: Division in Polar Form
items.content: z₁/z₂ = (r₁/r₂)[cos(θ₁−θ₂)+i sin(θ₁−θ₂)], for z₂ ≠ 0.

items.title: Quadratic Equation
items.content: A quadratic equation is ax²+bx+c=0, where a,b,c ∈ R and a ≠ 0.

items.title: Discriminant
items.content: For ax²+bx+c=0, the discriminant is D=b²−4ac.

items.title: Distinct Real Roots
items.content: D > 0 gives two distinct real roots.

items.title: Equal Real Roots
items.content: D = 0 gives two equal real roots.

items.title: Non-Real Complex Roots
items.content: D < 0 gives a pair of non-real complex conjugate roots.

items.title: Sum of Roots
items.content: If α and β are roots of ax²+bx+c=0, then α+β = −b/a.

items.title: Product of Roots
items.content: If α and β are roots of ax²+bx+c=0, then αβ = c/a.

items.title: Quadratic Equation from Roots
items.content: If α and β are roots, the equation is x²−(α+β)x+αβ=0.

items.title: Complex Roots Occur in Conjugate Pairs
items.content: For a quadratic equation with real coefficients, a non-real root occurs with its complex conjugate.

items.title: Square Root of a Negative Number
items.content: For a>0, √(−a) = i√a.

items.title: Negative Discriminant Root Form
items.content: If D<0, roots can be written as −b/(2a) ± i√(4ac−b²)/(2a).

items.title: Real Part Using z and Conjugate
Imaginary Part Using z and Conjugate
Condition for a Real Complex Number
items.content: z is real if and only if Im(z)=0, equivalently z=z̄.

items.title: Condition for a Purely Imaginary Number
items.content: z is purely imaginary if and only if Re(z)=0.

items.title: Zero Modulus
items.content: |z|=0 if and only if z=0.

items.title: Reciprocal of a Complex Number
items.content: For z≠0, 1/z = z̄/|z|².

items.title: Square Roots of −1
items.content: The two square roots of −1 are i and −i.

items.title: Complex Number Representation
items.content: Every complex number can be represented uniquely as a+ib with a,b real.

items.title: Linear Inequality
items.content: A linear inequality in one variable is an inequality of the form ax+b < 0, ax+b ≤ 0, ax+b > 0, or ax+b ≥ 0, where a and b are real and a ≠ 0.

items.title: Inequality Symbols
items.content: < means less than; > means greater than; ≤ means less than or equal to; ≥ means greater than or equal to.

items.title: Addition Property of Inequality
items.content: Adding the same real number to both sides of an inequality does not change its direction.

items.title: Subtraction Property of Inequality
items.content: Subtracting the same real number from both sides of an inequality does not change its direction.

items.title: Positive Multiplication
items.content: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a positive number does not change the inequality sign.

items.title: Negative Multiplication
items.content: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.

items.title: Solving ax+b > 0
items.content: If a>0, then ax+b>0 gives x>−b/a. If a<0, the inequality reverses and gives x<−b/a.

items.title: Solving ax+b ≥ 0
items.content: If a>0, then x≥−b/a. If a<0, then x≤−b/a.

items.title: Solving ax+b < 0
items.content: If a>0, then x<−b/a. If a<0, then x>−b/a.

items.title: Solving ax+b ≤ 0
items.content: If a>0, then x≤−b/a. If a<0, then x≥−b/a.

items.title: Solution Set
items.content: The solution set of an inequality is the set of all values of the variable that satisfy the inequality.

items.title: Interval Notation
items.content: Open intervals exclude endpoints: (a,b). Closed intervals include endpoints: [a,b]. Mixed intervals include one endpoint and exclude the other.

items.title: Infinite Interval
items.content: x>a is represented by (a,∞), while x≥a is represented by [a,∞).

items.title: Negative Infinite Interval
items.content: x<a is represented by (−∞,a), while x≤a is represented by (−∞,a].

items.title: Infinity and Interval Brackets
items.content: Infinity is never included as an endpoint, so ∞ and −∞ always use round brackets.

items.title: Number Line Representation
items.content: Use an open circle for a strict inequality (< or >) and a closed circle for an inclusive inequality (≤ or ≥).

items.title: Compound Inequality
items.content: A compound inequality combines two inequalities, such as a<x<b.

items.title: Three-Part Compound Inequality
items.content: a<x<b means x>a and x<b simultaneously.

items.title: Multiplying a Compound Inequality
items.content: When multiplying or dividing all three parts of a compound inequality by a negative number, reverse both inequality signs.

items.title: Graph of a Linear Inequality
items.content: A one-variable linear inequality is represented on the real number line by a ray or interval.

items.title: Intersection of Solution Sets
items.content: When two inequalities must both be satisfied, their solution is the intersection of their individual solution sets.

items.title: Union of Solution Sets
items.content: When either of two inequalities may be satisfied, their solution is the union of their individual solution sets.

items.title: Absolute Value Inequality: |x|<a
items.content: For a>0, |x|<a is equivalent to −a<x<a.

items.title: Absolute Value Inequality: |x|≤a
items.content: For a≥0, |x|≤a is equivalent to −a≤x≤a.

items.title: Absolute Value Inequality: |x|>a
items.content: For a>0, |x|>a is equivalent to x<−a or x>a.

items.title: Absolute Value Inequality: |x|≥a
items.content: For a≥0, |x|≥a is equivalent to x≤−a or x≥a.

items.title: Absolute Value as Distance
items.content: |x−a| represents the distance between x and a on the real number line.

items.title: Graphical Meaning of x>a
items.content: The solution consists of all points to the right of a on the number line, excluding a.

items.title: Graphical Meaning of x≥a
items.content: The solution consists of all points to the right of a on the number line, including a.

items.title: Graphical Meaning of x<a
items.content: The solution consists of all points to the left of a on the number line, excluding a.

items.title: Graphical Meaning of x≤a
items.content: The solution consists of all points to the left of a on the number line, including a.

items.title: Equality Boundary
items.content: For ≤ or ≥, the boundary value is included in the solution. For < or >, it is excluded.

items.title: Transitivity of Inequality
items.content: If a<b and b<c, then a<c.

items.title: Addition of Inequalities
items.content: If a<b and c<d, then a+c<b+d.

items.title: Order Preservation Under Positive Scaling
items.content: If a<b and k>0, then ka<kb.

items.title: Order Reversal Under Negative Scaling
items.content: If a<b and k<0, then ka>kb.

items.title: Real Number Ordering
items.content: For any two real numbers a and b, exactly one of a<b, a=b, or a>b is true.

items.title: Common Linear Inequality Forms
items.content: ax+b>c, ax+b≥c, ax+b<c, and ax+b≤c can all be solved by isolating x while applying the correct sign rule.

items.title: Linear Inequality Solution Method
items.content: Simplify both sides, collect variable terms on one side, collect constants on the other, divide by the coefficient of the variable, and reverse the sign if that coefficient is negative.

items.title: Checking an Inequality Solution
items.content: Substitute a test value from the proposed solution interval into the original inequality to verify the result.

items.title: No Solution Case
items.content: An inequality may have no solution when its simplified statement is always false, such as 0>5.

items.title: All Real Numbers Case
items.content: An inequality may be true for every real number when its simplified statement is always true, such as 0≤5.

items.title: Set Builder Form
items.content: A solution can be written in set-builder form, for example {x∈R : x>2}.

items.title: Strict vs Inclusive Inequality
items.content: Strict inequalities use < or >; inclusive inequalities use ≤ or ≥.

items.title: Multiplication by Zero
items.content: Multiplying both sides by zero does not preserve an equivalent inequality because both sides become equal.

items.title: Reciprocal Inequality for Positive Numbers
items.content: For positive a and b, if a<b, then 1/a>1/b.

items.title: Reciprocal Inequality for Negative Numbers
items.content: For negative a and b, reciprocal comparisons require careful sign consideration; taking reciprocals can reverse order when both numbers are negative.

items.title: Inequality Solution as a Set
items.content: Every inequality solution is a subset of the real numbers when the variable is real.

items.title: Empty Set Solution
items.content: If an inequality has no real solution, its solution set is ∅.

items.title: Universal Solution
items.content: If every real number satisfies an inequality, its solution set is R.

items.title: Boundary Point
items.content: The value where an inequality changes from true to false is called a boundary point; it is included only for ≤ or ≥.

items.title: Factorial
items.content: For a positive integer n, n! = n(n−1)(n−2)...2·1. Also, 0! = 1.

items.title: Factorial Recurrence
items.content: n! = n(n−1)! for n≥1.

items.title: Permutation
items.content: A permutation is an arrangement of objects in a definite order.

items.title: Combination
items.content: A combination is a selection of objects where order does not matter.

items.title: Permutation of n Objects Taken r at a Time
items.content: nPr = n!/(n−r)!, where 0≤r≤n.

items.title: Combination of n Objects Taken r at a Time
items.content: nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!], where 0≤r≤n.

items.title: Relation Between nPr and nCr
items.content: nPr = r! · nCr.

items.title: Combination from Permutation
items.content: nCr = nPr/r!.

items.title: Permutation in Terms of Combination
items.content: nPr = r!nCr.

items.title: Symmetry Property of Combinations
items.content: nCr = nC(n−r).

items.title: Boundary Combination Values
items.content: nC0 = nCn = 1.

items.title: Consecutive Combination Relation
items.content: nCr = nC(r−1) · (n−r+1)/r.
