items.title: Pascal Identity
items.content: nCr + nC(r−1) = (n+1)Cr.

items.title: Permutations of All n Distinct Objects
items.content: The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!.

items.title: Permutations with Repeated Objects
items.content: If n objects contain p identical objects of one kind, q identical of another, and so on, the number of arrangements is n!/(p!q!...).

items.title: Circular Permutation
items.content: For n distinct objects arranged around a circle, the number of arrangements is (n−1)!.

items.title: Circular Arrangements with Clockwise and Anticlockwise Identified
items.content: For arrangements where clockwise and anticlockwise orders are considered the same, the count is (n−1)!/2.

items.title: Linear vs Circular Arrangement
items.content: In a linear arrangement, positions are fixed in a row; in a circular arrangement, rotations are treated as equivalent.

items.title: Arrangements of r Objects from n
items.content: Choose and arrange r objects from n distinct objects: nPr.

items.title: Selection of r Objects from n
items.content: Select r objects from n distinct objects: nCr.

items.title: Order Matters Test
items.content: If changing the order produces a different outcome, use permutations. If order does not matter, use combinations.

items.title: nP1
items.content: nP1 = n.

items.title: nPn
items.content: nPn = n!.

items.title: nC1
items.content: nC1 = n.

items.title: nC(n−1)
items.content: nC(n−1) = n.

items.title: Choosing At Least One Object
items.content: The number of non-empty selections from n distinct objects is 2^n−1.

items.title: Choosing Any Number of Objects
items.content: The total number of selections from n distinct objects, including selecting none, is 2^n.

items.title: Sum of All Combinations
items.content: nC0+nC1+...+nCn = 2^n.

items.title: Alternating Combination Sum
items.content: nC0−nC1+nC2−...+(−1)^n nCn = 0 for n≥1.

items.title: Sum of Even-Indexed Combinations
items.content: The sum of combinations with even lower indices is 2^(n−1), for n≥1.

items.title: Sum of Odd-Indexed Combinations
items.content: The sum of combinations with odd lower indices is 2^(n−1), for n≥1.

items.title: Arrangements of n Objects with a Particular Object Fixed
items.content: If one specified object is fixed at a particular position among n distinct objects, the remaining arrangements are (n−1)!.

items.title: Objects Together in a Linear Arrangement
items.content: Treat a group required to stay together as one block, then arrange the blocks and multiply by the internal arrangements of the group.

items.title: Objects Not Together
items.content: Count all arrangements and subtract arrangements in which the specified objects occur together.

items.title: Permutation Problem Method
items.content: Identify n and r, determine whether order matters, then apply nPr or an appropriate arrangement rule.

items.title: Combination Problem Method
items.content: Identify n and r, confirm that order does not matter, then apply nCr.

items.title: Fundamental Counting Principle
items.content: If one operation can be performed in m ways and a second independent operation in n ways, the two operations together can be performed in mn ways.

items.title: Addition Principle
items.content: If mutually exclusive cases can occur in m and n ways respectively, the total number of ways is m+n.

items.title: Complementary Counting
items.content: Number of desired outcomes = total outcomes − number of undesired outcomes.

items.title: Permutation with Restrictions
items.content: For restricted arrangements, count the permitted cases using multiplication, addition, block, or complementary counting as appropriate.

items.title: Combination Ratio
items.content: nCr / nC(r−1) = (n−r+1)/r.

items.title: Permutation Ratio
items.content: nPr / nP(r−1) = n−r+1.

items.title: Distinct Objects
items.content: Objects are distinct when they can be individually distinguished from one another.

items.title: Identical Objects
items.content: Identical objects are indistinguishable for counting purposes.

items.title: Validity of nPr and nCr
items.content: Both nPr and nCr require integers n,r with 0≤r≤n.

items.title: Permutation as Ordered Selection
items.content: A permutation can be viewed as selecting r objects from n and then arranging those selected objects.

items.title: Combination as Unordered Selection
items.content: A combination counts each group of r selected objects once, regardless of the order in which they are selected.

items.title: Binomial Expression
items.content: An algebraic expression containing two terms is called a binomial.

items.title: Binomial Theorem
items.content: (a+b)^n = Σ(r=0 to n) nCr a^(n−r)b^r, where n is a non-negative integer.

items.title: General Term
items.content: T_(r+1) = nCr a^(n−r)b^r, for r=0,1,...,n.

items.title: First Term
items.content: The first term of (a+b)^n is a^n.

items.title: Last Term
items.content: The last term of (a+b)^n is b^n.

items.title: Number of Terms
items.content: The expansion of (a+b)^n contains n+1 terms.

items.title: Expansion of (a−b)^n
items.content: (a−b)^n = Σ(r=0 to n) nCr a^(n−r)(−b)^r.

items.title: Middle Term for Even n
items.content: If n is even, the expansion has one middle term: T_(n/2+1).

items.title: Middle Terms for Odd n
items.content: If n is odd, the expansion has two middle terms: T_((n+1)/2) and T_((n+3)/2).

items.title: Coefficient of First Term
items.content: The coefficient of the first term is 1.

items.title: Coefficient of Last Term
items.content: The coefficient of the last term is 1.

items.title: Symmetry of Binomial Coefficients
items.content: nCr = nC(n−r).

items.title: Pascal Identity
items.content: nCr + nC(r−1) = (n+1)Cr.

items.title: Sum of Binomial Coefficients
items.content: nC0+nC1+...+nCn = 2^n.

items.title: Alternating Sum of Coefficients
items.content: nC0−nC1+nC2−...+(−1)^n nCn = 0 for n≥1.

items.title: Sum of Even Coefficients
items.content: The sum of coefficients with even lower indices is 2^(n−1), for n≥1.

items.title: Sum of Odd Coefficients
items.content: The sum of coefficients with odd lower indices is 2^(n−1), for n≥1.

items.title: Coefficient of x^r in (1+x)^n
items.content: The coefficient of x^r is nCr.

items.title: Coefficient of x^r in (a+x)^n
items.content: The coefficient of x^r is nCr a^(n−r).

items.title: Coefficient of x^r in (a+bx)^n
items.content: The coefficient of x^r is nCr a^(n−r)b^r.

items.title: Term Independent of x
items.content: For a term independent of x, set the power of x in the general term equal to zero and solve for r.

items.title: Term Containing x^k
items.content: Use the general term and set its power of x equal to k to identify the required term.

items.title: Pascal Triangle Row
items.content: The coefficients of (a+b)^n form the nth row of Pascal’s triangle: 1, nC1, nC2, ..., 1.

items.title: Coefficient Pattern
items.content: In consecutive terms of a binomial expansion, the power of the first variable decreases by 1 while the power of the second increases by 1.

items.title: Term Indexing
items.content: The term containing r powers of b is T_(r+1), because the first term corresponds to r=0.

items.title: Successive Term Ratio
items.content: T_(r+2)/T_(r+1) = [(n−r)/(r+1)](b/a), whenever the terms are defined and a≠0.

items.title: Coefficient of x in (1+x)^n
items.content: The coefficient of x is n.

items.title: Coefficient of x² in (1+x)^n
items.content: The coefficient of x² is n(n−1)/2.

items.title: Coefficient of x^n in (1+x)^n
items.content: The coefficient of x^n is 1.

items.title: Binomial Expansion with a Negative Second Term
items.content: Apply the theorem directly with b replaced by −b; alternating signs arise according to the power of b.

items.title: Coefficient vs Term
items.content: A coefficient is the numerical or algebraic factor multiplying a variable term; a term includes both coefficient and variable factors.

items.title: Finding a Particular Term
items.content: Write the general term T_(r+1), substitute the required value of r, and simplify.

items.title: Finding a Particular Coefficient
items.content: Write the general term, identify the required power of the variable, solve for r, then extract the coefficient.

items.title: Finding a Constant Term
items.content: Write T_(r+1), equate the total variable exponent to zero, determine r, and substitute it into the term.

items.title: Binomial Coefficients Are Integers
items.content: For non-negative integer n and 0≤r≤n, nCr is an integer.

items.title: Combination Recurrence in Binomial Form
items.content: nCr = [(n−r+1)/r] nC(r−1), for r≥1.

items.title: Expansion of (a+b)^2
items.content: (a+b)^2 = a²+2ab+b².

items.title: Expansion of (a+b)^3
items.content: (a+b)^3 = a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³.

items.title: Expansion of (a−b)^2
items.content: (a−b)^2 = a²−2ab+b².

items.title: Expansion of (a−b)^3
items.content: (a−b)^3 = a³−3a²b+3ab²−b³.

items.title: Binomial Theorem Condition
items.content: The standard finite binomial theorem applies when the exponent n is a non-negative integer.

items.title: Coefficient Symmetry
items.content: Coefficients in the expansion of (a+b)^n are symmetric about the middle because nCr = nC(n−r).

items.title: Sum of Coefficients of a Polynomial Expansion
items.content: For a polynomial obtained from (1+x)^n, put x=1 to obtain the sum of coefficients: 2^n.

items.title: Alternating Coefficient Sum
items.content: For a polynomial obtained from (1+x)^n, put x=−1 to obtain the alternating coefficient sum: 0 for n≥1.

items.title: Power Progression in Expansion
items.content: Across successive terms, the exponent of b increases from 0 to n while the exponent of a decreases from n to 0.

items.title: Total Degree of Each Term
items.content: Every term in the expansion of (a+b)^n has total degree n.

items.title: Central Coefficient for Even n
items.content: When n=2m, the central coefficient is 2mCm.

items.title: Two Central Coefficients for Odd n
items.content: When n=2m+1, the two central coefficients are (2m+1)Cm and (2m+1)C(m+1), and they are equal.

items.title: Binomial Theorem and Combinations
items.content: The coefficient of each term in a binomial expansion is determined by a combination nCr.

items.title: End Coefficients
items.content: The first and last coefficients in every finite expansion of (a+b)^n are 1.

items.title: Sequence
items.content: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers following a definite rule.

items.title: Series
items.content: A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence.

items.title: Finite Sequence
items.content: A sequence containing a finite number of terms is called a finite sequence.

items.title: Infinite Sequence
items.content: A sequence continuing indefinitely is called an infinite sequence.

items.title: General Term
items.content: The nth term of a sequence is denoted by a_n and gives the term at position n.

items.title: Arithmetic Progression
items.content: An arithmetic progression is a sequence in which the difference between consecutive terms is constant.

items.title: Common Difference
items.content: For an AP, the common difference is d = a_(n+1) − a_n.

items.title: Sum of First n Terms of AP
AP Sum Using Last Term
items.content: S_n = n/2(a+l), where l is the nth or last term.

items.title: Arithmetic Mean
items.content: The arithmetic mean of a and b is (a+b)/2.

items.title: Arithmetic Mean Between Two Numbers
items.content: If A is the arithmetic mean between a and b, then A=(a+b)/2.

items.title: n Arithmetic Means
items.content: If n arithmetic means are inserted between a and b, the resulting AP has n+2 terms and common difference d=(b−a)/(n+1).

items.title: Geometric Progression
items.content: A geometric progression is a sequence in which the ratio between consecutive non-zero terms is constant.

items.title: Common Ratio
items.content: For a GP, the common ratio is r = a_(n+1)/a_n, where the denominator is non-zero.

items.title: Sum of First n Terms of GP
GP Sum for r=1
items.content: If r=1, every term equals a and S_n=na.

items.title: Infinite GP Sum
items.content: S_∞ = a/(1−r), provided |r|<1.

items.title: Condition for Infinite GP Sum
items.content: An infinite geometric series has a finite sum only when |r|<1.

items.title: Geometric Mean
items.content: The geometric mean of positive numbers a and b is √(ab).

items.title: Geometric Mean Between Two Positive Numbers
items.content: If G is the geometric mean between positive a and b, then G=√(ab).

items.title: n Geometric Means
items.content: If n geometric means are inserted between positive a and b, the common ratio is r=(b/a)^(1/(n+1)).

items.title: Relation Between AM and GM
items.content: For positive a and b, AM ≥ GM, i.e. (a+b)/2 ≥ √(ab), with equality when a=b.

items.title: Harmonic Mean
items.content: The harmonic mean of two positive numbers a and b is 2ab/(a+b).

items.title: Relation Among Means
items.content: For positive a and b, HM ≤ GM ≤ AM.

items.title: Equality of Means
items.content: For positive a and b, AM=GM=HM only when a=b.

items.title: Sum of First n Natural Numbers
Arithmetic Series
items.content: The sum of the terms of an arithmetic progression is called an arithmetic series.

items.title: Geometric Series
items.content: The sum of the terms of a geometric progression is called a geometric series.

items.title: Sequence vs Series
items.content: A sequence lists terms; a series adds those terms.

items.title: AP Constant Difference Test
items.content: A sequence is an AP if a_(n+1)−a_n is constant for all relevant n.

items.title: GP Constant Ratio Test
items.content: A sequence is a GP if a_(n+1)/a_n is constant wherever the ratio is defined.

items.title: Three Consecutive AP Terms
items.content: Three consecutive terms of an AP can be written as a−d, a, a+d.

items.title: Three Consecutive GP Terms
items.content: Three positive consecutive terms of a GP can be written as a/r, a, ar.

items.title: AP Middle-Term Property
items.content: For three consecutive AP terms x,y,z, 2y=x+z.

items.title: GP Middle-Term Property
items.content: For three positive consecutive GP terms x,y,z, y²=xz.

items.title: AP Term From Two Terms
items.content: If a_p and a_q are known in an AP, then d=(a_q−a_p)/(q−p).

items.title: GP Term From Two Terms
items.content: For a GP, a_q/a_p = r^(q−p), where the relevant terms are non-zero.

items.title: Sum of Consecutive AP Terms
items.content: The sum of n consecutive AP terms equals n times their arithmetic mean.

items.title: Average of AP Terms
items.content: The arithmetic mean of all terms of a finite AP equals (first term + last term)/2.

items.title: Number of Terms in AP
items.content: If first term a, last term l, and common difference d are known, n=(l−a)/d+1, when d≠0.

items.title: Sum of a GP Through Last Term
items.content: If first term a, last term l, ratio r≠1, and there are n terms, S_n=(lr−a)/(r−1).

items.title: GP Product Property
items.content: The product of terms equidistant from the beginning and end of a finite GP is constant.

items.title: Monotonic AP
items.content: For d>0 an AP increases; for d<0 it decreases; for d=0 it is constant.

items.title: Magnitude of GP Terms
items.content: For a non-zero GP, the magnitude of terms depends on |r|: it grows when |r|>1 and tends toward zero when |r|<1.

items.title: Infinite GP Convergence
items.content: When |r|<1, r^n tends to 0 as n becomes large, allowing the infinite GP sum formula.

items.title: Infinite GP Remainder
items.content: For |r|<1, the remainder after n terms is S_∞−S_n = ar^n/(1−r).

items.title: AP Sum When d=0
items.content: If d=0, every AP term equals a and S_n=na.

items.title: Series Partial Sum
items.content: The sum of the first n terms of a series is called its nth partial sum S_n.

items.title: Partial Sum Difference
items.content: The nth term of a series can be obtained from partial sums using a_n = S_n−S_(n−1), for n≥2.

items.title: Sigma Notation
items.content: Σ denotes summation. For example, Σ(k=1 to n) k = 1+2+...+n.

items.title: Arithmetic Sequence in Sigma Form
items.content: An AP can be written as a_k = a+(k−1)d.

items.title: Geometric Sequence in Sigma Form
items.content: A GP can be written as a_k = ar^(k−1).

items.title: Finite vs Infinite Series
items.content: A finite series has a fixed number of terms; an infinite series continues without a final term.

items.title: Coordinate Plane
items.content: The Cartesian plane is formed by two perpendicular coordinate axes, x-axis and y-axis, intersecting at the origin.

items.title: Coordinates of a Point
items.content: A point in the Cartesian plane is represented by an ordered pair (x,y), where x is the abscissa and y is the ordinate.

items.title: Slope of a Line
items.content: The slope of a non-vertical line measures its inclination to the positive x-axis and is denoted by m.

items.title: Slope from Two Points
items.content: For points (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂), m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), provided x₂≠x₁.

items.title: Slope and Inclination
items.content: m=tan θ, where θ is the angle made by the line with the positive x-axis.

items.title: Slope of Horizontal Line
items.content: A horizontal line has slope 0.

items.title: Slope of Vertical Line
items.content: A vertical line has undefined slope.

items.title: Angle Between Two Lines
items.content: If slopes are m₁ and m₂, then tan θ = |(m₂−m₁)/(1+m₁m₂)|, when 1+m₁m₂≠0.

items.title: Parallel Lines Condition
items.content: Two non-vertical lines are parallel if and only if their slopes are equal: m₁=m₂.

items.title: Perpendicular Lines Condition
items.content: Two non-vertical lines are perpendicular if m₁m₂=−1.

items.title: Distance Between Two Points
items.content: Distance between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is √[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²].

items.title: Section Formula Internal Division
items.content: If P divides the line segment joining (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) internally in ratio m:n, then P=((mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n),(my₂+ny₁)/(m+n)).

items.title: Midpoint Formula
items.content: Midpoint of (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is ((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2).

items.title: Section Formula External Division
items.content: If P divides the line joining (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) externally in ratio m:n, then P=((mx₂−nx₁)/(m−n),(my₂−ny₁)/(m−n)), where m≠n.

items.title: Centroid of Triangle
items.content: The centroid of a triangle with vertices (x₁,y₁),(x₂,y₂),(x₃,y₃) is ((x₁+x₂+x₃)/3,(y₁+y₂+y₃)/3).

items.title: Equation of a Line
items.content: A first-degree equation in x and y represents a straight line in the Cartesian plane, subject to the usual non-degenerate conditions.

items.title: Slope-Intercept Form
items.content: y=mx+c, where m is the slope and c is the y-intercept.

items.title: Point-Slope Form
items.content: y−y₁=m(x−x₁), for a line of slope m through (x₁,y₁).

items.title: Two-Point Form
items.content: (y−y₁)/(y₂−y₁)=(x−x₁)/(x₂−x₁), when the denominators are non-zero.

items.title: Intercept Form
items.content: x/a + y/b = 1, where a and b are the x- and y-intercepts respectively.

items.title: General Form of Line
items.content: Ax+By+C=0, where A and B are not both zero.

items.title: Slope from General Form
items.content: For Ax+By+C=0 with B≠0, slope m=−A/B.

items.title: x-Intercept from General Form
items.content: For Ax+By+C=0 with A≠0, the x-intercept is −C/A.

items.title: y-Intercept from General Form
items.content: For Ax+By+C=0 with B≠0, the y-intercept is −C/B.

items.title: Normal Form of Line
items.content: x cos α + y sin α = p, where p is the perpendicular distance from the origin and α is the angle made by the perpendicular with the positive x-axis.

items.title: Normal Form Parameters
items.content: In x cos α+y sin α=p, p≥0 represents the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line.

items.title: Slope of a Line Through Origin
items.content: A line through the origin with slope m has equation y=mx.

items.title: Line Through Two Given Points
items.content: Use the two-point form with the coordinates of the two given points.

items.title: Line Parallel to a Given Line
items.content: A line parallel to y=mx+c has slope m and can be written y=mx+k.

items.title: Line Perpendicular to a Given Line
items.content: If a line has slope m≠0, a perpendicular line has slope −1/m.

items.title: Distance of a Point from a Line
items.content: Distance from (x₁,y₁) to Ax+By+C=0 is |Ax₁+By₁+C|/√(A²+B²).

items.title: Distance Between Parallel Lines
items.content: Distance between Ax+By+C₁=0 and Ax+By+C₂=0 is |C₁−C₂|/√(A²+B²).

items.title: Area of Triangle from Coordinates
items.content: Area = 1/2 |x₁(y₂−y₃)+x₂(y₃−y₁)+x₃(y₁−y₂)|.

items.title: Collinearity Condition
items.content: Three points are collinear if the area of the triangle formed by them is zero.

items.title: Collinearity Determinant Condition
items.content: x₁(y₂−y₃)+x₂(y₃−y₁)+x₃(y₁−y₂)=0.

items.title: Intercepts
items.content: The x-intercept is the point where a line meets the x-axis; the y-intercept is where it meets the y-axis.

items.title: Line Parallel to x-Axis
items.content: A line parallel to the x-axis has equation y=k.

items.title: Line Parallel to y-Axis
items.content: A line parallel to the y-axis has equation x=k.

items.title: Line Through a Point Parallel to x-Axis
items.content: Through (x₁,y₁), the line parallel to the x-axis is y=y₁.

items.title: Line Through a Point Parallel to y-Axis
items.content: Through (x₁,y₁), the line parallel to the y-axis is x=x₁.

items.title: Inclination of a Line
items.content: The inclination θ of a line is the angle measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis to the line, with 0≤θ<π.

items.title: Inclination of Horizontal Line
items.content: For a line parallel to the x-axis, θ=0 and m=0.

items.title: Inclination of Vertical Line
items.content: For a vertical line, θ=π/2 and the slope is undefined.

items.title: Slope Through Origin and Point
items.content: For a line through origin and (x₁,y₁), m=y₁/x₁ when x₁≠0.

items.title: Same Line Test
items.content: Two equations represent the same line when their coefficients are proportional, including the constant term.

items.title: Parallel Line Test in General Form
items.content: Lines A₁x+B₁y+C₁=0 and A₂x+B₂y+C₂=0 are parallel when A₁B₂−A₂B₁=0.

items.title: Perpendicular Line Test in General Form
items.content: Lines A₁x+B₁y+C₁=0 and A₂x+B₂y+C₂=0 are perpendicular when A₁A₂+B₁B₂=0.

items.title: Angle Between General Form Lines
items.content: For A₁x+B₁y+C₁=0 and A₂x+B₂y+C₂=0, tanθ=|(A₁B₂−A₂B₁)/(A₁A₂+B₁B₂)|, when the denominator is non-zero.

items.title: Distance Between Point and Line Using Normal Form
items.content: For x cosα+y sinα=p, the signed perpendicular relation can be evaluated directly from the normal equation.

items.title: Foot of Perpendicular
items.content: The foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line is the point where the perpendicular meets that line.

items.title: Reflection Across a Line
items.content: Reflection problems can be handled by finding the perpendicular from the point to the line and extending the same distance on the opposite side.

items.title: Finding Equation of a Line
items.content: Identify a suitable form from the given information, substitute the known point/slope/intercepts, and simplify.

items.title: Finding Angle Between Lines
items.content: Find the slopes of the two lines and apply tanθ=|(m₂−m₁)/(1+m₁m₂)| when applicable.

items.title: Testing Parallel Lines
items.content: Compare slopes when defined, or use A₁B₂−A₂B₁=0 for general equations.

items.title: Testing Perpendicular Lines
items.content: Compare slopes using m₁m₂=−1 when defined, or use A₁A₂+B₁B₂=0 for general equations.

items.title: Distance from Origin to a Line
items.content: For Ax+By+C=0, distance from the origin is |C|/√(A²+B²).

items.title: Standard Coordinate Axes
items.content: The x-axis has equation y=0 and the y-axis has equation x=0.

items.title: Slope Sign
items.content: Positive slope means the line rises from left to right; negative slope means it falls from left to right.

items.title: Equal Slopes and Coincident Lines
items.content: Equal slopes indicate parallel or coincident lines; comparing intercepts distinguishes the two cases.

items.title: Locus
items.content: A locus is the set of all points satisfying a specified geometric condition.

items.title: Conic Section
items.content: A conic section is a curve obtained as the intersection of a plane with a right circular cone.

items.title: Circle
items.content: A circle is the locus of a point moving so that its distance from a fixed point is constant.

items.title: Parabola
items.content: A parabola is the locus of a point whose distance from a fixed point equals its distance from a fixed line.

items.title: Ellipse
items.content: An ellipse is the locus of a point for which the sum of distances from two fixed points is constant.

items.title: Hyperbola
items.content: A hyperbola is the locus of a point for which the absolute difference of distances from two fixed points is constant.

items.title: Focus
items.content: A focus is a fixed point associated with a conic that helps define the curve.

items.title: Directrix
items.content: A directrix is a fixed line associated with a conic and used in its geometric definition.

items.title: Eccentricity
items.content: Eccentricity e is the ratio of the distance of a point on a conic from the focus to its perpendicular distance from the directrix.

items.title: Eccentricity of Circle
items.content: For a circle, e=0.

items.title: Eccentricity of Parabola
items.content: For a parabola, e=1.

items.title: Eccentricity of Ellipse
items.content: For an ellipse, 0<e<1.

items.title: Eccentricity of Hyperbola
items.content: For a hyperbola, e>1.

items.title: Circle with Centre at Origin
items.content: A circle with centre (0,0) and radius r consists of all points at distance r from the origin.

items.title: Circle at Origin
items.content: x²+y²=r².

items.title: Circle with Centre (h,k)
items.content: (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r².

items.title: General Equation of Circle
items.content: x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0.

items.title: Centre of General Circle
items.content: For x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0, centre = (−g,−f).

items.title: Radius of General Circle
items.content: For x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0, r=√(g²+f²−c).

items.title: Real Circle Condition
items.content: For x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0, a real non-point circle requires g²+f²−c>0.

items.title: Parabola Opening Right
items.content: y²=4ax, with focus (a,0) and directrix x=−a.

items.title: Parabola Opening Left
items.content: y²=−4ax, with focus (−a,0) and directrix x=a.

items.title: Parabola Opening Upward
items.content: x²=4ay, with focus (0,a) and directrix y=−a.

items.title: Parabola Opening Downward
items.content: x²=−4ay, with focus (0,−a) and directrix y=a.

items.title: Vertex of Parabola
items.content: The vertex is the point where the parabola changes its direction and is closest to the directrix.

items.title: Vertex of Standard Parabola
items.content: For y²=±4ax and x²=±4ay, the vertex is (0,0).

items.title: Axis of Parabola
items.content: The axis of a parabola is the line passing through its vertex and focus and perpendicular to the directrix.

items.title: Length of Latus Rectum of Parabola
items.content: For y²=4ax or x²=4ay, the length of the latus rectum is 4a.

items.title: Endpoints of Latus Rectum
items.content: For y²=4ax, the endpoints are (a,2a) and (a,−2a).

items.title: Ellipse Standard Equation Horizontal
items.content: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, where a>b>0, has major axis along the x-axis.

items.title: Ellipse Standard Equation Vertical
items.content: x²/b² + y²/a² = 1, where a>b>0, has major axis along the y-axis.

items.title: Ellipse Focal Relation
items.content: For an ellipse, b²=a²(1−e²), equivalently a²=b²+c² when c is the focal distance.

items.title: Ellipse Focal Distance
items.content: For x²/a²+y²/b²=1 with a>b, c²=a²−b² and foci are (±c,0).

items.title: Ellipse Eccentricity
items.content: For an ellipse with semi-major axis a and focal distance c, e=c/a.

items.title: Ellipse Length of Major Axis
items.content: Major axis length = 2a.

items.title: Ellipse Length of Minor Axis
items.content: Minor axis length = 2b.

items.title: Ellipse Length of Latus Rectum
items.content: For an ellipse with semi-axes a and b, latus rectum length = 2b²/a.

items.title: Vertices of Ellipse
items.content: For x²/a²+y²/b²=1 with a>b, the vertices are (±a,0) and co-vertices are (0,±b).

items.title: Hyperbola Standard Equation Horizontal
items.content: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, with transverse axis along the x-axis.

items.title: Hyperbola Standard Equation Vertical
items.content: y²/a² − x²/b² = 1, with transverse axis along the y-axis.

items.title: Hyperbola Focal Relation
items.content: For a hyperbola, c²=a²+b².

items.title: Hyperbola Eccentricity
items.content: For a hyperbola, e=c/a, where c>a.

items.title: Hyperbola Foci Horizontal
items.content: For x²/a²−y²/b²=1, the foci are (±c,0), where c²=a²+b².

items.title: Hyperbola Foci Vertical
items.content: For y²/a²−x²/b²=1, the foci are (0,±c), where c²=a²+b².

items.title: Hyperbola Length of Transverse Axis
items.content: Transverse axis length = 2a.

items.title: Hyperbola Length of Conjugate Axis
items.content: Conjugate axis length = 2b.

items.title: Hyperbola Length of Latus Rectum
items.content: Latus rectum length = 2b²/a.

items.title: Asymptote of Hyperbola
items.content: An asymptote is a line that the hyperbola approaches as its points move far from the centre.

items.title: Asymptotes of Horizontal Hyperbola
items.content: For x²/a²−y²/b²=1, the asymptotes are y=±(b/a)x.

items.title: Asymptotes of Vertical Hyperbola
items.content: For y²/a²−x²/b²=1, the asymptotes are y=±(a/b)x.

items.title: Centre of Hyperbola
items.content: The centre is the midpoint of the segment joining the two vertices of the hyperbola.

items.title: Centre of Standard Conics
items.content: The standard circle, parabola, ellipse and hyperbola equations listed here are centred or positioned with respect to the origin unless translations are explicitly included.

items.title: Major Axis of Ellipse
items.content: The major axis is the longer axis of an ellipse and passes through its two foci.

items.title: Minor Axis of Ellipse
items.content: The minor axis is perpendicular to the major axis and passes through the centre.

items.title: Transverse Axis of Hyperbola
items.content: The transverse axis passes through the two vertices and foci of a hyperbola.

items.title: Conjugate Axis of Hyperbola
items.content: The conjugate axis is perpendicular to the transverse axis through the centre.

items.title: Circle as a Special Ellipse
items.content: A circle is obtained when the two semi-axes of an ellipse are equal: a=b.

items.title: Distance from Focus to Directrix for Parabola
items.content: For y²=4ax, the focus is (a,0) and the directrix is x=−a, so the focus-directrix distance is 2a.

items.title: Parabola Eccentricity Definition
items.content: For every point on a parabola, distance from focus equals perpendicular distance from directrix.

items.title: Ellipse Focal Definition
items.content: For every point on an ellipse, the sum of distances from the two foci is constant and equals 2a.

items.title: Hyperbola Focal Definition
items.content: For every point on a hyperbola, the absolute difference of distances from the two foci is constant and equals 2a.

items.title: Circle Diameter
items.content: Diameter of a circle = 2r.

items.title: Circle Area
items.content: Area of a circle = πr².

items.title: Circle Circumference
items.content: Circumference of a circle = 2πr.

items.title: Eccentricity Classification
items.content: e=0 corresponds to a circle, e=1 to a parabola, 0<e<1 to an ellipse, and e>1 to a hyperbola.

items.title: Identifying a Standard Conic
items.content: Compare the given equation with standard circle, parabola, ellipse, or hyperbola forms and identify the corresponding parameters.

items.title: Standard Parabola Parameter
items.content: In y²=4ax or x²=4ay, a is the distance from the vertex to the focus.

items.title: Standard Ellipse Parameter
items.content: For the standard ellipse, a is the semi-major axis and b is the semi-minor axis.

items.title: Standard Hyperbola Parameter
items.content: For the standard hyperbola, a is the semi-transverse axis and b is the semi-conjugate axis.

items.title: Translated Circle
items.content: A circle with centre (h,k) and radius r has equation (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r².

items.title: Translated Parabola
items.content: A right-opening parabola with vertex (h,k) has (y−k)²=4a(x−h).

items.title: Translated Ellipse Horizontal
items.content: An ellipse centred at (h,k) with horizontal major axis has (x−h)²/a²+(y−k)²/b²=1, a>b>0.

items.title: Translated Hyperbola Horizontal
items.content: A hyperbola centred at (h,k) with horizontal transverse axis has (x−h)²/a²−(y−k)²/b²=1.

items.title: Three-dimensional Coordinate System
items.content: A three-dimensional coordinate system represents a point by an ordered triple (x,y,z) with respect to three mutually perpendicular coordinate axes.

items.title: Coordinate Axes in 3D
items.content: The x-axis, y-axis and z-axis are three mutually perpendicular axes meeting at the origin.

items.title: Origin in 3D
items.content: The origin is the point O(0,0,0) where the three coordinate axes intersect.

items.title: Coordinates of a Point
items.content: A point in three-dimensional space is represented as P(x,y,z), where x, y and z are its coordinates.

items.title: Coordinate Planes
items.content: The three coordinate planes are the xy-plane, yz-plane and zx-plane.

items.title: Point on xy-plane
items.content: A point lies on the xy-plane if its z-coordinate is 0.

items.title: Point on yz-plane
items.content: A point lies on the yz-plane if its x-coordinate is 0.

items.title: Point on zx-plane
items.content: A point lies on the zx-plane if its y-coordinate is 0.

items.title: Point on x-axis in 3D
items.content: A point on the x-axis has coordinates (x,0,0).

items.title: Point on y-axis in 3D
items.content: A point on the y-axis has coordinates (0,y,0).

items.title: Point on z-axis in 3D
items.content: A point on the z-axis has coordinates (0,0,z).

items.title: Octants
items.content: The three coordinate planes divide three-dimensional space into eight regions called octants.

items.title: First Octant
items.content: In the first octant, x>0, y>0 and z>0.

items.title: Sign Pattern of Octants
items.content: The eight octants are distinguished by the positive or negative signs of x, y and z.

items.title: Distance Between Two Points in 3D
items.content: For P(x₁,y₁,z₁) and Q(x₂,y₂,z₂), PQ=√[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²+(z₂−z₁)²].

items.title: Distance from Origin
items.content: Distance of P(x,y,z) from the origin is √(x²+y²+z²).

items.title: Midpoint Formula in 3D
items.content: Midpoint of P(x₁,y₁,z₁) and Q(x₂,y₂,z₂) is ((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2,(z₁+z₂)/2).

items.title: Section Formula in 3D
items.content: If P divides A(x₁,y₁,z₁) and B(x₂,y₂,z₂) internally in ratio m:n, then P=((mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n),(my₂+ny₁)/(m+n),(mz₂+nz₁)/(m+n)).

items.title: External Section Formula in 3D
items.content: If P divides A(x₁,y₁,z₁) and B(x₂,y₂,z₂) externally in ratio m:n, then P=((mx₂−nx₁)/(m−n),(my₂−ny₁)/(m−n),(mz₂−nz₁)/(m−n)).

items.title: Collinearity of Three Points in 3D
items.content: Three points are collinear when the distance between one pair equals the appropriate sum of the other two distances.

items.title: Distance from a Point to an Axis
items.content: For P(x,y,z), distance from the x-axis is √(y²+z²).

items.title: Distance from Point to y-axis
items.content: For P(x,y,z), distance from the y-axis is √(x²+z²).

items.title: Distance from Point to z-axis
items.content: For P(x,y,z), distance from the z-axis is √(x²+y²).

items.title: Distance from Point to xy-plane
items.content: For P(x,y,z), perpendicular distance from the xy-plane is |z|.

items.title: Distance from Point to yz-plane
items.content: For P(x,y,z), perpendicular distance from the yz-plane is |x|.

items.title: Distance from Point to zx-plane
items.content: For P(x,y,z), perpendicular distance from the zx-plane is |y|.

items.title: Projection on xy-plane
items.content: The projection of P(x,y,z) on the xy-plane is (x,y,0).

items.title: Projection on yz-plane
items.content: The projection of P(x,y,z) on the yz-plane is (0,y,z).

items.title: Projection on zx-plane
items.content: The projection of P(x,y,z) on the zx-plane is (x,0,z).

items.title: Centroid of Four Points
items.content: For four points A(x₁,y₁,z₁), B(x₂,y₂,z₂), C(x₃,y₃,z₃), D(x₄,y₄,z₄), their coordinate average is ((x₁+x₂+x₃+x₄)/4,(y₁+y₂+y₃+y₄)/4,(z₁+z₂+z₃+z₄)/4).

items.title: Symmetric Point about Origin
items.content: The point symmetric to (x,y,z) about the origin is (−x,−y,−z).

items.title: Reflection in xy-plane
items.content: Reflection of (x,y,z) in the xy-plane is (x,y,−z).

items.title: Reflection in yz-plane
items.content: Reflection of (x,y,z) in the yz-plane is (−x,y,z).

items.title: Reflection in zx-plane
items.content: Reflection of (x,y,z) in the zx-plane is (x,−y,z).

items.title: Reflection in x-axis
items.content: Reflection of (x,y,z) in the x-axis is (x,−y,−z).

items.title: Reflection in y-axis
items.content: Reflection of (x,y,z) in the y-axis is (−x,y,−z).

items.title: Reflection in z-axis
items.content: Reflection of (x,y,z) in the z-axis is (−x,−y,z).

items.title: Distance Between Point and Origin Squared
items.content: For P(x,y,z), OP²=x²+y²+z².

items.title: Coordinate Difference Vector
items.content: The coordinate differences between P(x₁,y₁,z₁) and Q(x₂,y₂,z₂) are (x₂−x₁, y₂−y₁, z₂−z₁).

items.title: Finding Distance in 3D
items.content: Subtract corresponding coordinates, square the three differences, add them and take the positive square root.

items.title: Finding Midpoint in 3D
items.content: Add corresponding coordinates of the two points and divide each sum by 2.

items.title: Finding Section Point Internally
items.content: Use the internal section formula with the ratio coefficients opposite the corresponding endpoint coordinates.

items.title: Locus in 3D
items.content: A locus is the set of all points satisfying a specified geometric condition in three-dimensional space.

items.title: Point Equidistant from Coordinate Planes
items.content: A point P(x,y,z) is equidistant from the three coordinate planes when |x|=|y|=|z|.

items.title: Point Equidistant from Coordinate Axes
items.content: A point P(x,y,z) is equidistant from the three coordinate axes when y²+z²=x²+z²=x²+y².

items.title: Distance from Point to xz-plane
items.content: The distance from P(x,y,z) to the xz-plane is |y|.

items.title: xz-plane and zx-plane
items.content: The xz-plane and zx-plane are the same coordinate plane.

items.title: Coordinates on xy-plane
items.content: Every point on the xy-plane has the form (x,y,0).

items.title: Coordinates on yz-plane
items.content: Every point on the yz-plane has the form (0,y,z).

items.title: Coordinates on zx-plane
items.content: Every point on the zx-plane has the form (x,0,z).

items.title: Positive Coordinate Direction
items.content: The positive direction of each coordinate axis is determined by the chosen orientation of that axis from the origin.

items.title: Distance Between Points with Same z-coordinate
items.content: If z₁=z₂, then PQ=√[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²].

items.title: Distance Between Points with Same x-coordinate
items.content: If x₁=x₂, then PQ=√[(y₂−y₁)²+(z₂−z₁)²].

items.title: Distance Between Points with Same y-coordinate
items.content: If y₁=y₂, then PQ=√[(x₂−x₁)²+(z₂−z₁)²].

items.title: Midpoint and Equal Distances
items.content: The midpoint of a line segment is equidistant from its two endpoints.

items.title: Coordinate Geometry in Space
items.content: Three-dimensional coordinate geometry extends the coordinate-plane ideas of points, distances, sections and symmetry into space.

items.title: Absolute Coordinate Distance
items.content: Perpendicular distance to a coordinate plane is always non-negative and is obtained using the absolute value of the relevant coordinate.

items.title: Checking Whether a Point Lies on a Plane
items.content: For xy, yz and zx coordinate planes, check respectively whether z=0, x=0 or y=0.

items.title: Origin Belongs to All Coordinate Planes
items.content: The origin (0,0,0) lies simultaneously on the xy-plane, yz-plane and zx-plane.

items.title: Distance from Point to All Three Planes
items.content: For P(x,y,z), distances from the yz-plane, zx-plane and xy-plane are |x|, |y| and |z| respectively.

items.title: Quadrants versus Octants
items.content: In two dimensions the coordinate axes divide the plane into four quadrants; in three dimensions the coordinate planes divide space into eight octants.

items.title: Point on Intersection of xy and yz Planes
items.content: A point on both the xy-plane and yz-plane must have x=0 and z=0, so it lies on the y-axis.

items.title: Point on Intersection of yz and zx Planes
items.content: A point on both the yz-plane and zx-plane must have x=0 and y=0, so it lies on the z-axis.

items.title: Point on Intersection of zx and xy Planes
items.content: A point on both the zx-plane and xy-plane must have y=0 and z=0, so it lies on the x-axis.

items.title: Limit of a Function
items.content: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a is the value that f(x) approaches when x gets arbitrarily close to a.

items.title: Limit Notation
items.content: lim(x→a) f(x) denotes the limit of f(x) as x approaches a.

items.title: Left-hand Limit
items.content: The left-hand limit considers values of x approaching a from values less than a and is written lim(x→a−)f(x).

items.title: Right-hand Limit
items.content: The right-hand limit considers values of x approaching a from values greater than a and is written lim(x→a+)f(x).

items.title: Existence of Limit
items.content: lim(x→a)f(x) exists if and only if the left-hand and right-hand limits exist and are equal.

items.title: Constant Limit
items.content: lim(x→a)c = c.

items.title: Limit of x
items.content: lim(x→a)x = a.

items.title: Limit of Sum
items.content: lim(x→a)[f(x)+g(x)] = lim(x→a)f(x) + lim(x→a)g(x), when the individual limits exist.

items.title: Limit of Difference
items.content: lim(x→a)[f(x)−g(x)] = lim(x→a)f(x) − lim(x→a)g(x), when the individual limits exist.

items.title: Limit of Product
items.content: lim(x→a)[f(x)g(x)] = [lim(x→a)f(x)][lim(x→a)g(x)], when the individual limits exist.

items.title: Limit of Quotient
items.content: lim(x→a)[f(x)/g(x)] = lim(x→a)f(x) / lim(x→a)g(x), provided lim(x→a)g(x)≠0.

items.title: Limit of Scalar Multiple
items.content: lim(x→a)[cf(x)] = c lim(x→a)f(x).

items.title: Limit of a Polynomial
items.content: For a polynomial p(x), lim(x→a)p(x)=p(a).

items.title: Limit of a Rational Function
items.content: For a rational function p(x)/q(x), if q(a)≠0, then lim(x→a)p(x)/q(x)=p(a)/q(a).

items.title: Direct Substitution for Limits
items.content: First substitute the approaching value into the expression. If a finite defined value results, that is the limit.

items.title: Factorisation Method for Limits
items.content: If direct substitution gives an indeterminate 0/0 form, factorise and cancel common factors before taking the limit.

items.title: Rationalisation Method for Limits
items.content: For expressions involving surds that give 0/0, multiply by a suitable conjugate to simplify the expression before taking the limit.

items.title: Standard Limit sin x over x
items.content: lim(x→0) (sin x)/x = 1.

items.title: Standard Limit x over sin x
items.content: lim(x→0) x/(sin x) = 1.

items.title: Standard Limit tan x over x
items.content: lim(x→0) (tan x)/x = 1.

items.title: Standard Limit x over tan x
items.content: lim(x→0) x/(tan x) = 1.

items.title: Standard Limit 1−cos x
items.content: lim(x→0) (1−cos x)/x = 0.

items.title: Standard Limit 1−cos x over x²
items.content: lim(x→0) (1−cos x)/x² = 1/2.

items.title: Standard Limit sin ax over x
items.content: lim(x→0) sin(ax)/x = a.

items.title: Standard Limit sin ax over bx
items.content: lim(x→0) sin(ax)/sin(bx) = a/b, for b≠0.

items.title: Standard Limit tan ax over x
items.content: lim(x→0) tan(ax)/x = a.

items.title: Standard Limit tan ax over tan bx
items.content: lim(x→0) tan(ax)/tan(bx) = a/b, for b≠0.

items.title: Derivative at a Point
items.content: The derivative of f(x) at x=a is the limit of [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h as h approaches 0, when the limit exists.

items.title: Derivative by First Principle
items.content: f'(a)=lim(h→0)[f(a+h)−f(a)]/h.

items.title: Derivative Function Definition
items.content: f'(x)=lim(h→0)[f(x+h)−f(x)]/h.

items.title: Derivative as Slope
items.content: The derivative f'(a) represents the slope of the tangent to the graph y=f(x) at x=a.

items.title: Derivative as Rate of Change
items.content: The derivative represents the instantaneous rate of change of a function with respect to its variable.

items.title: Derivative Notations
items.content: Common notations include f'(x), dy/dx and D_x f(x).

items.title: Derivative of a Constant
items.content: d/dx(c)=0.

items.title: Derivative of x
items.content: d/dx(x)=1.

items.title: Derivative of x^n
items.content: d/dx(x^n)=nx^(n−1), for real n where the expression is defined.

items.title: Derivative of Scalar Multiple
items.content: d/dx[cf(x)] = c f'(x).

items.title: Derivative of sin x
items.content: d/dx(sin x)=cos x.

items.title: Derivative of cos x
items.content: d/dx(cos x)=−sin x.

items.title: Derivative of tan x
items.content: d/dx(tan x)=sec²x.

items.title: Derivative of cot x
items.content: d/dx(cot x)=−cosec²x.

items.title: Derivative of sec x
items.content: d/dx(sec x)=sec x tan x.

items.title: Derivative of cosec x
items.content: d/dx(cosec x)=−cosec x cot x.

items.title: Derivative of a^x
items.content: d/dx(a^x)=a^x ln(a), for a>0.

items.title: Derivative of e^x
items.content: d/dx(e^x)=e^x.

items.title: Derivative of log_a x
items.content: d/dx(log_a x)=1/(x ln a), for a>0 and a≠1.

items.title: Derivative of ln x
items.content: d/dx(ln x)=1/x, for x>0.

items.title: Product Rule
items.content: d/dx[f(x)g(x)] = f(x)g'(x)+g(x)f'(x).

items.title: Quotient Rule
items.content: d/dx[f(x)/g(x)] = [g(x)f'(x)−f(x)g'(x)]/[g(x)]², where g(x)≠0.

items.title: Chain Rule
items.content: If y=f(g(x)), then dy/dx=f'(g(x))g'(x).

items.title: Derivative of sin(ax+b)
items.content: d/dx[sin(ax+b)] = a cos(ax+b).

items.title: Derivative of cos(ax+b)
items.content: d/dx[cos(ax+b)] = −a sin(ax+b).

items.title: Derivative of tan(ax+b)
items.content: d/dx[tan(ax+b)] = a sec²(ax+b).

items.title: Derivative of e^(ax+b)
items.content: d/dx[e^(ax+b)] = a e^(ax+b).

items.title: Derivative of ln(ax+b)
items.content: d/dx[ln(ax+b)] = a/(ax+b), where ax+b>0.

items.title: Derivative of (ax+b)^n
items.content: d/dx[(ax+b)^n] = na(ax+b)^(n−1).

items.title: Differentiability
items.content: A function is differentiable at a point if its derivative exists there.

items.title: Differentiability Implies Continuity
items.content: If a function is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

items.title: Continuity Does Not Necessarily Imply Differentiability
items.content: A function may be continuous at a point without being differentiable there.

items.title: Derivative from Graph
items.content: The derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent line to the curve at that point.

items.title: First Principle Derivative Method
items.content: Find f(x+h), subtract f(x), divide by h, simplify, then take the limit as h approaches 0.

items.title: Derivative of Polynomial
items.content: Differentiate each term separately using the power rule and constant-multiple rule.

items.title: Derivative of Product
items.content: Identify the two factors and apply the product rule.

items.title: Derivative of Quotient
items.content: Identify numerator and denominator and apply the quotient rule.

items.title: Derivative of Composite Function
items.content: Identify the outer and inner functions and apply the chain rule.

items.title: Differentiation Variable
items.content: The derivative dy/dx measures the rate of change of y with respect to x.

items.title: Derivative of sin²x
items.content: d/dx(sin²x)=2sin x cos x.

items.title: Derivative of cos²x
items.content: d/dx(cos²x)=−2sin x cos x.

items.title: Derivative of sec²x
items.content: d/dx(sec²x)=2sec²x tan x.

items.title: Derivative of cosec²x
items.content: d/dx(cosec²x)=−2cosec²x cot x.

items.title: Tangent and Derivative
items.content: At a point where the derivative exists, the tangent slope equals the derivative value at that point.

items.title: Indeterminate 0/0 Form
items.content: The form 0/0 obtained during direct substitution does not itself determine a limit and requires further simplification.

items.title: Limit and Function Value
items.content: The existence of lim(x→a)f(x) does not require f(a) to equal the limit.

items.title: Derivative of a Constant Multiple of x
items.content: For constant c, d/dx(cx)=c.

items.title: Derivative of Linear Function
items.content: If f(x)=ax+b, then f'(x)=a.

items.title: Constant Function Slope
items.content: The derivative of a constant function is zero, so its graph has zero slope.

items.title: Derivative of Sum of Many Functions
items.content: The derivative of a finite sum is the sum of the derivatives.

items.title: Checking Differentiability at a Point
items.content: Use the derivative definition or compare the relevant one-sided derivatives when appropriate.

items.title: Statistics
items.content: Statistics is the study of collection, presentation, analysis and interpretation of data.

items.title: Data
items.content: Data are observations or measurements collected for a purpose.

items.title: Raw Data
items.content: Raw data are observations in their original unorganized form.

items.title: Grouped Data
items.content: Grouped data are observations arranged into classes or intervals with corresponding frequencies.

items.title: Frequency
items.content: Frequency is the number of observations falling into a particular value or class.

items.title: Class Interval
items.content: A class interval is a range of values used to group observations.

items.title: Class Limits
items.content: The smallest and largest values that can belong to a class are called its lower and upper class limits.

items.title: Class Boundaries
items.content: Class boundaries are the actual boundaries separating continuous class intervals.

items.title: Class Mark
items.content: The class mark is the midpoint of a class interval.

items.title: Class Mark Formula
items.content: Class mark = (Lower class limit + Upper class limit)/2.

items.title: Range
items.content: Range is the difference between the largest and smallest observations.

items.title: Range Formula
items.content: Range = Maximum value − Minimum value.

items.title: Measure of Dispersion
items.content: A measure of dispersion describes how far observations are spread around a central value.

items.title: Mean
items.content: The arithmetic mean is the sum of all observations divided by the number of observations.

items.title: Arithmetic Mean for Ungrouped Data
items.content: x̄ = Σx/n.

items.title: Mean for Discrete Frequency Distribution
items.content: x̄ = Σfx/Σf.

items.title: Mean for Continuous Frequency Distribution
items.content: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ, where xᵢ is the class mark.

items.title: Assumed Mean Method
items.content: x̄ = a + Σfd/Σf, where d=x−a.

items.title: Step-deviation Mean Method
items.content: x̄ = a + h(Σfu/Σf), where u=(x−a)/h.

items.title: Median
items.content: Median is the middle value of an ordered data set.

items.title: Median for Odd Number of Observations
items.content: For n odd, median is the ((n+1)/2)th observation after arranging the data.

items.title: Median for Even Number of Observations
items.content: For n even, median is the average of the (n/2)th and (n/2+1)th observations.

items.title: Mode
items.content: Mode is the observation that occurs most frequently in a data set.

items.title: Quartile
items.content: Quartiles divide ordered data into four equal parts.

items.title: Lower Quartile
items.content: The lower quartile Q₁ is the value below which approximately one-fourth of the observations lie.

items.title: Upper Quartile
items.content: The upper quartile Q₃ is the value below which approximately three-fourths of the observations lie.

items.title: Interquartile Range
items.content: IQR = Q₃ − Q₁.

items.title: Quartile Deviation
items.content: Quartile deviation is half the interquartile range.

items.title: Quartile Deviation Formula
items.content: QD = (Q₃−Q₁)/2.

items.title: Coefficient of Quartile Deviation
items.content: Coefficient of QD = (Q₃−Q₁)/(Q₃+Q₁).

items.title: Mean Deviation
items.content: Mean deviation is the arithmetic mean of the absolute deviations of observations from a chosen central value.

items.title: Mean Deviation from Mean
items.content: MD about x̄ = Σ|x−x̄|/n.

items.title: Mean Deviation from Median
items.content: MD about M = Σ|x−M|/n.

items.title: Mean Deviation for Frequency Data
items.content: MD = Σf|x−A|/Σf, where A is the chosen central value.

items.title: Variance
items.content: Variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the arithmetic mean.

items.title: Variance for Ungrouped Data
items.content: σ² = Σ(x−x̄)²/n.

items.title: Variance Frequency Distribution
items.content: σ² = Σf(x−x̄)²/Σf.

items.title: Standard Deviation Frequency Distribution
items.content: σ = √[Σf(x−x̄)²/Σf].

items.title: Variance Shortcut Formula
items.content: σ² = Σx²/n − x̄².

items.title: Frequency Variance Shortcut
items.content: σ² = Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

items.title: Assumed Mean Standard Deviation
items.content: σ = √[Σfd²/Σf − (Σfd/Σf)²].

items.title: Step-deviation Standard Deviation
items.content: σ = h√[Σfu²/Σf − (Σfu/Σf)²].

items.title: Coefficient of Variation
items.content: Coefficient of variation is the standard deviation expressed as a percentage of the mean.

items.title: Interpretation of Coefficient of Variation
items.content: A smaller coefficient of variation indicates less relative dispersion around the mean.

items.title: Effect of Change of Origin on Variance
items.content: Adding or subtracting a constant from every observation does not change the variance.

items.title: Effect of Change of Scale on Variance
items.content: Multiplying every observation by a constant k multiplies the variance by k².

items.title: Effect of Change of Scale on Standard Deviation
items.content: If every observation is multiplied by k, the standard deviation becomes |k|σ.

items.title: Effect of Change of Origin on Standard Deviation
items.content: Adding or subtracting a constant from every observation does not change the standard deviation.

items.title: Combined Mean of Two Groups
items.content: For groups of sizes n₁,n₂ and means x̄₁,x̄₂, combined mean = (n₁x̄₁+n₂x̄₂)/(n₁+n₂).

items.title: Combined Mean of Multiple Groups
items.content: Combined mean = Σnᵢx̄ᵢ/Σnᵢ.

items.title: Weighted Mean
items.content: Weighted mean = Σwx/Σw.

items.title: Frequency Distribution
items.content: A frequency distribution shows the values or classes of a variable together with their frequencies.

items.title: Discrete Frequency Distribution
items.content: A discrete frequency distribution lists distinct values of a variable with their corresponding frequencies.

items.title: Continuous Frequency Distribution
items.content: A continuous frequency distribution groups observations into continuous class intervals.

items.title: Inclusive Class Interval
items.content: An inclusive class interval includes both its lower and upper class limits.

items.title: Exclusive Class Interval
items.content: An exclusive class interval includes its lower boundary but excludes its upper boundary.

items.title: Converting Inclusive Classes to Continuous Form
items.content: For equal gap between consecutive classes, adjust class boundaries by half the gap on either side of the limits.

items.title: Finding Mean from Frequency Table
items.content: Find each class mark x, multiply it by frequency f, calculate Σfx and divide by Σf.

items.title: Finding Standard Deviation from Frequency Table
items.content: Calculate deviations from the mean or assumed mean, square them, weight by frequency and apply the standard deviation formula.

items.title: Finding Median of Ungrouped Data
items.content: Arrange observations in ascending or descending order and locate the middle observation(s).

items.title: Finding Mode of Ungrouped Data
items.content: Count frequencies and identify the observation with the highest frequency.

items.title: Finding Range
items.content: Subtract the smallest observation from the largest observation.

items.title: Central Tendency
items.content: Mean, median and mode are common measures of central tendency that describe a typical or central value.

items.title: Dispersion
items.content: Range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation describe different aspects of spread in data.

items.title: Standard Deviation is Non-negative
items.content: Standard deviation is always greater than or equal to zero.

items.title: Variance is Non-negative
items.content: Variance is always greater than or equal to zero.

items.title: Zero Standard Deviation
items.content: Standard deviation is zero only when all observations are identical.

items.title: Zero Variance
items.content: Variance is zero only when every observation has the same value.

items.title: Mean Using Deviations
items.content: If d=x−a, then x̄=a+Σfd/Σf.

items.title: Class Mark for Continuous Interval
items.content: For a continuous class interval with boundaries L and U, class mark = (L+U)/2.

items.title: Absolute Deviation
items.content: Absolute deviation |x−A| measures the non-negative distance of an observation x from a reference value A.

items.title: Why Squares Are Used in Variance
items.content: Squaring deviations removes their signs so positive and negative deviations do not cancel.

items.title: Mean Deviation Uses Absolute Values
items.content: Absolute deviations are used so deviations from the chosen central value do not cancel each other.

items.title: Notation for Mean
items.content: The arithmetic mean is commonly denoted by x̄.

items.title: Notation for Standard Deviation
items.content: Population-style standard deviation is commonly denoted by σ in school-level statistics.

items.title: Notation for Variance
items.content: Variance is commonly denoted by σ².

items.title: Relation Between Variance and Standard Deviation
items.content: Standard deviation is the positive square root of variance: σ=√σ².

items.title: Choosing a Dispersion Measure
items.content: Use range for a quick spread measure, quartile deviation for central spread, mean deviation for average absolute spread and standard deviation for squared-deviation-based spread.

items.title: Units of Variance
items.content: Variance is expressed in squared units of the original variable, while standard deviation has the same units as the variable.

items.title: Units of Mean Deviation
items.content: Mean deviation has the same units as the original observations.

items.title: Units of Range
items.content: Range has the same units as the original observations.

items.title: Coefficient of Range
items.content: Coefficient of range = (Maximum−Minimum)/(Maximum+Minimum).

items.title: Coefficient of Mean Deviation
items.content: Coefficient of mean deviation = MD/A, where A is the chosen central value.

items.title: Comparing Consistency Using CV
items.content: Calculate CV for each data set and compare the relative dispersion values; the smaller CV represents lower relative variability.

items.title: Outlier Sensitivity of Range
items.content: Range depends only on the minimum and maximum values, so an extreme observation can change it substantially.

items.title: Median and Extreme Values
items.content: Median is generally less affected by extreme observations than the arithmetic mean.

items.title: Mean and Extreme Values
items.content: The arithmetic mean can be affected by unusually large or small observations.

items.title: Frequency Sum
items.content: For a frequency distribution, total frequency N=Σf.

items.title: Mean in Terms of Total Frequency
items.content: x̄=Σfx/N, where N=Σf.

items.title: Range for Constant Data
items.content: If all observations are equal, the range is zero.

items.title: Mean of Constant Data
items.content: If all observations are equal to c, their mean is c.

items.title: Median of Constant Data
items.content: If all observations are equal to c, their median is c.

items.title: Mode of Constant Data
items.content: If all observations are equal to c, c is the mode.

items.title: Statistics Quick Workflow
items.content: Organize the data, identify the required measure, select the appropriate formula, substitute values carefully and interpret the result with its units.

items.title: Statistical Measure Selection
items.content: Mean, median and mode summarize central tendency; range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation summarize dispersion.

items.title: Random Experiment
items.content: An experiment whose outcome cannot be predicted with certainty in advance is called a random experiment.

items.title: Outcome
items.content: An outcome is a possible result of a random experiment.

items.title: Sample Space
items.content: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.

items.title: Sample Space Notation
items.content: The sample space is commonly denoted by S.

items.title: Event
items.content: An event is a subset of the sample space.

items.title: Elementary Event
items.content: An elementary event contains exactly one outcome.

items.title: Compound Event
items.content: A compound event contains more than one outcome.

items.title: Sure Event
items.content: The event containing all outcomes of the sample space is called the sure event.

items.title: Impossible Event
items.content: An event containing no outcome is called the impossible event.

items.title: Empty Event
items.content: The impossible event is represented by the empty set ∅.

items.title: Complementary Event
items.content: The complement of event A consists of all outcomes in S that are not in A.

items.title: Complement Notation
items.content: The complement of A may be written as A′ or Aᶜ.

items.title: Mutually Exclusive Events
items.content: Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur together.

items.title: Exhaustive Events
items.content: A collection of events is exhaustive if their union contains the entire sample space.

items.title: Equally Likely Outcomes
items.content: Outcomes are equally likely when each outcome has the same chance of occurring.

items.title: Classical Probability
items.content: When outcomes are equally likely, probability is based on the ratio of favourable outcomes to total outcomes.

items.title: Probability of an Event
items.content: P(A)=n(A)/n(S), when the outcomes are finite and equally likely.

items.title: Probability Range
items.content: For every event A, 0≤P(A)≤1.

items.title: Probability of Complement from Favourable Outcomes
items.content: P(A′)=[n(S)−n(A)]/n(S), for finite equally likely outcomes.

items.title: Addition Rule for Two Events
items.content: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).

items.title: Addition Rule for Mutually Exclusive Events
items.content: If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).

items.title: Intersection of Mutually Exclusive Events
items.content: If A and B are mutually exclusive, A∩B=∅ and therefore P(A∩B)=0.

items.title: Probability of Either Event
items.content: P(A or B)=P(A∪B).

items.title: Probability of Both Events
items.content: P(A and B)=P(A∩B).

items.title: Three Event Union
items.content: P(A∪B∪C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)−P(A∩B)−P(B∩C)−P(C∩A)+P(A∩B∩C).

items.title: Event as a Set
items.content: An event is represented as a subset of the sample space, so set operations can be used to combine events.

items.title: Union of Events
items.content: A∪B contains outcomes belonging to A, to B, or to both.

items.title: Intersection of Events
items.content: A∩B contains outcomes common to both A and B.

items.title: Complement of an Event
items.content: A′ contains outcomes in the sample space that do not belong to A.

items.title: Complement Union
items.content: A∪A′=S.

items.title: Probability of Union via Intersection
items.content: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).

items.title: Probability of Mutually Exclusive Union
items.content: For mutually exclusive A and B, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).

items.title: Probability of an Event Equal to One
items.content: P(A)=1 only when A is a sure event up to outcomes of zero probability in the given model; for finite equally likely sample spaces, A=S.

items.title: Probability of an Event Equal to Zero
items.content: P(A)=0 for an impossible event; in a finite equally likely sample space this means A=∅.

items.title: Favourable Outcomes
items.content: Favourable outcomes are the outcomes that belong to the event whose probability is being calculated.

items.title: Finding Probability by Counting
items.content: List the sample space, count total outcomes, identify favourable outcomes and divide favourable count by total count when outcomes are equally likely.

items.title: Probability Using Complement
items.content: When the complement is easier to count, calculate P(A′) first and use P(A)=1−P(A′).

items.title: Probability of Union
items.content: Add the individual probabilities and subtract the probability of their intersection to avoid double counting.

items.title: Double Counting in Union
items.content: When A and B overlap, outcomes in A∩B are counted twice by P(A)+P(B), so the intersection must be subtracted once.

items.title: Random Variable
items.content: A random variable assigns numerical values to outcomes of a random experiment.

items.title: Discrete Random Variable
items.content: A discrete random variable takes values that can be listed or counted.

items.title: Coin Toss Sample Space
items.content: For one toss of a fair coin, S={H,T}.

items.title: Two Coin Tosses Sample Space
items.content: For two coin tosses, S={HH,HT,TH,TT}.

items.title: Three Coin Tosses Number of Outcomes
items.content: Three independent two-outcome trials have 2³=8 possible ordered outcomes.

items.title: Number of Outcomes for n Binary Trials
items.content: For n independent trials with two possible outcomes each, total ordered outcomes=2ⁿ.

items.title: Die Sample Space
items.content: For one standard die, S={1,2,3,4,5,6}.

items.title: Probability of an Even Number on a Fair Die
items.content: For a fair die, P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2.

items.title: Probability of an Odd Number on a Fair Die
items.content: For a fair die, P(odd) = 3/6 = 1/2.

items.title: Probability of a Prime Number on a Fair Die
items.content: For a fair die, prime outcomes are 2,3,5, so P(prime)=3/6=1/2.

items.title: Two Dice Total Outcomes
items.content: When two standard dice are rolled, there are 6×6=36 ordered outcomes.

items.title: Probability of Sum 7 with Two Fair Dice
items.content: There are 6 ordered outcomes with sum 7, so P(sum 7)=6/36=1/6.

items.title: Deck of Cards Basic Count
items.content: A standard deck contains 52 cards, with 4 suits and 13 cards in each suit.

items.title: Probability of a Red Card
items.content: In a standard 52-card deck, 26 cards are red, so P(red)=26/52=1/2.

items.title: Probability of a Black Card
items.content: In a standard 52-card deck, 26 cards are black, so P(black)=26/52=1/2.

items.title: Probability of an Ace
items.content: A standard deck has 4 aces, so P(ace)=4/52=1/13.

items.title: Probability of a Face Card
items.content: A standard deck has 12 face cards, so P(face card)=12/52=3/13.

items.title: Probability of a King
items.content: A standard deck has 4 kings, so P(king)=4/52=1/13.

items.title: Probability of a Queen
items.content: A standard deck has 4 queens, so P(queen)=4/52=1/13.

items.title: Probability of a Jack
items.content: A standard deck has 4 jacks, so P(jack)=4/52=1/13.

items.title: Independent Trials in Elementary Probability
items.content: Repeated trials are often modeled independently when the outcome of one trial does not affect the probabilities of later trials.

items.title: With Replacement
items.content: When an object is replaced before another draw, the composition of the population remains unchanged for the next draw.

items.title: Without Replacement
items.content: When an object is not replaced, the composition of the population changes after each draw.

items.title: Equally Likely Does Not Mean Equally Common
items.content: Equally likely refers to equal probability for elementary outcomes, not necessarily equal frequency in a small observed sample.

items.title: Probability of Complement and Event Sum
Union with Entire Sample Space
items.content: A∪S=S, so P(A∪S)=1.

items.title: Intersection with Entire Sample Space
items.content: A∩S=A, so P(A∩S)=P(A).

items.title: Union with Empty Event
items.content: A∪∅=A, so P(A∪∅)=P(A).

items.title: Probability Monotonicity
items.content: If A is a subset of B, then P(A)≤P(B).

items.title: Probability of Disjoint Union
items.content: For pairwise mutually exclusive events A₁,A₂,...,Aₙ, P(A₁∪...∪Aₙ)=P(A₁)+...+P(Aₙ).

items.title: Pairwise Mutually Exclusive Events
items.content: Events are pairwise mutually exclusive when every pair of distinct events has empty intersection.

items.title: Checking Mutual Exclusivity
items.content: Check whether the events can occur together; if their intersection is empty, they are mutually exclusive.

items.title: Checking Exhaustiveness
items.content: Take the union of the events and check whether it equals the complete sample space.

items.title: Probability as a Number
items.content: Probability is a numerical measure between 0 and 1 that quantifies the chance of an event in the chosen probability model.

items.title: Experimental Probability
items.content: Experimental probability is estimated from observed frequencies over repeated trials and may differ from theoretical probability in a finite experiment.

items.title: Experimental Probability
items.content: Experimental probability of A = Number of times A occurs / Total number of trials.

items.title: Theoretical Probability
items.content: Theoretical probability is obtained from the structure of the probability model, especially by counting equally likely outcomes when applicable.

items.title: Probability of a Single Elementary Outcome
items.content: If a finite sample space has n equally likely elementary outcomes, each elementary outcome has probability 1/n.

items.title: Favourable Count from Probability
items.content: For equally likely finite outcomes, n(A)=P(A)n(S).

items.title: Complement Favourable Count
items.content: For equally likely finite outcomes, n(A′)=n(S)−n(A).

items.title: Sample Space Must Be Defined Carefully
items.content: A probability calculation is meaningful only after the possible outcomes and their probability model have been specified.

items.title: Writing a Sample Space
items.content: Identify the experiment, list every possible outcome without omission or duplication, then verify that the list represents the complete experiment.

items.title: Using Set Operations in Probability
items.content: Translate words such as either, both and not into union, intersection and complement before applying probability rules.

items.title: Either A or B
items.content: In probability notation, either A or B corresponds to A∪B and includes outcomes where both occur unless the events are mutually exclusive.

items.title: Both A and B
items.content: In probability notation, both A and B corresponds to A∩B.

items.title: Not A
items.content: Not A corresponds to the complement A′.

items.title: Overlapping Events
items.content: Events are overlapping when they have at least one common outcome, so their intersection is non-empty.

items.title: Probability Model
items.content: A probability model consists of a sample space together with probabilities assigned to its outcomes or events.

items.title: Total Probability of Finite Equally Likely Sample Space
items.content: If all n elementary outcomes are equally likely, the sum of their probabilities is n×(1/n)=1.

items.title: Sanity Check for Probability
items.content: After calculating a probability, verify that the result lies between 0 and 1.

items.title: Percentage Probability
items.content: A probability p can be expressed as 100p percent.

items.title: Percentage Form of Probability
items.content: Probability percentage = P(A)×100%.

items.title: Probability of Complement from Percentage
items.content: If P(A)=p, then P(A′)=1−p, or (100−100p)% in percentage form.

items.title: Probability and Certainty
items.content: Probability 0 represents impossibility in the model, while probability 1 represents certainty in the model.

items.title: Common Probability Language
items.content: Impossible corresponds to probability 0, certain to probability 1, and values between 0 and 1 represent varying degrees of likelihood.

items.title: Probability Exam Checklist
items.content: Define the sample space, identify the event, check whether outcomes are equally likely, choose the appropriate rule and simplify the final probability.
